docs.title: NØMAÐ
docs.text:
NØde Monitoring And Ðiagnostics — Lightweight HPC monitoring, visualization, and predictive analytics.

"Travels light, adapts to its environment, and doesn't need permanent infrastructure."

docs.title: What is NØMAÐ?
docs.text:
NØMAÐ is a self-contained monitoring and prediction system for HPC clusters. Unlike heavyweight solutions requiring complex infrastructure, NØMAÐ deploys quickly, runs with minimal resources, and provides actionable insights through:

  • Real-time monitoring of disk, CPU, memory, GPU, and SLURM jobs
  • Predictive analytics using machine learning and similarity networks
  • Educational analytics tracking computational proficiency development
  • Multi-cluster dashboards with partition-level views
  • Derivative analysis detecting accelerating trends before thresholds

docs.title: Philosophy
docs.text:
Inspired by nomadic principles:

Principle Implementation Travels light SQLite database, minimal dependencies, no external services Adapts to environment Configurable collectors, flexible alerts, cluster-agnostic Leaves no trace Clean uninstall, no system modifications required

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
pip install nomad-hpc
nomad demo                    # Try with synthetic data
nomad dashboard               # Open http://localhost:8050

For production deployment, see Installation.

docs.text:
• filesystems - disk usage snapshots
  • iostat_cpu - system %iowait
  • iostat_device - per-device I/O stats
  • mpstat_core - per-core CPU stats
  • mpstat_summary - CPU imbalance metrics
  • vmstat - memory pressure, swap
  • node_state - SLURM node allocation
  • gpu_stats - NVIDIA GPU metrics
  • nfs_stats - NFS I/O metrics

docs.title: CLI Commands
docs.text:
# Core commands
nomad status              # Full system overview
nomad syscheck            # Verify requirements
nomad collect --once      # Single collection cycle
nomad collect -i 60       # Continuous (every 60s)
nomad monitor -i 30       # Job I/O monitor (every 30s)

# Analysis
nomad disk /home          # Filesystem trends
nomad jobs --user X       # Job history
nomad similarity          # Similarity analysis
nomad alerts              # View alerts

# Bash helpers (source scripts/nomad.sh)
nstatus    nwatch    ndisk    njobs    nsimilarity
nalerts    ncollect  nmonitor nsyscheck nlog

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# 1. Initialize database
sqlite3 /var/lib/nomad/nomad.db < nomad/db/schema.sql

# 2. Verify system
nomad syscheck

# 3. Test collection
nomad collect --once

# 4. Start continuous collection
nohup nomad collect -i 60 > /tmp/nomad-collect.log 2>&1 &
nohup nomad monitor -i 30 > /tmp/nomad-monitor.log 2>&1 &

# 5. Check status
nomad status

docs.title: Contributing to NØMAÐ
docs.text: Thank you for your interest in contributing to NØMAÐ! This document provides guidelines and information for contributors.

docs.title: Code of Conduct
docs.text: By participating in this project, you agree to maintain a respectful and inclusive environment. We welcome contributors of all backgrounds and experience levels.

docs.title: Reporting Issues
docs.text:
• Bug reports: Use the GitHub issue tracker with the "bug" label
  • Feature requests: Use the "enhancement" label
  • Questions: Use the "question" label or start a discussion

When reporting a bug, please include: - NØMAÐ version - Python version - Operating system - SLURM version (if relevant) - Steps to reproduce - Expected vs actual behavior - Error messages and logs

docs.title: Contributing Code
docs.text:
1. Fork the repository
  2. Create a branch for your feature (git checkout -b feature/amazing-feature)
  3. Make your changes following our coding standards
  4. Add tests for new functionality
  5. Run the test suite (pytest)
  6. Commit with a clear message
  7. Push to your branch
  8. Open a Pull Request

docs.title: Pull Request Guidelines
docs.text:
• Keep PRs focused on a single feature or fix
  • Update documentation if needed
  • Add tests for new code
  • Ensure all tests pass
  • Follow the existing code style
  • Write a clear PR description explaining your changes

docs.title: Development Setup
docs.text:
# Clone your fork
git clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/nomad.git
cd nomad

# Create virtual environment
python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate

# Install in development mode with dev dependencies
pip install -e ".[dev]"

# Install pre-commit hooks
pre-commit install

docs.title: Python Style
docs.text:
• Follow PEP 8
  • Use type hints for function signatures
  • Maximum line length: 100 characters
  • Use ruff for linting: ruff check .
  • Use black for formatting: black .

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• Use docstrings for all public functions and classes
  • Follow Google docstring format
  • Update README.md for user-facing changes
  • Update docs/ for detailed documentation

docs.title: Example Function
docs.text:
def calculate_health_score(
    metrics: dict[str, float],
    weights: dict[str, float] | None = None,
) -> float:
    """
    Calculate job health score from metrics.

    Args:
        metrics: Dictionary of metric name to value.
            Expected keys: cpu_percent, mem_gb, nfs_write_gb, etc.
        weights: Optional custom weights for each metric.
            Defaults to empirically derived weights.

    Returns:
        Health score between 0.0 (catastrophic) and 1.0 (perfect).

    Raises:
        ValueError: If required metrics are missing.

    Example:
        >>> metrics = {'cpu_percent': 85, 'nfs_write_gb': 50}
        >>> score = calculate_health_score(metrics)
        >>> print(f"Health: {score:.2f}")
        Health: 0.72
    """
    ...

docs.title: Commit Messages
docs.text:
Follow the conventional commits format:

type(scope): brief description

Longer description if needed.

Fixes #123

Types: - feat: New feature - fix: Bug fix - docs: Documentation only - style: Formatting, no code change - refactor: Code restructuring - test: Adding tests - chore: Maintenance tasks

docs.title: Running Tests
docs.text:
# Run all tests
pytest

# Run with coverage
pytest --cov=nomad --cov-report=html

# Run specific test file
pytest tests/test_collectors.py

# Run specific test
pytest tests/test_collectors.py::test_disk_collector

docs.title: Writing Tests
docs.text:
• Place tests in tests/ directory
  • Mirror the source structure (e.g., tests/test_collectors/test_disk.py)
  • Use pytest fixtures for common setup
  • Mock external dependencies (SLURM commands, filesystem, etc.)

Example test:

import pytest
from unittest.mock import patch, MagicMock
from nomad.collectors.disk import DiskCollector

@pytest.fixture
def disk_collector():
    """Create a DiskCollector with test configuration."""
    config = {
        'filesystems': ['/home', '/scratch'],
        'quota_enabled': False,
    }
    return DiskCollector(config)

def test_parse_df_output(disk_collector):
    """Test parsing of df command output."""
    df_output = """Filesystem     1K-blocks      Used Available Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda1      102400000  51200000  51200000  50% /home"""

    result = disk_collector._parse_df_output(df_output)

    assert len(result) == 1
    assert result[0]['path'] == '/home'
    assert result[0]['used_percent'] == 50.0

@patch('subprocess.run')
def test_collect_filesystem_usage(mock_run, disk_collector):
    """Test filesystem usage collection."""
    mock_run.return_value = MagicMock(
        returncode=0,
        stdout="...",  # df output
    )

    result = disk_collector.collect()

    assert result is not None
    mock_run.assert_called_once()

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
An action is one nomad command that the Console (or nomad actions run on the hub) may start, on the hub or on a site. Actions come from a fixed catalog: each has its own command words and parameters, which are checked before anything runs. Nothing reaches a shell, and nothing outside the catalog can be asked for.

nomad actions list                              # the catalog
nomad actions run collectors --site c1          # on a site, through its agent
nomad actions run collectors                    # on the hub (every site's, from combined.db)
nomad actions run usage.report -p from=2025-10-01 -p to=2026-10-07 -p cluster=c1
nomad actions run syscheck --here               # on this host, as a site runs it

docs.title: The catalog
docs.text:
For now they only read: none changes settings or collected data. Actions that change something will come as a dry run followed by an apply, the way --apply works on the command line.

Action Runs on What it is version hub, sites nomad version config.check hub, sites nomad config check collectors hub, sites nomad collectors (days) syscheck sites nomad syscheck status hub, sites nomad status alerts hub, sites nomad alerts --unresolved (severity) per_user hub, sites nomad per-user --mask (days) insights.brief hub nomad insights brief (site, hours) console.roles hub nomad console roles --mask (netid) lab.show hub nomad lab show (lab) storage.use hub, sites nomad storage use (server, path, over, top, days) sync.status hub nomad sync status usage.report hub nomad usage-report (from, to, cluster, min_cell)

How parameters are checked: - Numbers must fall within their bounds. - Dates must be real dates; a period can be at most five years and can't end after tomorrow. - Names use letters, digits, ., _ and - (plus $ for a lab), and can't start with a dash. - Paths are absolute (/home), of letters, digits and . _ / + @ , : = - only. - Sizes are written as --over takes them: 500G, 1T, 2TB. - Sites must be among the hub's sites. - Unknown parameters are refused, not ignored.

On the hub, actions that read data read the combined database. The usage report writes into ~/.local/share/nomad/reports/ (readable only by its owner). The Console offers those files by name and nothing outside that directory.

alerts, per_user, lab.show and storage.use can name people or groups, as the commands do. The catalog marks them (names) so the Console shows them to administrators only.

docs.title: How the hub reaches a site
docs.text:
The hub uses a key of its own, not the key nomad sync uses. A site lets that key run one program only, nomad agent:

restrict,command="cd / && exec /usr/bin/env -u PYTHONHOME -u PYTHONPATH /path/to/python -m nomad.cli agent" ssh-ed25519 AAAA... nomad-actions@hub
  • command=: whatever the connection asks for, sshd runs the agent. The agent reads one request (JSON, at most 64 KB), checks it against the site's own catalog, runs it, and answers. The site never relies on the hub's checking.
  • restrict: no terminal and no port, agent or X11 forwarding.

The result is that whoever holds the hub's key, the hub included, can ask a site for catalog actions and nothing else. If the hub is compromised, the sites are exposed only to those actions.

A site whose host is localhost (collectors on the hub itself) needs no key: its actions run on the hub directly, as the account the Console or nomad actions runs as.

On the hub's side, the ssh command: - offers this key first and never reuses a shared connection (a master opened with a stronger key would otherwise carry the request); - refuses unknown host keys; - asks for no terminal.

Each answer says whether sshd ran the agent as the key's forced command. If it didn't, the hub doesn't use the answer and says why. That happens when the key was added by hand without command=, or when ssh fell back to another of the hub's keys named in ~/.ssh/config because the site doesn't have this one. [actions] allow_unrestricted = true in the hub's nomad.toml accepts such answers, which is not advised.

The hub treats a site's answer as data: - Size: it reads at most 16 MB and stops the connection beyond that. - Fields: it keeps only the known fields, with their expected types and sizes. - Files: it never takes a list of files from a site.

On the site: - One action at a time. One more request may wait up to 30 seconds; any others are refused at once. - Silent connections close. A connection that sends no request within 10 seconds is closed. - Every request is logged, refused ones too, one JSON line each in ~/.local/share/nomad/agent.log (readable only by its owner): time, source address, action, parameters, exit status. - The interpreter runs from /. cd / keeps a stray module in the home directory from being imported.

docs.title: Setting it up
docs.text:
On the hub, as the account that runs the Console and nomad sync:

nomad actions key

It makes the key the first time (~/.config/nomad/agent/id_ed25519, or [actions] agent_key in nomad.toml) and prints the line to run on each site.

On each site, as the account nomad runs as there:

nomad agent install-key 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA... nomad-actions@hub'           # what would change
nomad agent install-key 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA... nomad-actions@hub' --apply
  • It adds the line above to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, with a backup.
  • It uses the site's own Python, so the agent is the same nomad its collectors run.
  • An existing line holding the same key is replaced.
  • --from 10.0.0.5 also limits where the key may connect from.

Then, from the hub:

nomad actions run version --site SITE

The sites are those nomad sync reads (nomad.toml [hub], or sync.toml), and their host keys must already be known, as they are once sync has run.

docs.title: For the Console
docs.text:
from nomad import actions
actions.catalog()                            # every action, with each parameter's kind, bounds and choices
actions.targets()                            # {"hub": True, "sites": ["c1", "c2"]}
actions.run("collectors", {"days": 7}, site="c1", cancel=event, on_output=callback)
actions.report_file(name)                    # a file the usage report wrote, by bare name

run returns: - ok, exit_code, output and errors (each kept up to 1 MB), seconds; - timed_out and cancelled; - files, for an action that writes them; - for a site, also restricted and the site's nomad_version.

It raises ActionError when the request itself is refused.

  • Output is text from the site. Show it as text, never as HTML.
  • on_output streams output as it comes for actions on the hub. A site's output arrives when its action ends.
  • Cancelling stops the hub's side at once. A site may still finish the action on its own, within the action's time limit.
  • One usage report at a time. files lists what changed in the reports directory, so two reports at once would list each other's files.
  • Opening a report file: use actions.open_report_file(name). It refuses a file that was replaced by a link after the check.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text: NØMAÐ supports both threshold-based and predictive alerts.

docs.title: Threshold Alerts
docs.text:
Trigger when metrics exceed configured limits:

[alerts.thresholds.disk]
used_percent_warning = 80
used_percent_critical = 95

[alerts.thresholds.nfs]
retrans_percent_warning = 1.0
avg_rtt_ms_critical = 100

Before 1.7.16 [alerts.thresholds] was not read: every site alerted at the built-in values. The flat keys the example config used to show for disks (disk_warning_percent, disk_critical_percent) are read too.

The disk thresholds also cover the disks of other machines, each alert about that machine rather than the host that read it:

  • node_disk (1.14): a compute node's local disk, read from the head node ([collectors.node_disks]). Since 1.14.3 the message names the three largest owners of the data when the collector counted them in that sweep (it does for a disk that has just filled): who to ask. owners_in_alerts = false keeps the names out.
  • workstation_disk (1.14.2): a workstation's own disks (/, /home on a local drive, /localscratch, a data disk), from the workstation collector's mount readings. Network filesystems, fuse mounts and drives plugged in under /media are left out, and a device mounted at several places (btrfs subvolumes, a bind mount) is one disk. A machine collected as localhost is named as the host that collects it.

docs.title: Disk fill forecasts
docs.text:
Each disk reading fits the readings of the last forecast_window_hours ([collectors.disk], default 6) with a straight line. When the filesystem is filling, the reading stores the rate and when it will be full (filesystems.fill_rate_bytes_per_day, days_until_full), and an alert (disk_forecast) says so:

[WARNING] NØMAÐ spydur: Disk /home will be full in about 45 hours (filling 2.0 TB/day over the last 6 hours; 84% used)

[alerts.thresholds.disk]
full_within_hours_warning = 72
full_within_hours_critical = 24
full_within_hours_past_critical = 6   # once past used_percent_critical

[alerts.predictive]
enabled = true          # false: no forecasts

The forecast fits the space taken (size less free space), so a dataset on a shared pool is forecast as the pool fills. It needs four readings over at least an hour and growth of at least 0.1% of the filesystem over the window; readings of another filesystem (the path unmounted, df reading the one beneath: a different size and usage) are left out, and a disk already full gets the threshold alert instead. Past its critical threshold a disk has that alert, reminded of daily; a forecast is added only when the rest will be gone within full_within_hours_past_critical (6) hours. days_until_full_* under [alerts.predictive] and disk_fill_days_warning, which older configs carry for a forecast that never ran, are not read.

docs.title: Collection stopped (the hub, 1.14.5)
docs.text:
A site can keep syncing a database nothing writes to any more, and then the sync alert never fires while the pages show old or partial data. After each sync the hub reads the merged database and raises, with source collection (host = the site):

  • collection: nothing at all collected at the site for alert_after_minutes (120): nomad's cron or service there stopped.
  • collector NAME: a collector that runs regularly has not run, has failed every run, or -- one that nearly always collects something -- has collected nothing, for three of its usual intervals and at least alert_after_minutes. A failing one quotes its last message, with folders under /home, /scratch and the like, user@host, ~user, user=... and the usernames the hub knows taken out.
  • a GPU node: no GPU samples from it while the site's other GPU nodes report, for alert_after_minutes or three of the gpu collector's usual intervals there; all of them quiet is one alert for the site (or none, when the gpu collector's own alert says why).
  • DCGM on a GPU node: no DCGM samples from it for gpu_fallback_hours (24) while nvidia-smi still answers. GPU utilization in scores comes only from DCGM, so its jobs say "not measured" until DCGM (nv-hostengine) is back. Critical after a week. A node that never had DCGM is not this. The gpu collector now asks each node whether DCGM answers (and again every hour); it used to ask the first node and use that answer for all.

A warning, critical after a day; sent once, again when worse, then every reminder_hours, and forgotten when it recovers (kept in collection_alerts.json beside the hub's cached copies).

What is not raised:

  • A site is judged as of the hub's last live pull from it, so a site whose pull failed (the sync alert says so), or a combined database the hub held back, is not taken for one that stopped.
  • A collector is watched once it has run six times over more than a day in the last 30 days; its usual interval comes from its latest runs (runs under a minute apart count as one), and the longest gap of its last week counts too, so a collector moved to a longer schedule or tried by hand isn't "stopped". One that has not worked once in 30 days isn't a stop (nomad collectors says why). One disabled in the site's own settings (the copy the hub keeps) isn't watched.
  • A GPU node is watched once it has sent samples over more than a day. Collectors and nodes silent for more than 30 days are taken as retired.

Also (1.17.3):

  • runaway jobs: jobs Slurm's controller no longer lists (squeue -a) but its accounting still has running or waiting, for over a day. They count as running or waiting wherever sacct is read, nomad's pages included, and only Slurm's admin can clear them: sacctmgr show runawayjobs lists them and offers to fix them. The site's Slurm collector keeps them in runaway_jobs: each job its sacct pull or a lookup has active that squeue doesn't list, with when it was first and last seen so. When squeue may hide other people's jobs from the collecting account (PrivateData in scontrol show config includes jobs, read once a day, and the account is neither root nor SlurmUser; if that can't be read, when squeue listed no other account's job), a running job squeue doesn't list counts only once it is a day past its start and time limit (60 days with no limit), and a waiting one doesn't; a pending array range, whose id squeue cuts short, never does (a job only just ended is there until sacct catches up). One squeue lists again, that sacct has ended, or that is no longer stored as active goes, at the next run. The idle-condo report leaves the ones that never started out of the jobs that waited. A warning, with the count and the oldest one's submit date, no names.

To leave some out (name or site:name, shell wildcards allowed):

[hub]
alert_after_minutes = 120
gpu_fallback_hours = 24
quiet_collectors = []          # e.g. ["slurm_usage", "lab:workstation"]
quiet_nodes = []               # e.g. ["oldgpu07", "lab:*"]
collection_alerts = true

nomad collection-check lists the same, read-only (--send raises them; run it as the account that runs the sync).

docs.title: Node alerts sent by the hub (1.17.3)
docs.text:
A site's node alerts (a node down, not responding or draining) are raised by that site's own nomad, through the email, Slack or webhook in its nomad.toml. A site that can't send any -- a head node with no way to the mail server, or one set up with nomad init --quick, which writes nothing in [alerts] -- can leave them to the hub:

[[hub.sites]]
name = "cluster-b"
host = "headnode-b"
ssh_user = "monitor"
db_path = "~/.local/share/nomad/cluster-b.db"
alerts = "hub"                 # the hub sends this site's node alerts

After each sync the hub reads that site's latest node reading and raises each unhealthy node as the site's own collector would (critical for DOWN, NOT_RESPONDING, FAIL...; warning for DRAIN...; the hub's own [alerts.node_state] states apply), through the hub's [alerts] backends, with source node_state and the node as host. Sent once, again when worse, then every reminder_hours; a node healthy again is forgotten, so its return is news (kept in node_alerts.json beside the hub's cached copies). Each alert names the site, not the hub, in its subject and in the hub's alert records; two sites' nodes of the same name are separate alerts. A node's reason is sent without the name of whoever set it (Slurm's [user@time]) and with what could name a person masked. [hub] quiet_node_alerts (name, site:name, site:*, shell wildcards) leaves nodes out, a node kept down on purpose say; quiet_nodes is for the collection checks only (a GPU node without DCGM) and doesn't silence a node going down. A site not read for two hours is skipped: the sync and collection alerts say so. A send that failed is tried again when the hub's alert database says its retry is due (after 15 minutes, then longer), not a day later. Leave the site's own [alerts] without backends, or it sends them too.

docs.title: Email
docs.text:
[mail]                       # shared by everything that sends mail
host = "smtp.example.edu"
port = 587
starttls = "required"        # required | if-offered | off
from = "hpc@example.edu"     # a sender your mail server accepts

[alerts.email]
enabled = true
recipients = ["admin@example.edu", "hpc-team@example.edu"]

Alert email goes through [mail]; see nomad.toml.example for its other options (a certificate name, a missing intermediate, a login). Any of [mail]'s keys set in [alerts.email] itself override it, for alerts that must use a different server. nomad test-alerts --email checks the connection.

Each message names its cluster -- the name [clusters] gives, else the host name -- in the subject with the problem itself, so an inbox shared by several sites reads at a glance:

[WARNING] NØMAÐ spydur: Disk /scratch at 85.0% (1.9 TB free; threshold: 80%)

docs.title: Repeats
docs.text:
Each alert is about a condition: its source, its host, what on the host it is about -- the disk path, the NFS mount, the GPU, the node -- and the metric. /home and /scratch on one head node are two conditions. A condition is raised (stored and sent):

  • when it appears,
  • when it gets worse (warning → critical),
  • and once every reminder_hours while it lasts.
[alerts]
reminder_hours = 24
episode_gap_minutes = 60   # not seen this long: it has ended

What has been raised is kept in the alert_state table, so this holds across nomad collect --once runs from cron. A condition not seen for episode_gap_minutes has ended; if it comes back it is raised again (keep the gap longer than the collection interval). A short dip back (critical → warning → critical) raises nothing new; after episode_gap_minutes below its worst, getting worse again is raised. Two metrics of one thing (an NFS mount's latency and its retransmissions) are two conditions. If every backend fails to send, the alert is sent again after 15 minutes, then 30, an hour and so on up to reminder_hours (stored once). If the database cannot be written (nomad's own database on the disk that filled), what was sent is remembered in a small file in the local temporary directory instead, and the readings are checked even though they could not be stored. nomad test-alerts always sends its test.

Before 1.7.16 an alert was "the same" when its source, host and severity matched, whatever the path, with a 15-minute cooldown: a disk at 87% for weeks was stored and sent every 15 minutes, and a second disk's warning waited behind it. cooldown_minutes now applies only where alerts have no database.

nomad alerts lists the conditions active now (seen within the episode gap) before the alerts raised.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• The auth_failures and setuid_new signals (failed sudo/su per account, and a person's setuid/setgid files) can now be read unprivileged, by the probe itself, with no root helper and no cron — retiring the only part of the watch that needed root:
  • watch_auth (on by default): failed sudo/su in the last auth_window_hours (24), counted per account, read straight from the auth log (/var/log/secure or auth_log) wherever the collector's account may read it — e.g. where it's group-readable (installer is in securegrp on spydur). A no-op, with no error, where the log is root-only. The actor is taken from the log's structured fields, matched on the line's head before any COMMAND= so a command string can't inject a fake account, and su to root is counted against whoever ran it.
  • setuid_roots (off until set): the probe scans the directories listed (e.g. ["/localscratch"]) for a person's setuid/setgid files (basename only), staying on each root's own filesystem, following no symlink, bounded. "New" comes from the finding's first-seen — a file that appears alerts once.
  • The kinds, folding, severities and Console labels already existed (1.20), so these just add an unprivileged source. The root helper (scripts/watch_root_probe.py + root_report) still works where root is available instead. No database change.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• The policy watch gains behaviour signals: the tells an AI agent (or a careless script) driving the cluster over the user's own ssh leaves — which look like the user typing to the /proc watch, so the watch reads what was done, not who typed it. All read-only, thresholds in the TOML, info/warning only.
  • heavy (warning): a user process holding real CPU — by lifetime average (its whole CPU time / its age), so a steady computation shows and a brief spike doesn't — of at least heavy_cpu cores (default 2), on a login node only (a compute node is where jobs are meant to be heavy). The long-standing "work running on the head node" catch; no root needed.
  • job_burst (listed, not alerted): at least burst_jobs sbatches by one user within burst_minutes. An array counts as one, so a big array isn't a burst; listed rather than alerted because a parameter sweep bursts the same way.
  • fail_fast (warning): at least fail_fast_jobs of a user's jobs that FAILED within fail_fast_seconds — an agent resubmitting what it doesn't understand (node failures don't count).
  • job_churn (warning): the same job name resubmitted churn_repeats times with cancellations between — a cancel/resubmit loop.
  • Config: watch_heavy, heavy_cpu, heavy_min_seconds, watch_jobs, job_window_hours, burst_jobs, burst_minutes, fail_fast_jobs, fail_fast_seconds, churn_repeats in [collectors.policy_watch] (both watches on by default; each no-ops where there's nothing to see). The job signals read this site's jobs table; heavy adds --heavy to the probe. No database change — new kind values in policy_findings, already synced.
  • Console: the Policy watch page labels the four new kinds and names them in its intro (nomad_fix_73.py). No new route or scoping change.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• The policy watch reaches GPU workstations and keys on the GPU. workstations lists GPU boxes to probe over ssh (role "workstation"); the findings travel the same pipeline to the hub and the Console. With watch_gpu (on by default; nothing where there is no GPU), the probe reads GPU compute processes with nvidia-smi — unprivileged, and never graphics (Xorg, a browser), so a desktop's ordinary GPU use doesn't show:
  • gpu (listed, not alerted): a GPU compute process, with the memory held, whether it is detached (no terminal — the shape of an unattended job) and whether it is an AI agent.
  • gpu_served (warning): a GPU reachable from the network — it listens on a port open to the network, or its account also runs a tunnel/relay/forward. The shape of reselling or an open inference server.
  • gpu_min_mem (256 MiB) drops a trivial compute context; gpu_serve_hosts names boxes where serving a GPU is sanctioned (then listed, not alerted); ignore_programs/ignore_users apply as everywhere.
  • Under-claim by design: detached only annotates, never alerts on its own; per-process GPU attribution is opaque under MIG or in containers, and a GPU another account serves is caught through its account's exposure unless the probe runs as root. See docs/policy_watch.md.
  • Console: the Policy watch page labels the two new kinds (gpu, gpu_served) and names the workstations in its intro. No new route or scoping change.

docs.title: Fixes
docs.text: • Signals place an alert by what it is about, not where it was stored. A hub that raises a site's node alerts on its behalf (alerts = "hub", 1.17.3) stores them in its own rows (source_site = the hub) while naming the site in details.site; the Insight engine attributed them by source_site, so the hub's Signals (e.g. mingus) showed another site's "node down" and that site's own Signals (e.g. vadur) hid it. The alert signal now reads unscoped and places each alert by details.site, falling back to source_site. No database change; the Console picks it up once nomad is upgraded on the hub.

docs.title: Collectors
docs.text: nomad collect (usually nomad collect --once from cron, every 5 minutes) runs the collectors this host's nomad.toml turns on. Each writes its own tables; nomad sync copies every site's tables to the hub.

docs.title: Which run
docs.text:
Each collector is turned on or off in its own table:

[collectors.nfs]
enabled = false
Collector Default Where it belongs Needs Writes disk on every host df filesystems slurm on Slurm head node squeue, sacct queue_state, jobs job_metrics on Slurm head node sacct jobs, job_summary slurm_usage where slurm runs Slurm head node sreport cluster_usage iostat on every host iostat (sysstat) iostat_device, iostat_cpu mpstat on every host mpstat (sysstat) mpstat_summary, mpstat_core vmstat on every host vmstat vmstat node_state on Slurm head node scontrol node_state, partition_settings, partition_changes gpu on hosts with NVIDIA GPUs, or a head node reaching GPU nodes over SSH nvidia-smi (DCGM if present) gpu_stats, gpu_health nfs on hosts that mount NFS (client side) nfsiostat (nfs-utils, in /usr/sbin) nfs_stats groups on every site getent; sacct for job accounting group_membership, job_accounting interactive off hosts running RStudio or Jupyter — interactive_sessions, interactive_summary, interactive_daily, interactive_env_daily workstation off a hub reaching workstations over SSH ssh workstation_state, workstation_user_snapshot, ... per_user off login nodes, shared interactive hosts Python psutil per_user_sample, per_user_alert, per_user_daily oom off shared hosts without per-user memory limits (login nodes, interactive servers) journalctl, and reading the kernel's messages oom_kills storage off a host reaching ZFS/NFS servers over SSH ssh storage_state storage_use off a site or the hub reading the files nomad-storage.sh writes on storage servers ssh, or the files on this machine storage_owners, storage_paths, storage_tops, storage_folders, ... network_perf off any host; tests paths that start there ping; iperf3 for throughput network_perf cloud.aws off sites with AWS resources Python boto3 cloud_metrics

An enabled = [...] list under [collectors], which older example configs carried, is not read.

groups reads membership with getent group: on the head node of each [clusters] entry (over SSH when it has a host), on the first reachable workstation of a type = "workstations" cluster with an ssh_user, and on this host otherwise. Job accounting needs sacct and is skipped without it. On the same host it looks up each member with getent passwd and records whether they still have an account (has_account): a hand-kept /etc/group goes on listing people whose accounts were deleted long ago. "No account" needs every run for two days to find none (getent says the same for an unreachable directory), and a run where the lookup fails keeps the last known answer. Every run stamps what it saw with one time (collected_at), so a membership no longer listed stops being stamped. first_seen says when a membership was first seen (since 1.11; earlier ones are empty, not known): a course's students this term can be told from earlier terms' in a group nobody prunes. A membership missing from the runs for a week and listed again starts over (a student back for another course); one the collector simply did not run for keeps its date. A lab's members are the people listed in their cluster's latest run (give or take two days, for a failed run; a cluster not collected for 30 days while its site goes on is retired) who have an account; nomad console roles NETID says how many are not counted, and why.

node_state also reads each partition's settings (scontrol --all --oneliner show partition, hidden partitions and ones this account may not use included: limits, default and maximum time, default memory, who may use it, priority tier, preemption) and stores them only when something changes: partition_settings holds each partition as it is now, partition_changes when one appeared, changed (old and new values) or went. nomad partitions shows them; nomad partitions --changes, what changed. A cluster whose scontrol won't show partitions still has its nodes stored.

slurm records, from squeue, the last reason Slurm gave while a job waited (pending_reason: Resources, Priority, QOSMaxJobsPerUserLimit, Dependency...), since when it has waited for the cluster without a break (ready_since: Resources or Priority; cleared by a reading that shows it held by its own limits, and by a requeue) and how many nodes it asked for (req_nodes), from 1.18 on: whether, and from when, a job waited for the cluster rather than for its own limits. The first sync after upgrading sends each site's jobs table whole once (it gained columns).

nomad collect -C disk,nfs (or -C disk -C nfs) runs only those, if enabled. An unknown name is warned about and skipped; if no name is known, nothing runs and the command says so.

docs.title: Is it working?
docs.text:
nomad collectors

On a site, lists every collector: on or off and why, what it needs that this host lacks, and how its runs went over the last 7 days (from collection_log):

  nfs           on   on by default
                     needs: nfsiostat
                     2,016 runs, never any data, last 2026-10-01T07:20
                     nfsiostat not installed (nfs-utils)

On the hub, nomad collectors --db ~/.local/share/nomad/combined.db shows each site's collectors and marks those that run but collect nothing.

A collector that runs but has nothing to collect logs why — nfsiostat not installed, no NFS mounts on this host, no NVIDIA GPU here, psutil not installed: nothing collected, no network_tests configured — in collection_log.error_message of a successful run. Before 1.7.13 these logged "success, 0 records" (or, for groups and per_user, "1 records" whatever they held), which looked like a working collector. A command that isn't installed fails the run at once with the reason, without retrying.

Commands are looked for on the PATH and in /usr/sbin, /sbin, /usr/local/sbin and /usr/local/bin: cron's PATH is only /usr/bin:/bin, and nfs-utils installs nfsiostat in /usr/sbin.

docs.title: Jobs
docs.text:
The slurm collector reads running and pending jobs from squeue and every user's jobs of the last job_history_days (7) from sacct --allusers (without it, sacct run by anyone but root shows only that account's own jobs). squeue is run with -a, so hidden partitions and partitions the collector's account can't submit to are seen too. Jobs are recorded from every partition. partitions limits the queue snapshot (queue_state, pending and running counts per partition) to the partitions listed, and the old dashboard (nomad dashboard) shows those partitions' nodes; empty means all. Before 1.7.43 it limited the jobs too, and the setup wizard lists the partitions sinfo shows, which leaves out hidden ones: jobs in the partitions left out reached jobs only through job_metrics (finished, at least 10 seconds, a few states) and so every count about jobs was short. Partitions that share nodes don't count a job twice: a job runs in one partition, and questions about hardware go by the nodes in its node list. A job submitted to several partitions is stored with the list Slurm shows (a,b) while it waits, again after a requeue, and with the one it runs in once it starts; an ended job reported with its list keeps the partition it ran in. Jobs older than job_history_days from partitions that were left out before 1.7.43 stay as job_metrics recorded them.

A job that ended between two runs leaves squeue; if that run's sacct pull did not report it, it is looked up in sacct by number, and the answer is taken only if its submit time matches (Slurm reuses job numbers after its counter restarts). When sacct cannot account for the job yet, it is marked UNKNOWN: it has ended, its outcome is not known, it has no exit code or failure reason, and no success or failure count includes it. The next sacct pull corrects it. A pending array range (123_[5-10]) that left the queue is dropped, since each of its tasks has a row of its own. Nothing is concluded about any job in a run where squeue did not answer.

Before 1.7.19 such jobs were marked COMPLETED, with an end time in UTC where every other job time is local, so a failed job could count as a success. Those rows (COMPLETED, an end time without a T) are looked up in sacct too, 200 a run, and become UNKNOWN (end time moved to local) if sacct no longer has them.

From sacct (1.7.42) each job also gets account, alloc_tres (what Slurm allocated, e.g. cpu=6,gres/gpu:a40=1,gres/gpu=1,mem=32G,node=1), alloc_gpus (the GPUs in it: gres/gpu and gres/gpu:TYPE, never gres/gpumem or gres/gpuutil), and two parts of its working directory: work_root, the first (/home, /scratch), and work_tail, the last two (proj/run1). The whole path is not kept. squeue doesn't report these; what sacct stored stays.

A job's memory request (req_mem_mb) is its memory per node as sacct records it (1.14.1): what Slurm allocated (the mem= of its AllocTRES, the job's total, divided by its node=), else what was asked (ReqTRES, the same way), else ReqMem (4000Mc, a Slurm before 21.08's mark for per CPU, counts every CPU). squeue's %m, stored while a job waits, is the figure per CPU for a job submitted with --mem-per-cpu, with nothing to say so; until 1.14.1 it was never replaced, so such a job was stored as asking for one CPU's worth and its memory looked used several times over. Now sacct's figure replaces it once sacct reports the job. Stored jobs with an AllocTRES mem= were corrected on upgrading (migration 22); at a site whose AllocTRES has none, nomad import sacct --from DATE --apply reads them again.

A job's GPU count (req_gpus) is what sacct records when it records GPUs (1.14.4), and otherwise what squeue showed while the job waited or ran. Slurm records GPUs only where AccountingStorageTRES lists gres/gpu; before that, sacct gives a GPU job neither a GPU request nor GPUs in its AllocTRES, and nomad's reading of the queue is the only record of its GPUs. Until 1.14.4 the first count stored was never replaced, and the job-metrics collector built the job's summary from sacct alone: such jobs had used_gpu = 0 and so no DCGM utilization (avg_gpu_util). Now a reading with GPUs replaces the count, one without keeps it, and a job whose stored request has GPUs is a GPU job in its summary. Stored jobs were marked on upgrading, with a utilization where DCGM has samples on their nodes while they ran (migration 24). Jobs nomad never saw in the queue before GPU accounting began (short ones, or from before nomad ran) have no GPU record anywhere: the usage report counts them as a minimum and gives them no GPU-hours. To see when a site began: sacct -a -X -n -P -S DATE -o End,AllocTRES | grep gres/gpu | sort | head -1.

A Slurm that schedules cores only (SelectTypeParameters without Memory, e.g. CR_Core) puts no mem= in AllocTRES: it doesn't hold a job's --mem for it, jobs can use more than they ask for, and the impact report and nomad facts say so beside the memory share.

node_list is kept as Slurm writes it, in range form (n[01-04,07]). Code that needs the nodes themselves reads it with nomad.hostlist.expand_hostlist (or node_in); splitting on commas or matching with LIKE misses ranges.

docs.title: Job numbers that come back
docs.text: Slurm reuses job numbers: after its counter restarts (an outage that loses its state) or wraps at MaxJobId, number 4711 is a new job. Before 1.7.42 the new job's state, nodes and times were written onto the stored row, under the earlier job's user, partition, name and submit time. Now, when a job arrives whose number is stored with another submit time, and the stored job is another job (another user or job name, or it ended more than 30 days before, or it is still marked active but was submitted more than its time limit plus 30 days before -- a year without a limit -- as rows left RUNNING by an outage that lost Slurm's state are), the earlier job moves aside to NUMBER@SUBMIT-TIME (4711@2026-03-01T10:00:00; ~2 and so on if that is taken) in every table with a job id (jobs, job_summary, job_metrics, job_similarity, ...), and the number is the new job's. Rows in those tables dated (submit_time or timestamp) from the new job's submission on stay: they were written for the new job. A job moved aside while still marked active becomes UNKNOWN. A requeued job (same user and name) stays one job, and its submit time follows Slurm's (a requeue gets a new one). See nomad.db.jobkeys.place.

docs.title: Start times
docs.text: squeue reports a pending job's start as Slurm's estimate. It is never stored (before 16 Sep 2026 it was, and when the job's outcome then came from job_metrics, which did not update the start, the estimate stayed, with a wait to match). job_metrics now takes sacct's real start. Once per database, finished jobs whose start disagrees with end − runtime by more than two minutes are looked up in sacct and, when sacct's job is the same job, stored as sacct has it (no start for a job cancelled before it ran); those sacct no longer has are corrected to end − runtime only when their start is impossible (after the end, or before submission). At most 1,000 are looked up a run, so a backlog takes several runs; how far it got is kept in config (repair.job_start_times.after), and when done, what was done is recorded under repair.job_start_times. Rows from before 1.7.19 with an assumed end time are left to the outcome lookups above.

docs.title: Jobs from before nomad: nomad import sacct
docs.text:
nomad's job history starts when it was installed, and Slurm deletes its own job records after PurgeJobAfter. An export taken in time, or sacct itself for the months it still holds, fills that in, on the head node, into that site's database:

nomad import sacct /var/tmp/sacct_all.psv.gz          # what would change
nomad import sacct /var/tmp/sacct_all.psv.gz --apply
nomad import sacct --from 2025-10-01 --apply          # ask sacct, a month at a time

An export is any sacct -P output with its header line (sacct -a -X -P -o ALL -S DATE; not -n), plain or gzipped; fields are read by name. A record spread over lines (a field with newlines) is put back together: a line that reads as a record, or starts with one far enough to show a job id, starts a record, any other line goes on the one before. A | inside free-text fields (submit line, job name, working directory, comments) is put back where the other fields read as they should. Job steps and pending array ranges are skipped.

A job already stored only gets what it lacks (account, allocation, working directory, a partition instead of a list, a failure reason job_metrics left at 0), and its memory request as sacct records it (1.14.1, see Jobs). Its outcome changes only when nomad had none -- stored as running, pending or UNKNOWN, or an outcome assumed before 1.7.19 -- and the records show it ended; a stored outcome is never mixed with another. A job the records show running or pending, and nomad doesn't have, goes in as UNKNOWN with no end (an export is a snapshot). Numbers Slurm gave out again are kept apart (an older job as NUMBER@SUBMIT-TIME). Importing the same export twice changes nothing. The import commits every half second and gives way a moment after each commit, so the collectors writing the same database get in; with --from, each month is committed before sacct is asked about the next, and if sacct fails part way the months before stay written and the command says where it stopped. The database must exist (nomad collect makes it). Without --apply it is opened read-only and the counts say what would change, by month submitted (not counting what the import itself would change, such as a number used twice in the export).

docs.title: Usage history (sreport)
docs.text:
slurm_usage keeps Slurm's monthly usage totals in cluster_usage, one row per cluster, month and TRES (cpu, and gres/gpu where GPUs are accounted): hours allocated, down, planned down, idle, planned (held for waiting jobs; "Reserved" in older Slurm) and reported. Slurm usually keeps these for good (PurgeUsageAfter=NONE) after the job records are gone, so they are the long view of load. It runs where the slurm collector does, unless [collectors.slurm_usage] enabled says otherwise.

Each run asks sreport -P -t hours -T cpu,gres/gpu cluster utilization for at most months_per_run (24) months, newest first: this month and last month again every refresh_hours (6) until a month has been over two days (settled), and further back to the cluster's start or since = "YYYY-MM". The start is where Slurm has had nothing for three months in a row and nothing at all before them (one question about everything earlier, so a long outage isn't taken for it); it is kept in config as slurm_usage.nothing_before. Which months were asked, with which TRES and when, is in cluster_usage_asked; cluster_usage holds only what Slurm reported. A Slurm that says it doesn't account GPUs is asked for cpu alone from then on (slurm_usage.cpu_only); any other sreport error fails the run and the next tries again. A timeout ends the run without retries. A setting that doesn't read is warned about and its default used. Where two hosts report the same cluster, read one of them (the rows are the same).

Allocated, idle and planned are shares of the time nodes were up (reported − down); down is a share of all reported time. Never add cpu and gres/gpu rows together.

docs.title: Disks
docs.text: disk reads each of filesystems with df every run. Each reading also fits the readings of the last forecast_window_hours (default 6) with a straight line and stores the fill rate and when the filesystem will be full (fill_rate_bytes_per_day, days_until_full); a disk that will be full soon raises a disk_forecast alert (see docs/alerts.md).

docs.title: Compute nodes' local disks (node_disks)
docs.text:
Slurm knows a node's local disk only as configured (TmpDisk, often 0), and never how full it is. On the head node, node_disks asks every node that sinfo -a lists and that isn't down for df of each path in paths (default /localscratch), over ssh with BatchMode to the node's NodeHostname (the collector's account needs key or host-based access to the nodes, as it usually has inside a cluster), parallel nodes at a time, for at most max_seconds (120) in all, every interval_minutes (30; collect --once runs in between note when it last asked). The interval runs from when a sweep started, whatever came of it: one where no node answered (logins hanging on a dead home directory, say) is neither retried nor repeated at the next cron run. Off until enabled:

[collectors.node_disks]
enabled = true
paths = ["/localscratch"]

Each reading (node_disks: node, path, mount, device, size, used, free, percent) says which filesystem holds the path: mount = "/" means the path is a folder on the node's system disk, where a job that fills it can take the node down. Alerts (node_disk) at the disk thresholds of [alerts.thresholds.disk] (80 and 95% by default), one per node and path, raised and reminded of like the other disks; one ends when its disk hasn't been seen full for two and a half intervals (75 minutes), or episode_gap_minutes in [alerts] if longer, so a reading missed now and then doesn't raise it anew. A run says which nodes didn't answer, and fails only when none did. On the hub the readings are synced with the rest; the Console shows each node's latest.

docs.title: Who has the data
docs.text:
Since 1.14.3 a full disk comes with whom to ask. After a sweep's df readings, a few nodes chosen from them total each path by owner, on the node itself: find -xdev with its own block counts, as du (a file with several hard links counts once), summed there, so only one line per owner comes back over ssh. A path that is a link is counted where it leads. The count stays on that filesystem, runs at the lowest CPU and disk priority, ignores files that vanish while it runs, and stops after owners_seconds per path.

Which nodes, at most owners_per_sweep (and no more than parallel) per sweep:

  1. a disk at owners_above percent or more that wasn't when last counted: counted in the sweep that sees it full, so its alert names who has the data;
  2. counts due: never counted, or not for owners_every_hours;
  3. full disks, counted again at every sweep, the one counted longest ago first.

A node that didn't answer, or doesn't have the path, isn't counted. The counts run after the readings, so a sweep that counts takes up to owners_seconds per path (plus a few seconds) longer than the readings alone.

[collectors.node_disks]
# owners = true                # false: no counts
# owners_every_hours = 6
# owners_above = 80
# owners_seconds = 60          # per path
# owners_top = 5               # owners kept per node and path
# owners_per_sweep = 8         # default and most: parallel
# owners_in_alerts = true      # false: no names in alerts

node_disk_owner_counts has each count (node, path, how many owners, bytes counted, complete, and stopped: time limit, unreadable folders, no such folder, no access, count failed, no answer); node_disk_owners its largest owners and anyone with folders the count couldn't read (username as the head node names the uid, uid, bytes, files, unreadable folders). The collector's account reads what it counts: a folder it can't read is not counted, and its owner is named instead ("folders of X could not be read"), so an incomplete count never passes for the full picture.

A disk's alert names its three largest owners and their sizes. Alerts also go to Slack and webhooks when those are set up: owners_in_alerts = false keeps names out of every alert (the counts are still kept). The NØMAÐ Console shows the owners in a node's details, to staff.

To see whether the account reaches a node:

ssh -o BatchMode=yes NODE 'df -P /localscratch | tail -1'

docs.title: NFS
docs.text: On a host that mounts NFS, each run reads nfsiostat 5 2 and keeps the second report: what each mount did in those 5 seconds (sample_seconds in [collectors.nfs]). The first report averages everything since the share was mounted. Per mount: operations, read and write rates, and round-trip and execution times and retransmissions weighted over reads and writes — empty (NULL) for a mount with no reads or writes in the sample, rather than 0 ms. A host that mounts nothing says "no NFS mounts on this host"; turn nfs off there.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
Latency and packet loss from this host to the hosts you list, every run (ten pings, about two seconds per path):

[collectors.network_perf]
enabled = true

[[collectors.network_perf.network_tests]]
dest = "nas1"
path_type = "switch"
  • Each path starts on the host that runs it. A source naming another host (by name or address) is skipped, and the run says so; list that path in the other host's config.
  • A path with no reply at all is stored as unreachable.
  • Throughput is off unless throughput = true. It then runs at most once per throughput_interval (3600 s) per path — checked against the table, so it holds under cron — for iperf_duration seconds with iperf3, which needs iperf3 -s running on the destination. Without iperf3, or when no iperf3 -s answers, it times an SSH copy of 50 MB, which encryption may limit below what the network carries; if that fails too, no throughput is stored (never a 0).

docs.title: Heavy use of login nodes (per_user)
docs.text:
On a login node or another host people share, per_user says who used it heavily, with what, and for how long. Turn it on there:

[collectors.per_user]
enabled = true

Each run (every 5 minutes from cron) reads every process and averages its CPU and I/O over the 5 minutes since the previous run, from counters that run left in per_user_state. A process seen for the first time gets its average since it started; if that is above a rule's threshold, the next reading confirms it is still busy, and the flag is dated from the process's start — a process that has run flat out for two days is flagged as such five minutes after per_user is turned on. Where systemd puts each user's logins in a slice (user-<uid>.slice, cgroup v2 or v1 with CPU accounting), it also reads each user's CPU there, which counts processes that started and ended between two readings — a parallel make, a loop starting short programs. Work of another account inside a user's slice (sudo, su), and nomad's own when its cron session runs in its account's slice, is not counted as that user's.

What it keeps:

  • A sample (per_user_sample, with the command line) only for a process above a floor: floor_cpu_percent (10), floor_memory_gb (2) or floor_io_mb_per_s (10). Idle shells and daemons leave no row. Raw samples are deleted after sample_retention_days (30; 0 keeps them), a batch of 100,000 per run.
  • Flags (per_user_alert), kept. One row per episode — a process (or a user's processes together) above a rule's threshold without a break — and rule, written once the condition has held for the rule's duration and updated every run while it goes on: last_seen, sustained_for_seconds, occurrences (readings), and the episode's peaks.
  • Daily totals (per_user_daily), kept: for each user, host and day (local date), CPU seconds used, time busy (the user's processes together above the CPU floor), peaks of CPU and memory, and I/O where readable. An interval is added to the day it ends; one longer than two hours (the collector was stopped) is left out.

The rules (a duration is a minimum: readings come every 5 minutes, so a 2-minute CPU rule fires on the first 5-minute average above it):

Rule Over Condition Severity cpu_10pct_5min one process CPU ≥ 10% of a core for 5 min informational cpu_50pct_2min one process CPU ≥ 50% for 2 min actionable memory_4gb_10min one process resident memory ≥ 4 GB for 10 min informational memory_16gb_2min one process ≥ 16 GB for 2 min actionable user_cpu_200pct_10min a user's processes together ≥ 2 cores for 10 min actionable user_memory_32gb_10min a user's processes together ≥ 32 GB for 10 min actionable io_50mbs_10min one process reads + writes ≥ 50 MB/s for 10 min informational

A user's memory is the resident memory of their processes added up, so memory that forked workers share counts once for each.

[[collectors.per_user.rules]] tables replace them (see nomad.toml.example). System accounts (uid below min_uid), users, user_commands and processes started from parent_paths are never flagged; they are stored, marked, when above the floor.

I/O is what a process read and wrote through system calls — files on any filesystem, NFS included, pipes and sockets — so a large copy to NFS or a transfer through the host shows. Reading another user's I/O counters, and the executable path that parent_paths matches, needs root: run as another account, only that account's own processes have them. For a script run by an interpreter (python3 /usr/local/sw/backup/backup.py), parent_paths and user_commands also match the script, read from the command line, which needs no root: user_commands = [["backupuser", "backup.py"]].

If /proc is mounted with hidepid, an account other than root sees only its own processes; the run says so (nomad collectors).

nomad per-user                       # this host's database
nomad per-user --db ~/.local/share/nomad/combined.db --days 30   # every site, on the hub
nomad per-user --mask                # user and command names replaced, for sharing

Each host is named with its role, as its role setting says (from its latest sample or flag): login1 (login node), rstudio1 (interactive server), node01 (compute node). Each flagged line is a process (or a user's processes together) and a stretch of time: from when the condition began to when it was last seen, the rules it broke (! actionable, i informational), and its peaks.

docs.title: Interactive servers (RStudio, JupyterHub)
docs.text:
On a server people use through RStudio Server or JupyterHub, interactive records each session every run (interactive_sessions: who, which kind, its memory) and keeps each person's day in small totals, kept for good (interactive_daily, one row per day, server, person and kind):

  • sessions open that day (one running across midnight counts on both days), and session_seconds, the time they were open (two notebooks for an hour are two session-hours);
  • busy_seconds of that time, when a session used CPU (at least 2% of one core between two runs), out of cpu_measured_seconds, and cpu_seconds used;
  • mem_mb_seconds, memory held over time (/ 3.6e6 is GB-hours), and peak_mem_mb, the most one session held.

A session is a process tree: an RStudio session (rsession), a Jupyter kernel (ipykernel, IRkernel), or a person's Jupyter server (jupyterhub-singleuser, jupyter-lab, ...), with the workers it forked that kept its command line (R's mclapply, Python's multiprocessing with fork) folded in: their memory and CPU are the session's. A kernel is a session of its own, apart from the server that started it, so a person with JupyterLab open and two notebooks has three. Programs are told by what runs (for Python, the module or script after any interpreter options: python -Xfrozen_modules=off -m ipykernel_launcher), not by a word anywhere in the command line: pip install ipykernel is not a session. So that a person's time is not counted once per session, each person also has a row of kind (any): session_seconds there is the time they had at least one session open, busy_seconds the time at least one was busy, memory and CPU their sessions' together, peak_mem_mb the most they held at once, and sessions all their sessions that day, of every kind (JupyterLab and two notebooks: 3). Counts of people and hours come from (any); the other rows say which kinds.

Environments (since 1.12.5): each session also says which software environment it runs from (environment in interactive_sessions): the name of a conda environment whose program it runs (.../envs/demo101/bin/python, or R's .../envs/demo101/lib/R/bin/exec/R: demo101), or nothing for the base installation. Only the program counts (the command line's first word, or what /proc says a bare python is), not a path anywhere in its arguments. An environment the session's own account owns, or keeps in its home, is marked as its own (own): anyone can name one like a course, so the hub counts such sessions only for faculty members. A Jupyter server records none: it runs from the hub's installation whatever its kernels use. A class often has an environment of its own, a Jupyter kernel named for its course, so who used which says who is in which class (courses). Each person's day per environment is kept for good in interactive_env_daily (day, server, person, environment, own: sessions, session_seconds, busy_seconds, cpu_seconds), counted once whatever the kind of session. On the hub a person is one of an environment's users after sessions in it on two days of a term. A site whose environments live elsewhere says where with environment_patterns: regular expressions matched against the program, the name in a group called env (else the first group); one that isn't a regular expression is skipped, with a warning.

By the hour (since 1.11.1, also kept for good), for peaks and for when a class works:

  • interactive_hourly, one row per hour and server: runs (readings in the hour; measured_runs of them with a known interval), the most people on at once (people_max) and their sum over readings (people_sum / runs is the hour's average), the same for people with a busy session (busy_people_max, busy_people_sum, over measured readings, out of measured_people_sum: their ratio is the share busy), sessions_max, person-seconds open and busy (open_seconds, busy_seconds), cpu_seconds, and mem_mb_max, the most memory everyone held at once. A reading with nobody on counts as zero people, so averages cover the whole hour; an hour the collector did not run has no row. Busy means computing (at least 2% of a core between readings): someone reading or typing in a notebook is on, not busy.
  • interactive_person_hourly, one row per hour, server and person with a session: open_seconds, busy_seconds (out of measured_seconds), cpu_seconds, mem_mb_max and runs — when a class or a lab works, for the views that sum them by course or lab.

Hours are local time (2026-10-13T14); as for days, the time between two readings goes to the later one's hour. The hour repeated when daylight time ends holds both (twice the readings, averages unaffected) and the skipped hour has no row. Peaks at once are as seen at the readings, five minutes apart. Like the daily totals, these rows are kept for good, whatever sample_retention_days does to the raw snapshots, and they start at the upgrade (earlier hours can be rebuilt only roughly, from the raw snapshots: who was on, not who was busy).

CPU is read from each process's own counter at every run (interactive_state, this host's working state, not synced): ps's %CPU is an average over a process's whole life, so it calls a notebook idle that is busy now after a day of nothing. A session's counter includes the workers it has finished with; workers started another way (multiprocessing with spawn, subprocess) are not part of the session while they run, and their CPU is counted when they end and the session collects them. Not for a Jupyter server: the children it collects are kernels, whose CPU was counted as theirs. Memory is resident memory added up over a session's processes, so pages forked workers share count once per worker. The time between two runs is measured on the system clock, not local time (the change to or from daylight time adds or loses no hour) and goes to the day of the later run; a gap over two hours (the collector was stopped) adds no time, and a run that could not list processes is not taken for nobody being on. Accounts are named from their uid (ps aux shortens names over 8 characters, which then match no group).

The weeks before 1.11: nomad interactive backfill, on the server, rebuilds the daily and hourly totals for the days before nomad kept them from the raw snapshots: who was on at each reading and for how long, and the memory they held (a reading with nobody on still counts: the collector's run log says when it ran). Not what was computing: the old snapshots kept ps's lifetime average. Rebuilt rows are marked (rebuilt = 1), carry no CPU and no session count (the old snapshots counted processes), and say so wherever they are read. Names ps aux cut to 8 characters ("abcdefg+") are matched to the one known name they can be. It runs on the server (a hub's combined database is refused: the hub copies the server's at its next sync). It shows what it would rebuild; --apply writes it, a day at a time; --redo replaces an earlier rebuild. The day nomad 1.11 was installed is not rebuilt: its totals begin at the upgrade.

[interactive]
enabled = true
server_id = "web1"
sample_retention_days = 0   # raw snapshots kept this many days (0: all); the daily totals are always kept
# environment_patterns = ['/envs/(?P<env>[^/]+)/']   # the default: conda's layout

On such a server, per_user with role = "interactive" keeps its daily per-person totals (CPU and memory for everyone, terminal users included) without the login-node rules, which would flag every busy notebook. Its rules there flag one person holding a large share of the machine for long:

[collectors.per_user]
enabled = true
role = "interactive"
Rule Over Condition Severity interactive_user_cpu_800pct_30min a user's processes together ≥ 8 cores for 30 min informational interactive_user_memory_64gb_30min a user's processes together ≥ 64 GB for 30 min informational

docs.title: Out-of-memory kills (oom)
docs.text:
Without per-user memory limits, one person's work can use up a shared host's memory; the kernel then kills a process to free some -- often someone else's notebook in the middle of a lab, who sees only a dead kernel. oom records each kill from the kernel's messages in the journal (journalctl _TRANSPORT=kernel, every boot the journal keeps: kills just before a restart are the ones that matter most, and journalctl -k reads only the current boot): when, the program and its pid, whose (uid and account), the control group it ran in, and the memory it held (oom_kills). Each run reads on from where the previous one stopped; the first looks back lookback_days (30; 0 starts from now). The account needs to read the kernel's messages (usually the systemd-journal or adm group); when it cannot, the run says so (a first look back that finds no kernel message at all says so once, and the look then starts from that run: to look back again after giving the account access, delete the rows of oom_state). A journal kept only in memory (Storage=volatile, or auto without /var/log/journal) loses what came before a restart.

[collectors.oom]
enabled = true

docs.title: Workstations over SSH
docs.text: workstation runs its commands and probes on each machine over SSH (BatchMode: a key, no password prompt), as the user ~/.ssh/config gives for that host, and runs them directly on a machine listed under the collecting host's own name. Some lab machines print a banner on every login, interactive or not, from a shell startup file. Since 1.7.27 nomad prints a marker before each command and reads only what follows it, so such a banner is never read as the machine's figures. To keep the banner off non-interactive logins anyway, wrap it in if [[ $- == *i* ]]; then ... fi.

docs.title: Workstation mounts
docs.text:
Each workstation run also checks every mount on each machine (NFS, and local filesystems other than the system's own). A small probe goes over the same SSH connection to the machine's own python3 (3.6 or later), so nothing is installed on the workstations. It checks all mounts at once, each in its own thread with a 3-second limit, and records whether stat() answered (workstation_mount_state: is_responsive, response_ms). A call on a dead NFS server cannot be interrupted, so a thread still waiting at the limit is abandoned, the mount recorded as not responding, and the probe ends anyway: a dead NAS costs one limit, and the other mounts are still reported.

Since 1.7.24 it also records the size of the filesystem behind each mount, as df shows it: total_bytes, used_bytes and avail_bytes (what users can still write). These are empty for a mount that did not answer, and in rows from before 1.7.24. For an NFS mount they are the server's figures for that export, so the lab machines report their NAS's space without nomad reaching the NAS. "Used" is the whole export's, whoever wrote it.

Exports that are datasets of one ZFS pool each report their own used space but share the pool's free space, and each one's total is its own used space plus that shared free space. So their totals overlap and must not be added up. When two exports of one server are read with the same free space (within 0.1%, at most 1 GiB) in one run, whether by the same lab machine or by two (an export mounted on a single machine is read by no other), nomad console roles says "free space shared with ...", leaves out each one's total, and adds a line with their space together: their used space summed, the free space counted once. Exports on different server addresses are never put together, even if the same NAS answers on both.

Only the collecting host needs 1.7.24 for the sizes; the hub's combined database gains the columns at its next sync.

A machine's own disks among them (not NFS or other network filesystems, not fuse mounts, not drives plugged in under /media) raise workstation_disk alerts at the disk thresholds, one per machine and disk (1.14.2; see docs/alerts.md), and are the Console's Local disks.

docs.title: Storage servers
docs.text:
[collectors.storage]
enabled = true

[[collectors.storage.storage_devices]]
hostname = "nas1"
type = "zfs"

[[collectors.storage.storage_devices]]
hostname = "nfs-home"
type = "nfs"
paths = ["/export/home"]

Reached over SSH with BatchMode (a key, no password prompt) unless hostname is this host. type = "zfs" reads pool health and capacity: the space users have, from each pool's root dataset (zfs list), so RAIDZ parity isn't counted as it is in zpool list, and a boot pool (boot-pool, freenas-boot, bpool) isn't counted at all. It works on TrueNAS CORE (FreeBSD) as on Linux. Any type reads NFS exports and connected clients. A login banner is skipped, as for workstations. nomad lab add-nas adds a NAS (see docs/config.md). Without ZFS, capacity comes only from the paths listed (df) — never from the server's root disk. An unreachable server is stored as offline with its capacity unknown (NULL), not as an empty server.

Who holds a server's space (each owner's use, quotas, and how old their folders are) is the storage_use collector's: see Storage use.

[[storage_devices]] and [[network_tests]] at the top level of nomad.toml, where older examples put them, are still read, with a warning to move them.

docs.title: Condo reports
docs.text:
A condo is a set of nodes a lab bought, lent to everyone else through a guest partition while the lab isn't using them. nomad usage-report condos writes each condo's monthly report for its owner, and a summary of every condo for research computing, grouped by cluster.

nomad usage-report condos init               # draft the condos into report.toml
nomad usage-report condos init --apply       # ... and add them to it (in a terminal, it asks how reports go out)
nomad usage-report condos status             # what is left to set up
nomad usage-report condos set --labs mail_domain=example.edu --labs review_to=rc@example.edu \
                              --confirm smith,jones --owner lee=klee --apply
nomad usage-report condos                    # last month's reports, written
nomad usage-report condos --send             # ... and mailed
nomad usage-report condos --month 2026-09 --cluster c1 --condo smith
sudo nomad usage-report condos timer --apply # make and mail them on the 1st

The Console does the same for admins, under Settings > Condo reports: the settings, the condos with nomad's owner guesses, a preview of each report, and sending a month for review.

docs.title: Setting it up
docs.text:
nomad init asks whether to register condos: for each Slurm cluster, the guest partition (the one named like "condo" by default), then each condo it finds there with its owner's NetID (an owner typed there is confirmed; left blank, it is set later), the owners' mail domain and who reviews the reports first. It writes them to report.toml beside nomad.toml. The reports are made where a cluster's data is gathered: on that machine, or on the hub that syncs it (copy report.toml there, or set it up there as below).

On a hub:

  1. nomad usage-report condos init --apply drafts every cluster's condos into report.toml, each owner guessed and not confirmed. In a terminal it then asks what a first setup needs and isn't set yet: the owners' mail domain, who reviews the reports first (review_to), the sender and the line at the foot (--no-input skips this).
  2. Check each owner and confirm it (condos set --confirm NAME --apply, or the Console).
  3. Read last month's reports (nomad usage-report condos). With review_to set, --send mails them all there; without it, --send mails each confirmed owner theirs.
  4. nomad usage-report condos timer --apply, as root, installs the timer that makes and mails them on the 1st.
  5. When the reviewed reports read right, clear review_to: from then on each goes to its owner.

nomad usage-report condos status says what is left at any point:

  • condo partitions on the nodes that report.toml doesn't list (a new condo), and condos it lists that are gone from the nodes;
  • owners not confirmed (their reports don't go out);
  • confirmed condos without an address (no mail_domain, no email), and no sender;
  • the timer, not installed or not enabled;
  • notes: review mode (every report goes to review_to) and no PDF (fpdf2 missing).

Most lines say what to run. nomad config check on a hub (or wherever report.toml lists condos) shows the same in counts, naming no condos or owners, and the Console lists it at the top of Settings > Condo reports.

It reads the hub's combined database (--db names another) and the same report.toml as nomad usage-report (--config names another).

docs.title: What an owner gets
docs.text:
Each report names the cluster it covers, in its title and on a badge, so an owner with condos on two clusters can tell them apart.

  1. The nodes: how many, their cores, memory and GPUs, and the partition.
  2. The month on the nodes: of the core-hours the nodes were in service, the share the owner's lab used, the share guests used, and the share nobody used, as a bar and as figures; the node-hours in service, down, drained, in maintenance and not read; how many guest jobs ran there, how many were preempted, and how many ran longer than the guest limit.
  3. The lab's jobs on its own nodes: of the jobs submitted to the condo's partition in the month, the share that started within the guarantee (owner_start_minutes, from when the job could start: Slurm's Eligible time, else its submission), whenever they started: a job submitted on the 30th that starts on the 1st is the month's. A job still waiting when the report is made counts as late once it has waited longer than the guarantee. A later start is put down to guest jobs on the nodes at the time, the lab's own jobs filling them, or neither (dependencies, a request larger than the nodes, nodes out of service). Then how the jobs that ended did (completed, failed, out of memory, timed out, cancelled) and how much of the cores and memory they held they used.
  4. The lab elsewhere: the lab's use of the cluster's shared nodes, of other condos as guests, and of other clusters: core-hours, GPU-hours, people, failures, CPU and memory used, and median wait.
  5. Members: each member of the lab who ran anything, by NetID, with their core-hours on the condo, on the shared nodes, on other condos and on other clusters (name_members); the others are counted. People who ran in the condo's partition without being members are listed too, marked, with their jobs there only. Guests on the owner's nodes are only ever totals.
  6. Storage: the lab's scratch quota and the home quota from [report.policy]. Not measured yet: once NØMAÐ reads quotas, this shows what is used.
  7. The past 12 months: the lab, guest and idle shares month by month.
  8. What the figures rest on: node-hours not read, jobs not measured, and what a figure can't count.

A run limited by --cluster or --condo writes and sends no summary: a summary of some condos would stand for the month's.

Research computing's summary has one table per cluster, a row per condo (owner, nodes, shares, guest core-hours, preemptions, how many owner jobs started within the guarantee, node-hours out of service) and a bar per condo. A cluster without condos is listed as having none. It also lists what needs attention: condo partitions on the nodes that report.toml doesn't list, condos whose partition is gone, and owners not confirmed.

docs.title: How the figures are made
docs.text:
• Node-hours come from the node readings (every 5 minutes). Each reading stands for the time until the node's next one, up to twice the node's usual interval that month (the median gap, and at least 10 minutes); the rest is "not read", counted as in service, and the report says how much there was. The interval is each month's own, so a site that read its nodes more often earlier in the year isn't measured by that interval now. A node counts from its first reading only when the cluster's other nodes were reporting before it (a new node), and until its last only when they went on after it (a node retired). Months before a cluster's first reading have no readings.
  • Core-hours are each job's cores (Slurm's allocation, else the request) times the hours it ran inside the month, split evenly over its nodes. A job that left the queue with no outcome recorded (UNKNOWN) ran until NØMAÐ saw it gone. GPUs are the allocation's, or the request's where the site's accounting doesn't count GPUs.
  • Owner or guest: a job on the condo's nodes is the owner's when it ran in the condo's partition, under the lab's Slurm account (account), or for a member of the lab; any other job there is a guest's. Idle is what is left of the in-service core-hours.
