  • Preempted guest jobs are those that ended PREEMPTED. A guest job that was requeued keeps its job number and only its last run is kept, so the count is a lower bound.
  • Members: members in report.toml (a Unix group, a Slurm account, or a list); else each owner's labs by [console.labs] in nomad.toml (the group named for them by group_pattern, and the groups they lead), and the owners.

docs.title: Idle condos while jobs waited elsewhere
docs.text:
nomad usage-report condos idle [--month 2026-09] [--json] [--mask] measures what sharing condos more widely would offer, before anything changes in Slurm:

  • Idle core-hours: free cores (CPUTot - CPUAlloc) on the condo's nodes while in service, each reading standing for the time until the next one, as the monthly report counts them. Open: those on nodes that take jobs (not draining, reserved or planned for a job); only open cores can take a waiting job.
  • Waiting elsewhere: jobs waiting in partitions that don't reach the condo's nodes (not the condo's own, not a guest partition over it). Once a job runs Slurm keeps only the partition it ran in, so a job that also listed a guest partition while it waited, and ran elsewhere, is counted.
  • Waiting for the cluster: since squeue last began showing the job waiting for Resources or Priority (or its partition's nodes down) without a break. A job held by its own limits (QOS, association, a dependency, a hold, nodes it named) waited for those, and one never seen waiting for the cluster is left out. This is recorded from nomad 1.18 on; older jobs count from when they could start, and the command says how many had no reason recorded. Jobs submitted in the month that started after it count too.
  • Wanted by a waiting job: at each reading, the waiting jobs whose request fits on one free node -- cores, memory, GPUs -- with a time limit within guest_max_days (no limit stored: how long it ran, once it ended; still running or never ran: left out) are placed, the longest-waiting first. The cores placed are the idle core-hours a waiting job could have used. It is the opportunity at each moment, not a simulation: a job placed at one reading is placed again at the next if it was in fact still waiting. For a job sacct hasn't reported (never started, or not yet) nomad has only what squeue showed: its memory is read per core (the larger reading), and GPUs asked for with --gpus aren't seen.
  • Jobs that could have started earlier, by at least 10 minutes, and by how much (the median, and the job-hours in all, which is at most: two such jobs may have wanted the same cores later). A job given up while it waited counts until it was given up.
  • Left out: jobs asking for several nodes, longer than guest_max_days, with no time limit and no finished run, too big for any of the condo's nodes, or held by their own limits.
  • Idle stretches: the share of wholly idle, open node-hours in stretches of at least 2, 6, 12 and 24 hours, and the length half of them reached: long stretches are where guest jobs would rarely be pushed off.

Each condo is measured on its own: one waiting job may count at several, so the condos' figures don't add up; the cluster's line counts each job once. No job or person is named; condos go by their names in report.toml (--mask for stand-ins).

docs.title: Finding the condos
docs.text:
Nothing new runs at the sites: each node reading carries the node's partitions. The guest partition is the one named in guest_partitions, or one named like "condo". A condo is a partition whose nodes all sit inside the guest partition. A partition over every condo node is another way in for guests, unless it is the only condo there is.

The owner is guessed from two kinds of evidence, because each alone misleads: a partition can be named for another of the PI's surnames, and a condo lent out a lot is used mostly by other labs.

  • The name. owner_patterns ({name}, {name}lab, {name}_lab and {name}-lab by default) give a last name, a number at the end being a second condo of the same lab (smith2). The owner is a NetID of up to two initials and that name, perhaps with a number after it (jsmith3), cut short where the institution's NetIDs stop (netid_max_length, 8: tanderso for Anderson): first one with a lab group named for it, then one that leads a lab in nomad.toml, then one that ran jobs in the partition, then an account. Several accounts that fit, none of them a lab's PI, are listed rather than guessed from. Two last names joined (smithjones) are two owners, when one of them at least is a lab's PI.
  • The users. The lab groups (by [console.labs] group_pattern) of the people who ran jobs in the partition over the past year, the one holding the most of them first. When it holds more than half of them (two at least), it names the owner where the name names nobody, or only an account.

When the two point at different labs, the name's owner is kept and the draft says to check. init writes each guess with its evidence and confirmed = false; a report goes to its owners only once someone sets it to true.

docs.title: Changing the settings
docs.text:
nomad usage-report condos set changes report.toml without opening it:

  • --labs KEY=VALUE and --policy KEY=VALUE: a [report.labs] or [report.policy] setting; lists as A,B, numbers and true/false as such;
  • --confirm A,B and --unconfirm A,B: which condos' reports may go to their owners;
  • --owner CONDO=NETID[,NETID]: a condo's owner, or owners.

A condo is its name, or CLUSTER/NAME when two clusters have one of that name. Without --apply it shows the change and writes nothing. With it, the file is copied first and keeps its owner and permissions, and nothing is written unless the result reads as condo settings (a misspelled setting or an address that isn't one is refused). --mask prints counts instead of names.

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text:
Reports are written to OUT/<cluster>/<condo>/<YYYY-MM>.{html,pdf,json,md} and OUT/summary/<YYYY-MM>.*, readable only by the account that writes them: they name people. OUT is out_dir in [report.labs], else reports/condos in nomad's data directory, else --out.

The email is HTML made for mail readers (tables, inline styles), with a plain-text part and the PDF attached. Each report is headed like the Console's sign-in page, from [console.branding] in nomad.toml: the logo, the institution and the unit lines under it (unit = ["Research Computing", "Office of the Provost"]). The logo must be a PNG or JPEG at a full path; it goes inside the HTML file, inline in the email (so mail readers show it without fetching anything), and in the PDF. branding = false in [report.labs] leaves it all out; without [console.branding], institution in [report.labs] names the sender. The PDF needs fpdf2:

pip install 'nomad-hpc[report]'

Without it the reports are written and sent without a PDF, and the email says so.

Mail goes through [mail] in nomad.toml. While review_to is set, every report goes there, marked with whom it would have gone to, and so does the summary when summary_to names someone else; clear it to send reports to their owners and the summary to summary_to. What was sent each month is kept in OUT/summary/<YYYY-MM>.sent.json, so a second run doesn't mail the same report twice (--resend does).

docs.title: On the first of each month
docs.text:
nomad usage-report condos timer prints the timer for this install (the nomad in use, its nomad.toml, and the nomad account, or --user), and --apply (as root) installs and starts it; --at changes when (systemd's OnCalendar, the 1st at 07:00 by default, after the night's syncs). A timer already set up with the same settings is left as it is. It is this, on the hub:

# /etc/systemd/system/nomad-condo-reports.service
[Unit]
Description=NOMAD condo reports
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
User=nomad
ExecStart=/opt/nomad/venv/bin/nomad -c /etc/nomad/nomad.toml usage-report condos --send

# /etc/systemd/system/nomad-condo-reports.timer
[Unit]
Description=NOMAD condo reports, on the 1st

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-01 07:00
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now nomad-condo-reports.timer

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Everything one institution may do differently goes in report.toml:

[report.labs]                          # how the reports go out
mail_domain = "example.edu"            # owner's address: NETID@mail_domain
send_from = "Research Computing <rc@example.edu>"
review_to = ["rc@example.edu"]         # while set, every report goes here
summary_to = ["rc@example.edu"]        # the summary (default: review_to)
name_members = true                    # an owner's report names their lab's members
formats = ["html", "pdf", "json"]      # also "md"
owner_patterns = ["{name}", "{name}lab", "{name}_lab", "{name}-lab"]
netid_max_length = 8                   # NetIDs cut short here; 0: never
contact = "Questions: rc@example.edu"  # the line at the foot of each report
out_dir = "/var/lib/nomad/reports/condos"
institution = "Research Computing"     # the name at the top, without [console.branding]
branding = true                        # head reports with [console.branding]: logo and lines

[report.policy]                        # what the reports check against
owner_start_minutes = 5                # an owner's job starts on its own nodes within
guest_max_days = 10                    # the longest a guest job may run
guest_grace_minutes = 5
home_quota_gb = { soft = 50, hard = 60 }
lab_scratch_quota_tb = { soft = 20, hard = 24 }
scratch_path = "/scratch/{lab}"
use_below = 0.25                       # below this share of what jobs ask for, say so

[report.clusters.c1]
label = "Cluster 1"                    # how the reports name the cluster
guest_partitions = ["condos"]          # default: partitions named like "condo"

[report.clusters.c1.condos.smith]      # drafted by `nomad usage-report condos init`
owner = "jsmith"                       # or several: ["jsmith", "rjones"]
partition = "smith"                    # default: the table's name
nodes = "c[01-04]"                     # default: the partition's nodes
members = "group:smith$"               # or "account:smith", or a list of NetIDs
account = "smith"                      # the lab's Slurm account, if it has one
email = "jsmith@example.edu"           # or a list; default: each owner@mail_domain
cc = ["manager@example.edu"]
confirmed = true
lab_scratch_quota_tb = 30              # an agreed larger quota

A cluster with a condos table is reported as listed there. One without is reported from what its nodes say, every condo unconfirmed, until init drafts it. A setting nobody reads is refused (reveiw_to would otherwise send reports to owners). A site's own database, with no hub, is the cluster this-cluster, or the one cluster of its nomad.toml that report.toml lists condos for (as nomad init writes them).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: NØMAÐ uses TOML configuration files.

docs.title: Configuration Locations
docs.text: Install Type Path User ~/.config/nomad/nomad.toml System /etc/nomad/nomad.toml

docs.title: When the file can't be read
docs.text:
A file with a mistake in it is not read at all: nomad then runs with none of its settings (database, collectors, roles, labs), and the Console shows no PIs or labs. It is not replaced by the next file either (/etc/nomad/nomad.toml behind a broken ~/.config one): only nomad's packaged defaults apply. So nomad says so instead of carrying on quietly:

  • every command prints, on stderr, which file and which line (when nobody is at a terminal, as under cron, once an hour for the same problem);
  • nomad syscheck marks it ✗, and nomad console roles says the Console has no labs until it is fixed;
  • nomad lab refuses to edit it.

After editing the file by hand, check it:

$ nomad config check
✗ /home/hpcadmin/.config/nomad/nomad.toml can't be read
  line 211: `leads` is set twice in [console.labs] (first on line 209); keep one of them
    209 | leads = { jdoe = ["pi1$"] }
  > 211 | leads = {}

A key set twice in the same table (as above), or a table declared twice, is the usual cause. The exit status is 1 while the file can't be read, 0 once it does; the messages name keys and tables, never values from the file.

docs.title: Example Configuration
docs.text:
# nomad.toml

[general]
cluster_name = "spydur"
data_dir = "/var/lib/nomad"
log_level = "INFO"

[database]
path = "/var/lib/nomad/nomad.db"

[collectors]
interval = 60  # seconds, for `nomad collect` without --once

# Each collector is turned on or off in its own table (see Collectors).
[collectors.nfs]
enabled = false

[collectors.disk]
filesystems = ["/", "/home", "/scratch"]
quota_enabled = true

[collectors.slurm]
partitions = ["compute", "gpu", "highmem"]

[dashboard]
host = "127.0.0.1"
port = 8050

[alerts]
enabled = true

[mail]
host = "smtp.example.edu"
from = "hpc@example.edu"

[support]
email = "hpc-support@example.edu"
institution = "Example University"

[alerts.email]
enabled = true
recipients = ["admin@example.edu"]

[alerts.slack]
enabled = true
webhook_url = "https://hooks.slack.com/services/..."

[alerts.thresholds]
disk_warning = 85
disk_critical = 95
gpu_temp_warning = 80

[ml]
enabled = true
similarity_threshold = 0.7

docs.title: Console access
docs.text:
Who may see what in the Console is set in nomad.toml on the machine that runs it:

[console.roles]
admin = ["jtonini"]            # everything, settings included
operator = []                  # everything, no settings
viewer = []                    # named: their own work, whatever else says

[console.labs]
group_pattern = "{netid}$"     # the group a faculty member leads, by its name
leads = { NETID = ["chemlab$"] }   # exceptions and extra groups
not_labs = ["svc$"]            # never a lab, whatever else says (1.17.10)

[console.labs.resources."NETID$"]
name = "Smith Lab"             # how the lab is shown (else its group)
workstations = ["adam", "eve"] # the lab's own machines
storage = ["sarahvaughan"]     # its storage: a server, or server:/export

[console.labs.assistants]
"NETID$" = ["eve"]             # research assistants: see the lab as its PI does

[console.labs.attention]       # what My lab's Needs attention lists (1.17.6); the defaults:
# days = 7                     # the jobs, and the growth of data, looked at
# waiting_hours = 24           # a job waiting longer for something that won't change by itself,
# waiting_max_days = 60        # and no longer (an old record, not a job)
# failing_jobs = 3             # failed jobs, at least half of a member's that ran to an end
# storage_pct = 90             # a lab storage server this full
# holders = 3                  # the lab's biggest holders of data named (0: none),
# holder_gb = 100              # each holding this much or more,
# growth_gb = 100              # and anyone whose data grew this much in `days` (0: none)
# quota_pct = 90               # a member this close to a quota
# over_cpu_hours = 100         # core-hours held by measured jobs,
# over_cpu_pct = 25            # used under this share of them
# over_memory_pct = 20         # memory used under this share of what jobs asked for,
# over_memory_jobs = 3         # over this many measured jobs
# workstation_hours = 2        # a lab workstation silent this long

[console.storage."10.0.0.28"]  # a storage server, as the mounts name it
name = "sarahvaughan"
note = "community $HOME, all users"

[console.machines."labhead1"]   # what a machine is, beside its name (1.17.7)
note = "the Smith lab's head node: collects its workstations"

nomad console role NETID admin|operator|viewer|none changes one person's role here (--apply writes it): only their name in the admin, operator and viewer lists changes, and each list's line and comment stay. viewer names them a viewer whatever else would make them more (a directory admin group, an older role in the Console's own records); none takes them off every list, so the Console's own record decides. Roles written inline (roles = {...}), a list spread over several lines, or a multi-line string are left to be changed by hand. It refuses to write when the file changed since it was read, keeps the file's line endings, and keeps the newest 20 of its backups (nomad.toml.bak-role-*; ones named by hand stay). Give it the file the Console reads. Saving writes in the file's folder (the backup, then the new file swapped in), so run it as an account that can write that folder, or as root (sudo -u nomad nomad -c /etc/nomad/nomad.toml console role jdoe operator --apply where the nomad account or its group may write /etc/nomad; else sudo nomad -c ...).

  • Viewer: anyone the file does not name who signs in. They see their own work, and the aggregates (queues, capacity, storage) everyone sees.
  • PI: a viewer who leads a lab also sees its members, one by one. They lead the group group_pattern names for them, when that group exists in the groups collector's data, and any group listed for them in leads (nomad lab lead LAB NETID adds one, below). Members are the people the group lists now who still have an account; someone taken out of the group, or whose account was deleted while a group file still names them, is not one (see the groups collector). group_pattern is empty by default: a site that has not said how its groups work gets no lab view rather than a wrong one. A group that is a course this term ([console.courses]: listed, as nomad course add on an instructor's own group does, or named like a course) is a class, not a lab: that term it is not the instructor's lab, unless storage or machines are listed for it under [console.labs.resources] or a leads entry names it (nomad lab lead LAB NETID writes one, for the instructor too: its PI and research assistants then see its members, the class's students, one by one); a workstation only tagged with the group doesn't count. nomad console roles NETID and nomad facts lab NETID say when someone's own group is a class this term. nomad course add says so when it makes a lab a class. It is a lab again the term it isn't a course. The condo reports' members are the owner's group either way.
  • Research assistant: a viewer listed for a lab under [console.labs.assistants] (nomad lab assistant LAB NETID, below, or the PI from the lab's Members page in the Console) sees it as its PI does: its members one by one, its machines and storage -- but for whoever leads it: the PI's own work stays theirs. Only while they are one of the lab's members: someone who leaves the group stops being its assistant with nothing to edit, and nomad console roles lists the entries that no longer apply. Only a lab has them: a group named in [console.labs] (machines, storage, a name, a lead) or the one group_pattern names for one of its own members, not any group with members; a lab that is a class this term (above) has none that term. Names that aren't NetIDs are reported and left out.
  • Not a lab: not_labs lists groups that are never labs, whatever the rules above say (1.17.10): a service account's group, a mistyped one, the group of someone who left. The Console leaves them out (Labs, search, Groups, My lab), nobody leads them or is their research assistant, and nomad facts lab and nomad console roles say why. Nothing on the clusters changes and their data stays: the condo reports count a hidden group's members as before, and hiding one of an owner's labs moves no condo onto another. Taking a group off the list makes it a lab again. nomad lab hide LAB writes it (below). A name, machines or a lead nomad.toml gives a group it lists are kept but don't apply, and nomad config check says so.
  • A lab's machines: a PI also sees their labs' workstations and storage. On those machines, people outside the lab appear as "another user". A workstation belongs to a lab when the collector that monitors it tags it with the lab's group: department = "NETID$" in its [[collectors.workstation.workstations]] entry, on the machine that collects it. The tag reaches the hub with the data, so a workstation is assigned once, where it is added. A machine moved to another lab follows its latest tag. Workstations can also be listed under [console.labs.resources."group"] (one not collected, say), and storage is listed there: a storage server's name, or one export (server:/export) as the workstations mount it. Nothing is guessed from names.
  • Needs attention: the lab's PI (and its research assistants, and staff) see at the top of each lab what needs them: members' jobs stuck waiting, out of memory, out of time or mostly failing, the lab's storage filling, who holds the most data and where, someone near a quota, jobs holding far more than they use, a workstation gone quiet (details). [console.labs.attention] sets each limit; nomad config check reports a value it can't use (its default applies). nomad facts lab NETID --each prints the same list.
  • Storage servers: [console.storage."SERVER"] gives a server a name and a note, shown wherever its exports are (and beside a member's data in Needs attention: a note saying what it is, "spydur's /home and /scratch", tells a PI where that is). When the storage collector reads that server (under its address, or under that name, as an ssh alias), its state, space and pools' health go on the server's line. SERVER is the server as the mounts name it, the part before the colon in server:/export (often an address). A server that everyone shares should say so in its note: its used space is everyone's, and would otherwise read as the lab's own.
  • What each machine is: [console.machines."NAME"] gives any machine (a head node, the hub, a NAS, a cluster, a workstation) a note, a short line saying what it is: the Console shows it when the pointer is over the machine's name (and under the name on a lab's Workstations), and nomad facts, nomad lab show print it. NAME as nomad shows the machine, compared without case; at most 200 characters. A storage server's [console.storage] note is used when it has none here. nomad machine note NAME "..." shows the change and --apply writes it (with a backup, nomad.toml.bak-machine-*, the newest 20 kept; only the note line changes, the table's other keys and comments stay); --remove takes it away; nomad machine list lists them. A storage server has one description under its address and its name. A note is seen by whoever sees the machine named: a site, a storage server or a cluster's node is everyone's (a site that is also a lab's head node is a site; a machine listed or collected as storage is storage); a workstation is its lab's PI's, research assistants' and staff's; a name nomad can't place, staff's.
  • Operator: sees everything, changes no settings.
  • Admin: everything, settings included.

NetIDs are compared without regard to case. For anyone named here the file wins over the Console's own records (users.json), which keep only what is private or automatic: the break-glass password, and the record made at someone's first login. A setting that is wrong is reported and left out, never guessed at.

docs.title: Adding machines and labs: nomad lab
docs.text:
nomad lab edits these settings in nomad.toml for you: it backs up the file first, keeps its comments, and writes nothing that doesn't read back as intended. Each command shows the change; --apply writes it.

nomad lab show [LAB]
nomad lab add-machine LAB HOST          a workstation collected here, tagged with the lab
nomad lab add-nas LAB HOST [--name NAME] [--note "..."] [--type zfs|nfs] [--path P]
                                        a NAS collected here (its pools), listed as the lab's
nomad lab add-storage LAB SERVER[:/export] [--name NAME] [--note "..."]
                                        storage the lab's machines mount, listed as the lab's
nomad lab name LAB "NAME"               how the lab is shown, e.g. "Smith Lab"
nomad lab lead LAB NETID [--remove]     NETID leads LAB too (or no longer)
nomad lab assistant LAB NETID [--remove]
                                        NETID is a research assistant of LAB (or no longer)
nomad lab hide LAB [--remove]           LAB is never a lab, not shown (or a lab again)
nomad lab remove LAB HOST

For storage that is everyone's, LAB is shared: nomad lab add-nas shared HOST --note "community $HOME" collects it and names it, listed for no lab. It stays collected when a lab that also lists it removes it.

LAB is the PI's NetID when group_pattern is set (jdoe is jdoe$ with "{netid}$"), or the lab's group itself.

  • add-machine goes on the host that collects the workstation (a lab's own head node, or the hub for a lab without one). It turns the workstation collector on there if needed, and says whether the host answers over SSH with a key.
  • add-nas is for a NAS the storage collector reads over SSH: pool health, and the space users have (each pool's root dataset, so RAIDZ parity isn't counted; a boot pool isn't storage). A host listed as a workstation moves to storage. It says whether cron on this host runs the storage collector.
  • add-storage goes on the Console's machine: an export the lab's machines mount, or a server, with an optional name and note for the server.
  • lead goes on the Console's machine: someone besides the PI who leads the lab (a co-PI, a lab manager, a test account) sees its machines and, one by one, its members. LAB may also be the lab's name as nomad lab show prints it, and must be a lab nomad knows (listed machines or storage, tagged workstations, or members in the groups data) unless --new-group is given: a mistyped NetID could be another PI's lab. It writes [console.labs.leads]; a leads = {} line in [console.labs], as in nomad.toml.example, becomes that table. Editing leads by hand risks setting it twice, which makes the whole file unreadable. The PI group_pattern names needs no entry.
  • assistant goes on the Console's machine: a research assistant sees the lab as its PI does while one of its members (above). LAB as for lead, and a lab by nomad's rules (above), not just any group with members; taking a name off works for any. It says how many members the lab has, and when NETID isn't one of them in the groups data now (the entry applies once they are), and writes [console.labs.assistants], which goes when its last name does. Like leads, the table is written whole: comments inside it aren't kept, and an entry nomad can't read is left for a person to fix first.
  • hide goes on the Console's machine: LAB is not a lab (above), so the Console doesn't show it; nothing on the clusters changes. It writes the not_labs = [...] line of [console.labs] on one line (a list spread over several lines is left to change by hand), says when nomad knows no such group here (a mistyped name hides nothing; --db gives the groups data when nomad can't find it), and --remove makes it a lab again. A group nomad knows by that very name (research, a workstation tag) is taken as it is, not as a PI's NetID; LAB may also be the lab's name as nomad lab show prints it ("Smith Lab"). nomad lab show lists them.
  • remove takes a host out of a lab: no longer collected here, no longer listed.

A workstation's lab travels with its data, so it is added where it is collected; storage listings and server names are read on the Console's machine. On a hub that also collects a lab, one command does all of it.

nomad console roles shows what the file grants, and anything wrong in it; nomad console roles NETID shows what that person would see, with each lab's size, and whether each of their machines is online (and when it last was) or whether each storage export is mounted and responding, by server (with its name and note), with its space when the lab machines report it: percent used, used of total and free, in decimal units (those of df -H), and for exports of one pool "free space shared with ..." and a line with their space together (see docs/collectors.md, Workstation mounts), and for a NAS the storage collector reads, its state, space and pools' health. A machine or NAS whose latest record is over an hour old shows as "no report since ..."; a workstation with no record in two days no longer counts as its lab's. A machine known only by its tag is marked [tagged] (--db for the database holding group membership, such as the hub's combined database; --mask for counts only).

docs.title: Courses: nomad course
docs.text:
A course is a Unix group (demo101, say), a software environment, or both. Its instructors see it in nomad facts course (and the Console): the class this term, each student as a row, when the class works. Nothing is a course until [console.courses] is there: a site that hasn't said how its classes work gets no course view rather than a wrong one. nomad course setup asks, showing what it finds here for each answer.

[console.courses]
sources = ["groups", "environments"]     # how classes get access (below)
pattern = "^[a-z]{2,6}[0-9]{3}[a-z]?$"   # which groups and environments are courses, by name
faculty_group = "faculty"                # whose members can teach one
term_start = "2026-08-24"                # this term's first day
min_students = 0                         # fewer students this term: counts only
names = false                            # instructors see students by name
not_teaching = ["jdoe"]                  # in the faculty group, teaches no course (staff)

[console.courses.groups."demo101"]
name = "Econometrics"
instructors = ["jdoe"]                   # teaches it every term
exclude = ["asmith"]                     # in the group and faculty, never teaches it
environments = ["datakit"]              # whoever used it this term is in the class

[console.courses.groups."demo101".terms."2026-08-24"]
instructors = ["bsmith"]                 # teaches it this term
exclude = ["cjones"]                     # doesn't teach it this term

[console.courses.groups."lab201"]
course = false                           # named like a course, but isn't one
  • How classes get access differs from one institution to the next; sources says which of these happen here (default ["groups"]):
  • groups: a Unix group per course, named for it. A group whose name matches pattern is a course; its members are the course's people.
  • environments: a software environment per course, a conda environment or a Jupyter kernel named for it. The interactive servers record which environment each session runs from (nomad 1.12.5; environment_patterns under the interactive collector, collectors), and whether it is the person's own (they own it, or keep it in their home): anyone can name one like a course, so a session from one's own counts only for a faculty member (an instructor who built their course's). An environment named like a course group (pattern) counts for that course: whoever used it this term, on two days or more, is one of its members, whatever groups they are in. Shared software is named like courses too (py311, cuda121): an environment with no group of its name is a course only when listed (nomad course env NAME NAME).
  • own_groups: an instructor's own group (jdoe$, by [console.labs] group_pattern) holds their class. Such a group is often their lab too, so none becomes a course by itself: nomad course discover proposes the ones with people active this term, and one becomes a course when someone is added to it. A course this term, it is not their lab that term (see the PI under Console access): add one that mostly holds a class.

Whatever the sources, a group listed under groups is a course (unless course = false), and a course's environments add whoever used them this term to its students (nomad course env GROUP ENV): for a class whose environment isn't named like its course. They add no one to choose its instructors among: an environment two courses share says who is in a class, not who teaches it (its users are students of both). An environment listed under a course counts for that course, not as one of its own. Environments are listed for good; a group listed only by a term's decisions (someone added to an instructor's own group for a term) is a course that term only. - A course's instructors this term, in this order: 1. anyone listed (nomad course add), this term or every term. When anyone is, they alone teach it that term: nothing below adds anyone, and nobody is asked about it in the Console. A group reused from an earlier term keeps that term's instructor among its members, so adding this term's takes the earlier one out; list a co-instructor or a TA too; 2. otherwise, of its members in faculty_group (its group's, and whoever used the environment named for it), those who said in the Console that they teach it this term (nomad course answers); 3. when none has, its one faculty member, when it has one; 4. when it has several, those who joined its group this term; 5. when none did, those who used its environment this term; 6. when none did, those active this term where the course's students work (the servers and clusters most of its active students used: research on another cluster says nothing about a course).

Groups are reused term after term and nobody takes last term's instructor out; when nothing above settles it, nomad can't tell who teaches it, and nobody does until someone says so or is added. Left out: anyone excluded from the group (nomad course exclude), this term or every term; anyone who said they don't teach it this term; anyone in not_teaching (staff in the faculty group, old accounts, people who retired; nomad course not-teaching) unless added to the course by name. nomad.toml wins over what people said, and both over nomad's guess. A course with no instructor is shown to no one; nomad course list names those last. - Decisions hold for a term. Who teaches a course changes from term to term, so nomad course add and exclude write under the term's own table and stop applying when term_start moves on (they stay in nomad.toml as a record); --every-term writes them for good. So do the answers people give in the Console: each is for one term. - term_start must move on. When it is set, a new term begins only when it is changed (nomad course setup --term-start YYYY-MM-DD); nomad course list says when the calendar's term has moved past it. Left unset, it is the Monday on or after 15 August, 1 January or 1 June (a US academic calendar); set it to the first day of classes, or the weeks before would count in each student's range as weeks of nothing. - Activity is a person's, not a course's: a faculty member active this term where a course's students work counts in every group of several they are in, and one who teaches without using the server is left out. nomad course list shows why each instructor is there; check it once a term. course add takes no one off. Join dates say more than activity: an instructor added to a reused group shows as joined that term (a membership nomad saw before 1.11, on any site, has no date); someone added only for access counts as joined too: exclude them. - What people say is kept beside the hub's combined database (course_answers.db, readable by its owner only), not in nomad.toml. Only the course's faculty members can answer (in its group, or a user of the environment named for it; not those excluded, staff, or those already added by name); nomad course answer GROUP NETID --yes|--no|--clear records an answer someone gave you another way. - Its students are its other people; of those, this term's joined its group since term_start or used an interactive server or a cluster since then (groups nobody prunes keep earlier terms' students). For a course whose class is in its environment rather than its group -- more of the environment's users are outside the group than the group has students who joined or were active this term; or, early in a term, a faculty member outside the group uses it, none of the group's does, and fewer than half the group's active students do -- the environment says it: this term's students joined its group this term or used its environment, an earlier student's work this term in another class doesn't count, and its group's faculty members count only if they joined it this term or used the environment (left out otherwise: not last term's instructor shown this term's class). One outsider in a course's kernel changes nothing. nomad records when a membership began from 1.11 on; before that, a member who hasn't been active this term can't be told from an earlier term's, and is left out (and counted as such). - A group named like a course that isn't one (a project's or a lab's) is marked course = false (nomad course ignore GROUP): otherwise every faculty member in it would see its other members as a class. nomad course list shows every group taken for a course. - min_students defaults to 0: a small institution's course may have three students. With so few, even figures for the class together are close to each student's, and unnamed rows are not anonymous to someone who knows the class. names (default false) decides whether instructors see each student by name: both are for the institution to decide (FERPA).

A faculty member who used the environment named for a course on two days or more this term is among those it chooses its instructors from when they are in its group, or when its class is in the environment (above); with several, those who used it count as teaching it. A faculty member outside a course's group who used its environment counts only when people besides faculty outside the group used it too (a colleague who borrowed a group course's kernel is not one). nomad course list shows why; exclude whoever doesn't teach it. Its students' figures are all their work this term, as for a group's students, not only in its environment.

nomad course discover (read-only) lists what may be a course that nomad.toml doesn't say is one yet: each environment people had a session in this term (how many, the faculty members among them, the course it counts for, the group most of its users are in), and groups with a faculty member and at least three people active this term besides faculty (whose own group each is, and the environment most of them used). Then what to do, as commands that each show their change first: environments named like a course group (setup --sources ...,environments), one named like a course with no group (course env NAME NAME), an environment four in five of whose users are in a course's group (course env), an instructor's own group whose people are active (course add, for this term, when own_groups is a source). Nothing for an environment several faculty members use: that is shared software, not a class's. --mask numbers groups, environments and NetIDs. Run it a week or two into a term.

nomad course setup in a terminal with no setting given asks: how classes get access (the sources, with how many groups and environments here are named like a course and how many instructors' own groups have people active), which names are courses' (and what they match), the faculty group (and its size), the term's first day, min_students and names; then shows how many courses those settings make, what discover would suggest, and what would change, and asks before writing (--apply: without asking). Each setting is also an option (--sources groups,environments), for scripts; --ask asks even then.

nomad course setup                           turn courses on: asks how classes get access
nomad course setup --term-start 2026-08-24   start a new term (or --sources, --pattern, ...)
nomad course discover                        what here may be a course, and what to do
nomad course list                            each course: instructors (and why), students
nomad course env GROUP ENV [--remove]        whoever used environment ENV is in GROUP's class
nomad course add GROUP NETID                 NETID teaches GROUP this term
nomad course exclude GROUP NETID             in GROUP and faculty, not teaching it this term
                                             (add, exclude: --every-term for good)
nomad course remove GROUP NETID              off either list
nomad course name GROUP "Econometrics"       how the course is shown
nomad course ignore GROUP [--undo]           named like a course, but isn't one
nomad course not-teaching NETID [--undo]     in the faculty group, teaches no course
nomad course answers                         what faculty members said this term
nomad course answer GROUP NETID --yes|--no   record what someone said

Like nomad lab, each change is shown first and written with --apply, after a backup, only if the file still reads back as intended.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text: Variable Description NOMAD_CONFIG Config file path NOMAD_DB Database path NOMAD_LOG_LEVEL Log level (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR) NOMAD_CONSOLE_HOST The machine serving the Console, for nomad console NOMAD_LOGIN_HOST This cluster's name as people's computers reach it, for nomad console

docs.title: Collectors
docs.text: See ARCHITECTURE.md for detailed collector documentation.

docs.title: Console access
docs.text: The Console, NØMAÐ's web interface, listens only on the machine that serves it (127.0.0.1:8000 by default). Nothing on the network can reach it directly, and that is deliberate: the Console asks for passwords, and until it sits behind HTTPS they must not cross the network where they could be read. People reach it through an SSH tunnel instead, which encrypts everything, passwords included.

docs.title: Opening it from your own computer
docs.text:
Run this on the computer you are sitting at, the one with the browser:

nomad console launch NETID@console-host.example.edu

It opens the tunnel, waits until the Console answers through it, and opens your browser. Keep the window open while you use the Console; press Ctrl-C to close the tunnel. ssh asks for your password itself; nomad never sees it.

When the Console's machine can only be reached through another one (a lab workstation, a gateway), go through that one with --via:

nomad console launch NETID@console-host --via NETID@gateway

The machine names of the last launch that worked are remembered (~/.config/nomad/console_launch.json), so next time nomad console launch alone is enough.

Option --via [USER@]HOST Go through this machine first (ssh's -J). --port N Port on this computer. Default: the Console's own number (8000) if free here, else any free port. --remote-port N The Console's port on its machine (default 8000). --no-browser Don't open the browser; only print the address. --print Only print the ssh command, to run it by hand.

docs.title: What it needs
docs.text:
• An ssh client. macOS and Linux have one; on Windows 10 and 11, add OpenSSH Client under Settings › System › Optional features.
  • An account that can log in to the Console's machine. It can be a tunnel-only one (below).
  • nomad itself: pip install nomad-hpc (Python 3.10 or later). That brings NumPy, pandas and SciPy along. A computer that only needs the launcher can use the single file nomad/console/launch.py instead, with Python 3.8 or later: python3 launch.py NETID@console-host (on Windows, py launch.py ...).

docs.title: By hand
docs.text:
nomad console launch --print shows the same tunnel as a command to type:

ssh -N -L 8000:localhost:8000 NETID@console-host

Then open http://localhost:8000. The launcher itself adds a few options: it keeps a connection of its own even when ~/.ssh/config shares connections (ControlMaster), binds the port to 127.0.0.1 only, and has ssh say when the tunnel is in place, so that it never mistakes another program on the same port for the Console.

docs.title: When it doesn't work
docs.text:
• ssh stopped (exit 255): ssh could not reach the machine or log in; its own message is printed above.
  • The tunnel is up, but nothing answers: the Console isn't running on that machine, or the machine doesn't allow a tunnel to that port.
  • Port N is already in use: leave out --port, or choose another.

Ctrl-C, closing the window, or ending the launcher with kill closes the tunnel. On Windows, ending Python from Task Manager does not: end ssh.exe there too, or use Ctrl-C.

docs.title: From a cluster
docs.text:
Typed in a shell on a cluster over SSH, nomad console (the same as nomad console launch) knows a browser there would not be on your screen, and prints the one line to run on your own computer, through the cluster:

$ nomad console
A browser started on spydur would not be on your screen. On your own computer, run:

    ssh -N nomad-console

It opens the Console in your browser; that window keeps it open, and Ctrl-C there closes it.

The first time on that computer (Mac or Linux), set it up once there with:

    bash -c "$(ssh NETID@spydur.example.edu /usr/local/sw/bin/nomad console --key-setup)"

and send the line it prints to your research computing contact.

Until then, or on Windows, this works with your password:

    ssh -N -L 8000:localhost:8000 ... -J NETID@spydur.example.edu NETID@console-host.example.edu
...

Your own computer then needs nothing but ssh.

docs.title: No password: a key for the Console
docs.text:
nomad console --key-setup prints a short bash script; the line above runs it on the person's own computer, fetched over ssh from the cluster (with $( ): in bash <( ) ssh runs in the background and can't ask for the password). It

  • makes a key just for the Console, ~/.ssh/nomad_console;
  • tries the Console's machine directly: when it answers, the entry goes straight there, otherwise through the cluster (and copies the key to the person's own account there, asking their password once);
  • puts a nomad-console entry first in ~/.ssh/config, keeping a copy of the old file and everything that was in it, after a Host * line (ssh takes the first value it finds for each setting); run again, it replaces its own entry;
  • prints the public key, for whoever adds Console keys on the server (below).

ssh -N nomad-console then opens the tunnel and, once it is up, the browser (open on a Mac, which keeps the key's passphrase in the Keychain; xdg-open on Linux). At a workstation's own screen, nomad console uses the key when there is one and otherwise says how to set it up. NOMAD_CONSOLE_CONTACT names who adds keys; NOMAD_COMMAND gives the shared nomad by its full path, since a command over ssh gets a shorter PATH than a login. Two names come from the environment, which a cluster's shared nomad command sets for everyone: NOMAD_CONSOLE_HOST (the machine that serves the Console) and NOMAD_LOGIN_HOST (the cluster, as people's computers reach it). --here opens the tunnel and browser on the cluster after all (a remote desktop, say).

A shared install is one virtual environment every user can read (for example /usr/local/sw/nomad) and a small nomad script on everyone's PATH:

#!/bin/bash
export NOMAD_CONSOLE_HOST="${NOMAD_CONSOLE_HOST:-console-host.example.edu}"
export NOMAD_LOGIN_HOST="${NOMAD_LOGIN_HOST:-cluster.example.edu}"
exec env -u PYTHONHOME -u PYTHONPATH /usr/local/sw/nomad/bin/nomad "$@"

Clearing PYTHONHOME and PYTHONPATH keeps a site's own Python settings (an Anaconda in the login scripts, say) from breaking nomad's environment. Users can run every command, but nomad's databases stay readable only by the account that collects them, so what anyone sees of other people goes through the Console's own scoping.

docs.title: On the server: accounts that may only open the tunnel
docs.text:
To let people open the Console without giving them a shell on its machine, sshd can limit everyone outside a group to this one tunnel. Put this block at the end of /etc/ssh/sshd_config; anything after it would belong to the Match:

Match Group *,!console-shell User *,!root
    AllowTcpForwarding local
    PermitOpen localhost:8000 127.0.0.1:8000
    PermitTTY no
    X11Forwarding no
    AllowAgentForwarding no
    AllowStreamLocalForwarding no
    PermitTunnel no
    GatewayPorts no
    ForceCommand echo "This login is for the NOMAD Console tunnel only."

Members of console-shell and root keep everything. Everyone else who can log in gets the tunnel to the Console and nothing more: no shell, no file copy, no other forwarding (including jumps through the machine).

Before reloading sshd:

  1. Create the group and add yourself and anyone who works on that machine or jumps through it: groupadd console-shell, gpasswd -a NAME console-shell.
  2. Check the file: sshd -t.
  3. Check what an account will get: sshd -T -C user=NAME,host=x,addr=127.0.0.1 | grep -E 'forcecommand|permitopen|permittty'. A group member shows forcecommand none and permittty yes.
  4. Reload, and keep a root session open until a new login works.

On a machine joined to the campus directory (sssd), this lets anyone with a campus account open the Console without an account being created for them; the Console's own login then decides what each person sees.

docs.title: Keys for those accounts
docs.text:
They can't write anything on the machine, so their keys come from a folder the admin keeps, in a second block after the first, with the same Match:

Match Group *,!console-shell User *,!root
    AuthorizedKeysFile /etc/ssh/nomad_keys/%u

/etc/ssh/nomad_keys is root's (mode 755), one file per account (644). Each key line starts with options that hold it to the tunnel even without the block above:

restrict,port-forwarding,permitopen="localhost:8000",permitopen="127.0.0.1:8000" ssh-ed25519 AAAA... nomad-console

A key in the account's own home is not read. Passwords keep working.

docs.title: Later: a web address
docs.text: The tunnel is the way in until the Console sits behind HTTPS on a named host: a reverse proxy with a certificate, ideally with campus single sign-on. Then people open an address and nothing needs installing.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text: The NØMAÐ dashboard provides real-time monitoring of your HPC cluster(s).

docs.title: Launching
docs.text:
nomad dashboard

Open http://localhost:8050 in your browser.

docs.title: Cluster Tabs
docs.text: Per-cluster views showing: - Node status (idle, allocated, down) - Partition utilization - CPU and memory pressure indicators - Active jobs count

docs.title: Network
docs.text: 3D job similarity network visualization: - Jobs as nodes, colored by health - Edges connect similar jobs - "Safe zone" and "danger zone" regions emerge from data - Failure clustering analysis

docs.title: Resources
docs.text: Resource usage views for administrators: - CPU hours by cluster/group - Filter by cluster, group, and time period - Resource consumption patterns - Quietest hours for job scheduling

docs.title: Activity
docs.text: Job activity and history: - Recent job completions - Failed job categories - Interactive session monitoring (RStudio/Jupyter)

docs.title: Planned Features
docs.text: • Education Tab: Visual proficiency trajectories and per-student breakdowns (CLI available now via nomad edu)

docs.title: Remote Access
docs.text:
By default, the dashboard only listens on localhost. For remote access:

  1. SSH Tunnel (simple): 

       ssh -L 8050:localhost:8050 user@hpc-head

  2. Reverse Proxy (production): See System Install

docs.title: GPU Panel
docs.text: The node detail panel shows GPU metrics for any node with NVIDIA GPUs.

docs.title: nvidia-smi utilization
docs.text: The primary GPU utilization bar reflects the kernel-launch duty cycle reported by nvidia-smi. This is the standard metric available on all NVIDIA GPU nodes.

docs.title: Real Utilization (DCGM)
docs.text:
When DCGM is active on a node, a second bar labeled Real Util appears below the nvidia-smi bar. Real Utilization is a weighted composite of pipeline activity counters (SM, Tensor, DRAM, GR engine) that reflects what the GPU is actually computing, not just whether any kernel is scheduled.

A significant gap between nvidia-smi utilization and Real Util is a signal worth investigating — see GPU Monitoring.

docs.title: Workload badge
docs.text: A color-coded badge below the utilization bars shows the dominant workload category for the node's GPUs: tensor-heavy compute, FP64 / HPC compute, memory-bound, compute-active, idle, and others. Colors follow the Okabe-Ito colorblind-safe palette. See Workload Classification for the full category definitions.

docs.title: Health indicator
docs.text: A WARN, HOT, or CRIT badge appears next to the GPU name when hardware health issues are detected via DCGM (PCIe replay errors, high temperature, ECC errors, or row remap failures). No badge means OK.

docs.title: DCGM pill
docs.text: A small DCGM pill next to the GPU name indicates that enhanced metrics are active for that node. Nodes without DCGM show the nvidia-smi bar only and no badge or Real Util row.

docs.title: Developer Toolchain
docs.text: The nomad dev command family provides scaffolding, validation, and contribution tools for NØMAÐ module development. It codifies architectural patterns into CLI tools so contributors focus on logic, not plumbing.

docs.title: Philosophy
docs.text:
• Codify patterns, don't document them. The scaffolding tool enforces correct structure rather than relying on contributors to read a wiki.
  • Lower the barrier to the creative work. Plumbing (file creation, registration, wiring, test boilerplate) is identical for every module of the same type. The toolchain handles all plumbing so the contributor focuses on implementation.
  • Quality by construction. Rather than catching problems in code review, prevent them from being created. Every scaffolded module comes with tests, documentation stubs, proper registration, and linting compliance built in.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# First-time setup (installs ruff, pytest, pre-commit hooks)
nomad dev setup

# Interactive wizard — walks you through everything
nomad dev guide

# Direct scaffolding if you know what you want
nomad dev new collector zfs

# Validate your work
nomad dev check

# Submit when ready
nomad dev submit

docs.title: nomad dev guide
docs.text:
Interactive contribution wizard. Asks what you want to build, gathers parameters, scaffolds the module, and provides step-by-step next instructions.

Supports 8 module types:

Type Description Example collector Gather metrics from a new data source nomad dev new collector zfs command Add a user-facing CLI command nomad dev new command topology analysis Add analytical capability nomad dev new analysis spectral metric Add to nomad dyn nomad dev new metric resilience view Add a dashboard visualization nomad dev new view network_health page Add a Console feature nomad dev new page ecosystem alert Add a new alerting mechanism nomad dev new alert pagerduty insight Add to the Insight Engine nomad dev new insight disk_community

docs.title: nomad dev new <type> <name>
docs.text:
Direct scaffolding for experienced contributors. Creates:

  • Source file with proper base class inheritance and method stubs
  • Database schema (collectors)
  • Test file with test stubs for each expected behavior
  • Configuration template
  • Next-step instructions with references to similar modules

docs.title: nomad dev check
docs.text:
Validates codebase structural integrity:

  • Module Registration — all modules imported and registered
  • Test Coverage — every module has a test file
  • Documentation — docstrings present, reference entries exist
  • Code Quality — ruff linting
  • Architecture Consistency — base class inheritance, Click patterns
  • Integration Points — schemas, alerts, insights wired
  • Config Consistency — all sections have matching modules

Options:

nomad dev check              # Standard check
nomad dev check --fix        # Auto-fix registration issues
nomad dev check --strict     # Treat warnings as errors (for CI/CD)
nomad dev check --module zfs # Check only a specific module (fast)
nomad dev check -f json      # JSON output

docs.title: nomad dev test
docs.text:
Targeted testing with git-aware file detection.

nomad dev test                    # Test only changed files (default)
nomad dev test all                # Full test suite
nomad dev test collector zfs      # Test specific module
nomad dev test collectors         # Test all collectors
nomad dev test changed            # Explicit: test what changed since last commit
nomad dev test --coverage         # Show coverage report

docs.title: nomad dev status
docs.text: Shows current branch, changes from main, and readiness for submission: check results, test collection status, and ahead/behind count.

docs.title: nomad dev submit
docs.text:
Full contribution pipeline:

  1. Runs nomad dev check --strict
  2. Runs test suite
  3. Runs ruff linting
  4. Analyzes changes, detects contribution type
  5. Creates branch, commits, pushes
  6. Opens PR (or generates patch file with --patch)

Authentication tiers:

  • Institutional token in nomad.toml — seamless submission
  • Personal token in ~/.config/nomad/dev.toml — set up via nomad dev setup
  • Browser fallback — opens GitHub with fields pre-filled
  • Patch export — nomad dev submit --patch for email-based contribution

docs.title: nomad dev setup
docs.text:
One-time environment configuration:

  1. GitHub token (fine-grained, with Contents + PRs + Issues permissions)
  2. Development dependencies (ruff, pytest, pytest-cov)
  3. Pre-commit hooks (ruff check + module validation on changed files)

docs.title: nomad dev bump
docs.text:
Version management:

nomad dev bump patch    # 1.2.5 -> 1.2.6
nomad dev bump minor    # 1.2.5 -> 1.3.0
nomad dev bump major    # 1.2.5 -> 2.0.0
nomad dev bump patch --dry-run  # Show what would change

Updates pyproject.toml, __version__, CHANGELOG, and creates a git tag.

docs.title: nomad dev deps
docs.text:
Module dependency graph — shows upstream dependencies, downstream dependents, and related modules:

nomad dev deps collector disk

docs.title: Scaffolding Templates
docs.text: Each module type has a template that embodies NØMAÐ's architectural patterns.

docs.title: Collector Template
docs.text:
Every scaffolded collector includes:

  • BaseCollector subclass with collect(), store(), get_history() stubs
  • @registry.register decorator
  • Metric definitions
  • Dependency checking (for external packages)
  • SQL schema file
  • Config template for nomad.toml
  • 6 test stubs (init, collect, parse, store, config, error handling)

docs.title: CLI Command Template
docs.text:
• Click decorators with --format (table/json/plain) and --no-color flags
  • Pass-through context for config access
  • 4 test stubs (default, options, format, error)

docs.title: Analysis Module Template
docs.text:
• Result dataclass with to_dict() and to_narrative()
  • Alert integration via to_alert()
  • Insight Engine integration via to_insight()
  • 4 test stubs (known input, edge cases, alert, insight)

docs.title: Dynamics Metric Template
docs.text:
• compute(), trend(), to_insight(), visualize() methods
  • CLI registration for nomad dyn <name>
  • 4 test stubs (compute, trend, insight, edge cases)

docs.title: CI/CD Integration
docs.text:
Use nomad dev check --strict in your CI pipeline to enforce quality:

# GitHub Actions example
- name: NØMAÐ codebase validation
  run: |
    nomad dev check --strict
    nomad dev test all --coverage

Pre-commit hooks (installed by nomad dev setup) run ruff and module validation automatically before each commit.

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text: The nomad diag commands provide targeted analysis for common HPC issues, helping administrators quickly identify root causes of performance problems.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
nomad diag network    # Network performance analysis
nomad diag storage    # Storage health and I/O patterns
nomad diag node       # Node-level resource bottlenecks
nomad diag workstation HOST   # A departmental workstation's latest reading

docs.title: Network Diagnostics
docs.text:
Analyze network performance between nodes. 

nomad diag network
nomad diag network --src node01 --dst node02
nomad diag network --threshold 100   # Flag if <100 MB/s

docs.title: What It Checks
docs.text:
• Bandwidth: Measures throughput between node pairs
  • Latency: Round-trip time for packets
  • Packet loss: Percentage of dropped packets
  • Path analysis: Identifies bottleneck links

The network collector pings every run. It measures throughput (and the TCP retransmits during it) only with throughput = true under [collectors.network_perf], at most hourly, with iperf3 -s (or ssh) at the far end. Without it the diagnostic says "Throughput Not Measured" rather than showing 0 Mbps as a reading, and it shows the last measured throughput when the newest row is ping only.

docs.title: Output Example
docs.text:
Network Diagnostics Report
======================================================================

Path Analysis: node01 -> node02
  Hops: 2 (node01 -> switch01 -> node02)
  Latency: 0.3ms (excellent)
  Bandwidth: 9.2 Gbps (92% of 10G link)
  Packet Loss: 0.00%

Path Analysis: node01 -> storage01
  Hops: 3 (node01 -> switch01 -> switch02 -> storage01)
  Latency: 0.8ms (good)
  Bandwidth: 4.1 Gbps (41% of 10G link)  [!] Below expected
  Packet Loss: 0.01%

Summary:
  Total paths tested: 12
  Degraded paths: 1
  Recommendation: Check switch02 port utilization

docs.title: Storage Diagnostics
docs.text:
Examine storage health and I/O patterns. 

nomad diag storage
nomad diag storage --path /home
nomad diag storage --detailed

docs.title: What It Checks
docs.text:
• NFS performance: Read/write throughput, latency
  • Disk utilization: Space usage, inode counts
  • I/O patterns: Sequential vs random, read/write ratio
  • Queue depth: Outstanding I/O requests
  • Error rates: Failed operations, retries
  • Fill rate: growth by least squares over daily averages, from at least a week of readings in the last 30 days, and the days until full at that rate: under 30 days is noted, under 14 is flagged, under 3 is high. A server read for less than a week has no fill rate.

docs.title: Output Example
docs.text:
Storage Diagnostics Report
======================================================================

/home (NFS: storage01:/export/home)
  Capacity: 45.2 TB / 100 TB (45%)
  Inodes: 12M / 50M (24%)
  Read throughput: 850 MB/s (good)
  Write throughput: 420 MB/s (good)
  Latency: 2.1ms avg, 15ms p99
  Active clients: 47

/scratch (NFS: storage02:/export/scratch)
  Capacity: 82.1 TB / 100 TB (82%)  [!] High utilization
  Inodes: 45M / 50M (90%)  [!] Critical
  Read throughput: 1.2 GB/s (excellent)
  Write throughput: 180 MB/s  [!] Degraded
  Latency: 8.3ms avg, 250ms p99  [!] High latency spikes
  Active clients: 89

Recommendations:
  - /scratch approaching inode limit - clean old files
  - /scratch write performance degraded - check ZFS pool status

docs.title: Node Diagnostics
docs.text:
Drill into node-level resource bottlenecks. 

nomad diag node
nomad diag node gpu-01
nomad diag node --all

docs.title: What It Checks
docs.text:
• CPU: Utilization, load average, steal time
  • Memory: Usage, swap activity, OOM events
  • GPU: Utilization, temperature, memory, errors
  • I/O: Wait percentage, disk throughput
  • Network: Interface utilization, errors

docs.title: Output Example
docs.text:
Node Diagnostics: gpu-03
======================================================================

CPU
  Utilization: 78% (32/40 cores active)
  Load Average: 28.5, 27.2, 25.8
  Steal Time: 0.0%
  Status: [OK] Normal

Memory
  Used: 187 GB / 256 GB (73%)
  Swap: 2.1 GB / 32 GB (6%)  [!] Swap activity detected
  OOM Events (24h): 0
  Status: [!] Monitor swap usage

GPU (4x NVIDIA A100)
  GPU 0: 92% util, 68C, 38/40 GB mem
  GPU 1: 88% util, 65C, 35/40 GB mem
  GPU 2: 0% util, 42C, 0/40 GB mem  [!] Idle
  GPU 3: 95% util, 71C, 39/40 GB mem
  ECC Errors: 0
  Status: [!] GPU 2 underutilized

I/O
  Wait: 3.2%
  Read: 450 MB/s
  Write: 120 MB/s
  Status: [OK] Normal

Recommendations:
  - Swap activity on memory-bound workload - consider job memory limits
  - GPU 2 idle while others near capacity - check job GPU allocation

docs.title: Workstation Diagnostics
docs.text:
A workstation's latest reading from the workstation collector, judged; the Console's Workstation Diagnostic panel shows the same. 

nomad diag workstation labws1

docs.title: What It Checks
docs.text:
• Memory: above 85% used is flagged, above 95% critical
  • Local disk: above 85% is flagged, above 95% critical
  • Load: above the core count is flagged, above twice the core count critical
  • Swap: more than 1 GB in use
  • Zombie processes: any; more than 10 is flagged as many
  • Not reporting: the latest reading is more than an hour old
  • Incomplete reading: a figure the collector couldn't read (it stores zeros when a command fails on the machine) is named as missing, not passed as 0%

The last day's readings are summarized (samples, average load and memory, most users). They are not judged for trends: readings five minutes apart are too noisy for a slope and acceleration from the last three.

docs.title: Common Options
docs.text:
All nomad diag commands support:

Option Description --db PATH Specify database path --json Output as JSON --quiet Minimal output (exit code only) -v, --verbose Detailed output

docs.title: Exit Codes
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 All checks passed 1 Warnings detected 2 Critical issues found 3 Error running diagnostics

Useful for scripting and automated monitoring.

docs.title: System Dynamics
docs.text:
The nomad dyn command family applies quantitative frameworks from ecology and economics to research computing resource usage patterns.

Every command takes --db PATH, --hours N and --site NAME. On a hub's combined database (nomad sync), --site reads one site through read-only views; nothing is copied. A combined database needs --site: pooling sites mixes their nodes and jobs (two sites' node01 become one node flapping between states).

docs.title: Full Summary
docs.text:
nomad dyn summary --db nomad.db
nomad dyn summary --db ~/.local/share/nomad/combined.db --site spydur
Generates a comprehensive narrative combining all dynamics metrics.

docs.title: Diversity
docs.text:
nomad dyn diversity --by user --hours 720
nomad dyn diversity --by group
nomad dyn diversity --by partition
Computes Simpson's and Shannon diversity indices over people, research groups, or partitions.

Simpson's D = 1 - sum(p_i^2) — probability that two randomly chosen jobs belong to different categories.

Shannon H' = -sum(p_i * ln(p_i)) — information-theoretic uncertainty about category membership.

Pielou's J = H' / ln(S) — evenness of distribution across categories.

When one category holds more than 60% of the jobs, the result says so ("One person accounts for 94% of the 7,946 jobs in this window"). The trend leaves out weekly windows with fewer than 20 jobs; with fewer than three left it is "too few weeks", not "stable".

docs.title: Niche Overlap
docs.text:
nomad dyn niche --hours 720
Measures pairwise resource usage overlap between research groups using Pianka's overlap index. Needs a group per job (below).

docs.title: Carrying Capacity
docs.text:
nomad dyn capacity
Multi-dimensional capacity: CPU cores and memory allocated on the nodes that can take jobs (allocated ÷ what they have, per snapshot), GPU utilization as measured, the busiest disk's utilization (an average over every disk hides the one that is saturated), and queue pressure (pending jobs per running job, 3 counted as full). Each is averaged per hour; "current" is the latest hour.

The busiest resource is named; it is called the binding constraint only at 75% or more (BINDING_AT). At 28% nothing binds. The queue is shown but never binds: pending jobs include held, dependent and throttled ones.

docs.title: Resilience
docs.text:
nomad dyn resilience
Recovery time after disturbances: a node going down or stopping to respond, and hours when jobs failed at more than twice the usual rate (with at least 10 jobs and 5 failures in the hour; an hour with fewer jobs ends a spike, and one still running at the end of the window is reported as ongoing). Node states are read as whole Slurm tokens, so POWERED_DOWN is a cloud node at rest and IDLE* is not responding. With fewer than four recovered events the trend is "too few events", not "stable".

Drains are listed but not scored. Most are an administrator taking a node out on purpose — maintenance, vendor repair — and scoring them made planned work look like fragility. With no node states or jobs to read, the score is empty ("nothing to read"), not 100.

docs.title: Externality
docs.text:
nomad dyn externality --hours 720
Looks for pairs of groups where one group's resource use rises and falls with another group's failure rate (failed, node failure, out of time or memory; cancelled jobs left out), over at least 12 shared hours. A correlation, not proof that one causes the other. Needs a group per job (below).

docs.title: Groups need a group per job
docs.text:
Diversity by group, niche overlap and externalities count jobs per group. Joining jobs to group_membership by username counts a job once for every group its owner belongs to: on one real cluster 7,946 jobs became 38,971 rows, groups sharing one busy member looked identical (overlap 1.00), and group-to-group correlations were drawn from the same jobs counted several times.

So these analyses run only when each job can be placed in one group (nomad.dynamics.attribution):

  1. the job records a group itself — an account column on jobs, or group_name — when at least two groups of two or more people hold 80% of the jobs and no single one covers more than 80% of the people (a catch-all Unix group such as people, or one private group per user, says nothing). nomad's job collector does not record the Slurm account on jobs yet; or
  2. membership is unambiguous — everyone who ran jobs belongs to at most one research group (leaving out umbrella groups that hold more than 80% of users), there are at least two groups of two or more people, and they account for 80% of the jobs.

Otherwise the result is available: false with the reason, for example: "Jobs don't record a group, and 12 of the 40 people who ran jobs in the last 12 weeks belong to more than one group, so their jobs can't be placed in one. Group views need a group per job, such as a Slurm account." The reason names the period it counts: diversity by group places jobs over its trend windows (12 weeks by default), the other analyses over the window asked for. Diversity by person is always computed.

In Python, attribution="membership" forces the old join for callers that want it knowingly; the reason then says how many people are counted once per group.

docs.title: JSON
docs.text: nomad dyn summary --json (and DynamicsEngine(...).to_dict()) returns diversity (by group, with available and reason), diversity_by_user, niche, capacity (with binding_constraint, busiest), resilience (with counted_events, drains), externality, attribution, site and hours.

docs.title: Theoretical Foundation
docs.text: These metrics are adapted from ecological and economic frameworks for their mathematical properties, not as ontological claims. Users are intentional agents shaped by decisions and incentives, not natural selection. See Tonini (2026), Ecological, Economic, and Governance Metrics for Research Computing.

docs.title: Educational Analytics
docs.text: NØMAÐ Edu bridges the gap between infrastructure monitoring and educational outcomes, helping instructors, mentors, and users track the development of computational proficiency.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Traditional HPC metrics tell you what happened. NØMAÐ Edu tells you how well users are learning to use HPC effectively.

Use cases:

  • Instructors: Track class-wide skill development, identify struggling students
  • Research mentors: Monitor graduate student onboarding progress
  • HPC staff: Evaluate workshop and training effectiveness
  • Users: Self-assess and improve HPC practices

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# Explain a job with proficiency scores and recommendations
nomad edu explain 12345

# Track a user's improvement over time
nomad edu trajectory alice

# Generate a report for a course or research group
nomad edu report cs301

# Your own jobs: score, trend and what to change
nomad edu me

docs.title: nomad edu explain
docs.text:
Analyze a single job with proficiency scores and actionable recommendations. 

nomad edu explain <job_id> [options]

Options:

Option Description --db PATH Database path (default: configured DB) --json Output as JSON --no-progress Skip historical comparison

Example output: 

  NØMAÐ Job Analysis — 1104
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  User: alice    Partition: compute    Node: node03
  State: COMPLETED    Runtime: 33h 38m / 48h 00m requested

  Proficiency Scores
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    CPU Efficiency       ██░░░░░░░░   22.6%   Needs Work
    Memory Efficiency    █████████░   90.4%   Excellent
    Time Estimation      ██████████   97.4%   Excellent
    I/O Awareness        ███████░░░   68.8%   Good
    ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    Overall Score        ███████░░░   69.8%   Good

  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

      Very low CPU utilization at 21% — requested 4
      cores but used ~1. This wastes resources and
      may delay other users' jobs.

          If your code is single-threaded, request 1 core.

  Your Progress (last 30 jobs)

    Memory Efficiency     90.0% →  90.4%  → stable

docs.text:
Track a user's proficiency development over time. 

nomad edu trajectory <username> [options]

Options:

Option Description --db PATH Database path --days N Lookback period (default: 90) --json Output as JSON

Example output:

  Stable proficiency

  Score Progression
