docs.title: nomad edu report
docs.text:
Generate aggregate reports for courses, research groups, or any Linux group. 

nomad edu report <group_name> [options]

Options:

Option Description --db PATH Database path --days N Lookback period (default: 90) --json Output as JSON

Example output: 

  NØMAÐ Group Report — cs101
  Last 90 days · 4 members · 4 ran jobs · 4 scored · 935 of 935 jobs measured · demo-cluster

  Median overall: 72/100 across 4 people (middle half 69–73)
  Over the period: 1 of 4 improved, 3 steady, 0 declined

  By dimension (median, people):
    CPU        51   (4)
    Memory     87   (4)
    Time       81   (4)
    I/O        69   (4)
    GPU        70   (4)

  Most common to work on:
    CPU: 4 of 4
    I/O: 2 of 4

  Member             Jobs  Measured  Overall  Change  Weakest
  diana               200       200       66      +1  I/O
  charlie             243       243       70      +9  CPU
  alice               260       260       73      +2  CPU
  bob                 232       232       73      -2  CPU

Every figure says how many people and jobs it rests on. A job counts when it finished in the period (completed, failed, timed out or ran out of memory) and is scored only when NØMAÐ measured it; members with no jobs are listed apart, never averaged in as zero. Figures over people are medians. "Change" compares a member's first and last week with measured jobs, and needs two such weeks.

The members are the group's members now, as nomad facts lab counts them: listed in the groups collector's latest run, with an account (1.17.8; before, anyone the group had ever listed); for a group with no one in it now the command says so. The Console shows the same report under the group's row on Groups.

docs.title: nomad edu me
docs.text:
Your own jobs over the last 90 days (--days N), scored by the same rules as nomad edu report: every finished job is counted, only jobs NØMAÐ measured are scored, the overall score is the mean of your dimension averages, and the trend compares your first and last week with measured jobs. Your line in a group report and this page therefore show the same numbers, and so do the Console's Trajectory and My Activity pages. With --detailed:

  Your NØMAÐ Profile — alice
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  25 jobs in the last 90 days, 15 measured and scored
  Overall score: 52 / 100  (improving, +6 since your first week)
  By dimension (average over measured jobs): CPU 43, memory 62, time 50

  Top issues across your measured jobs:
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

  [HIGH]     CPU Efficiency (spydur/basic) — ↑ improving
    5/7 jobs scored below threshold (avg score: 21.8)

    Your jobs:    request 8 (typical)
                  use 2.0 median (range 1.0–3.0 cores)
                  that's 25.0% utilization

    Try:          #SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
                  (or --ntasks=2, if the job runs several tasks: srun, MPI)

The CPU advice names the flag the jobs asked for their cores with: --cpus-per-task for -c (cores for one program), --ntasks for -n (several tasks: srun, MPI). nomad reads it from the submit command line and the jobs' steps; for a job whose #SBATCH lines are inside its script and that ran one task, it can't tell, and names --cpus-per-task with --ntasks as the other possibility.

An issue is listed when most of your measured jobs on a cluster and partition fall below the threshold for that dimension. --detailed adds the line with your score in each dimension; --json gives everything as JSON; admins can pass --user. With jobs but none measured, it says so instead of showing a score.

Each suggested value says where it comes from: for memory and time, how many of the flagged jobs it fits ("fits what each of the 5 flagged jobs used, with a 2x safety buffer"; for one job, "fits what the flagged job used"); for cores and GPUs, how many flagged jobs needed it, from what they used.

docs.title: Workstation sessions
docs.text:
Your workstation sessions of the last 7 days can add one piece of advice, listed first:

  • Memory: two or more sessions that used at least 80% of the workstation's memory for 12 hours or more, or ten or more that used that much at any length. Depending on the cluster's nodes it says to move to the cluster (a node with at least twice the peak), that the workstation is the right tool, or that the work is too big for both.
  • Long computation: sessions of 12 hours or more that kept at least half the workstation's cores (and at least 2) busy on average, adding up to a day or more. One long run counts. It says to run such work on the cluster, with a batch script sized from the session: cores it kept busy, twice its memory peak, and 1.5 times its length. A site without a cluster gets no such advice.

docs.title: Setting Up Groups
docs.text: NØMAÐ uses Linux groups for course/lab membership. To track a class:

docs.title: Option 1: Use existing Linux groups
docs.text:
If your users are already in groups (e.g., bio301, cs101): 

# Collect group membership
nomad collect -C groups --once

# Generate report
nomad edu report bio301

docs.title: Option 2: Create dedicated groups
docs.text:
# Create group for course
sudo groupadd cs301

# Add students
sudo usermod -aG cs301 student01
sudo usermod -aG cs301 student02
# ...

# Collect and report
nomad collect -C groups --once
nomad edu report cs301

docs.title: Option 3: Manual group file
docs.text:
Create a CSV file and import: 

username,group_name,gid,cluster
alice,cs301,3001,spydur
bob,cs301,3001,spydur

nomad edu import-groups groups.csv

docs.title: Dashboard Integration
docs.text:
The dashboard includes an Education tab showing:

  • Class-wide proficiency distributions
  • Individual student progress
  • Common problem areas
  • Improvement trends over time

Access via: nomad dashboard → Education tab

docs.title: For Instructors
docs.text:
1. Baseline early: Collect data from the first week to establish starting points
  2. Check weekly: Review group reports to identify struggling students early
  3. Focus on trends: Individual job scores vary; trajectories matter more
  4. Share reports: Let students see class-wide (anonymized) progress

docs.title: For Mentors
docs.text:
1. Onboarding checkpoint: Review trajectory after first 10 jobs
  2. Specific feedback: Use explain output to guide discussions
  3. Celebrate improvement: Recognize when dimensions improve

docs.title: For Users
docs.text:
1. Review failed jobs: Use explain to understand what went wrong
  2. Track your trajectory: Check weekly to see improvement
  3. Act on recommendations: The suggestions are data-driven

docs.title: Technical Details
docs.text:
For detailed information on how proficiency is computed:

  • Proficiency Scoring — Formulas, dimensions, and scoring rubrics
  • Database Schema — How scores are stored

docs.title: "Job not found in database"
docs.text:
Job 12345 not found in database.

Hint: Specify a database with --db or run 'nomad init' to configure.
  Example: nomad edu explain 12345 --db ~/nomad_demo.db

Solutions:

  1. Specify the database: nomad edu explain 12345 --db /path/to/db
  2. Run nomad init to configure the default database
  3. Ensure data collection is running: nomad collect

docs.title: "Not enough data for user"
docs.text: The user needs at least 3 completed jobs for trajectory analysis.

docs.title: "No data found for group"
docs.text:
Ensure group membership data has been collected: 

nomad collect -C groups --once

docs.title: Extending NØMAÐ-HPC
docs.text: This guide explains how to add new modules to NØMAÐ-HPC, including collectors, diagnostics, and alert backends.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                           NØMAÐ-HPC Architecture                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                         │

docs.title: Adding a New Collector
docs.text: Collectors gather metrics from various sources. All collectors inherit from BaseCollector.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Collector File
docs.text:
# Create new collector in nomad/collectors/
touch nomad/collectors/my_collector.py

docs.title: Step 2: Implement the Collector
docs.text:
"""
my_collector.py - Collect metrics from my data source
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional, Dict, Any
from .base import BaseCollector

@dataclass
class MyMetrics:
    """Data class for my metrics."""
    timestamp: str
    value: float
    status: str
    # Add your fields here

class MyCollector(BaseCollector):
    """Collector for my data source."""

    def __init__(self, config: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None):
        super().__init__(config)
        self.name = "my_collector"
        # Initialize any state

    def collect(self) -> Optional[MyMetrics]:
        """
        Collect metrics from the data source.

        Returns:
            MyMetrics object or None if collection fails
        """
        try:
            # Your collection logic here
            # Example: run a command, parse output
            result = self._run_command("my-command --json")

            if result is None:
                return None

            # Parse and return metrics
            return MyMetrics(
                timestamp=self._get_timestamp(),
                value=float(result.get("value", 0)),
                status=result.get("status", "unknown")
            )
        except Exception as e:
            self.logger.error(f"Collection failed: {e}")
            return None

    def collect_to_db(self, db_path: str) -> bool:
        """
        Collect metrics and store in database.

        Args:
            db_path: Path to SQLite database

        Returns:
            True if successful
        """
        metrics = self.collect()
        if metrics is None:
            return False

        # Store in database
        import sqlite3
        conn = sqlite3.connect(db_path)
        cursor = conn.cursor()

        cursor.execute("""
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS my_metrics (
                timestamp TEXT,
                value REAL,
                status TEXT
            )
        """)

        cursor.execute(
            "INSERT INTO my_metrics VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
            (metrics.timestamp, metrics.value, metrics.status)
        )

        conn.commit()
        conn.close()
        return True

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Diagnostic File

docs.title: Step 2: Implement the Diagnostic
docs.text:
"""
my_diagnostic.py - Diagnostic analysis for my data source
"""
from typing import Dict, Any, List, Optional
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

@dataclass
class MyDiagnosticResult:
    """Results from my diagnostic analysis."""
    status: str  # 'healthy', 'warning', 'critical'
    score: float  # 0-100
    metrics: Dict[str, Any]
    issues: List[str]
    recommendations: List[str]

def diagnose_my_source(
    db_path: str,
    hours: int = 24,
    thresholds: Optional[Dict[str, float]] = None
) -> MyDiagnosticResult:
    """
    Analyze my data source health.

    Args:
        db_path: Path to database
        hours: Hours of history to analyze
        thresholds: Custom thresholds (optional)

    Returns:
        MyDiagnosticResult with analysis
    """
    import sqlite3

    # Default thresholds
    thresholds = thresholds or {
        "warning": 80.0,
        "critical": 95.0,
    }

    # Query recent data
    conn = sqlite3.connect(db_path)
    cursor = conn.cursor()

    cutoff = (datetime.now() - timedelta(hours=hours)).isoformat()
    cursor.execute("""
        SELECT value, status FROM my_metrics
        WHERE timestamp > ?
        ORDER BY timestamp DESC
    """, (cutoff,))

    rows = cursor.fetchall()
    conn.close()

    if not rows:
        return MyDiagnosticResult(
            status="unknown",
            score=0,
            metrics={},
            issues=["No data available"],
            recommendations=["Ensure collector is running"]
        )

    # Analyze data
    values = [r[0] for r in rows]
    avg_value = sum(values) / len(values)
    max_value = max(values)

    issues = []
    recommendations = []

    # Determine status
    if max_value >= thresholds["critical"]:
        status = "critical"
        score = 20
        issues.append(f"Value exceeded critical threshold: {max_value:.1f}")
        recommendations.append("Immediate investigation required")
    elif max_value >= thresholds["warning"]:
        status = "warning"
        score = 60
        issues.append(f"Value exceeded warning threshold: {max_value:.1f}")
        recommendations.append("Monitor closely")
    else:
        status = "healthy"
        score = 95

    return MyDiagnosticResult(
        status=status,
        score=score,
        metrics={
            "average": avg_value,
            "maximum": max_value,
            "samples": len(rows),
        },
        issues=issues,
        recommendations=recommendations
    )


def format_my_diagnostic(result: MyDiagnosticResult) -> str:
    """Format diagnostic result for CLI output."""
    lines = []

    # Status header with color
    status_colors = {
        "healthy": "\033[92m",   # Green
        "warning": "\033[93m",   # Yellow
        "critical": "\033[91m",  # Red
        "unknown": "\033[90m",   # Gray
    }
    reset = "\033[0m"
    color = status_colors.get(result.status, "")

    lines.append(f"\n{'='*60}")
    lines.append(f"  MY DIAGNOSTIC REPORT")
    lines.append(f"{'='*60}")
    lines.append(f"  Status: {color}{result.status.upper()}{reset}")
    lines.append(f"  Score:  {result.score:.0f}/100")

    # Metrics
    lines.append(f"\n  Metrics:")
    for key, value in result.metrics.items():
        if isinstance(value, float):
            lines.append(f"    {key}: {value:.2f}")
        else:
            lines.append(f"    {key}: {value}")

    # Issues
    if result.issues:
        lines.append(f"\n  Issues:")
        for issue in result.issues:
            lines.append(f"    ⚠ {issue}")

    # Recommendations
    if result.recommendations:
        lines.append(f"\n  Recommendations:")
        for rec in result.recommendations:
            lines.append(f"    → {rec}")

    lines.append(f"{'='*60}\n")

    return "\n".join(lines)

docs.title: Step 4: Add CLI Command

Edit nomad/cli.py to add the diagnostic command: 

@diag.command()
@click.argument('target')
@click.option('--hours', '-h', default=24, help='Hours of history')
@click.option('--json', 'as_json', is_flag=True, help='JSON output')
def mysource(target, hours, as_json):
    """Diagnose my data source health."""
    from nomad.diag import diagnose_my_source, format_my_diagnostic

    result = diagnose_my_source(get_db_path(), hours=hours)

    if as_json:
        click.echo(json.dumps(asdict(result), indent=2))
    else:
        click.echo(format_my_diagnostic(result))

docs.text: Alert backends send notifications when thresholds are exceeded.

docs.title: Step 1: Create the Backend
docs.text:
# In nomad/alerts/backends.py or new file

class MyAlertBackend:
    """Send alerts to my notification system."""

    def __init__(self, config: Dict[str, Any]):
        self.api_url = config.get("api_url")
        self.api_key = config.get("api_key")

    def send(self, alert: Alert) -> bool:
        """
        Send alert notification.

        Args:
            alert: Alert object with severity, message, etc.

        Returns:
            True if sent successfully
        """
        import urllib.request
        import json

        payload = {
            "severity": alert.severity,
            "title": alert.title,
            "message": alert.message,
            "timestamp": alert.timestamp,
        }

        req = urllib.request.Request(
            self.api_url,
            data=json.dumps(payload).encode(),
            headers={
                "Content-Type": "application/json",
                "Authorization": f"Bearer {self.api_key}",
            }
        )

        try:
            urllib.request.urlopen(req)
            return True
        except Exception as e:
            logger.error(f"Failed to send alert: {e}")
            return False

docs.title: Facts
docs.text:
Three questions every front to nomad asks, answered once, as data:

What it answers Who may ask, in the Console sites every site now (freshness, nodes, CPU, memory and GPUs in use, jobs running and waiting, storage, alerts, workstations) and its jobs over a window anyone signed in: aggregates only me one person's work: their jobs over a window, running and waiting now, score and advice that person lab the labs a person leads: members, their jobs taken together, the lab's workstations, storage and condo nodes the lab's PI; staff for any lab course the courses a person teaches, this term: the class together, each student as a row, when the class works the course's instructors; staff for any course busy when each cluster, interactive server and group of workstations is busiest: the most in use at once and when, a typical week, the busiest and quietest hours (1.14.7) anyone signed in; each workstation by name for staff only

The Console serves them at /api/v1/sites, /api/v1/me and /api/v1/lab; a dashboard widget elsewhere (an Open OnDemand page, say) or an assistant answering questions reads the same answers, so no two of them can disagree. On the command line:

nomad facts sites                 # every site, jobs over the last 30 days
nomad facts me NETID --days 90    # one person
nomad facts lab NETID             # the labs NETID leads
nomad facts lab NETID --each      # each member too, by NetID, and what needs attention
nomad facts sites --json          # the data itself
nomad facts lab NETID --mask      # no NetID, lab, machine or storage names, for sharing
nomad facts course --instructor NETID   # the courses NETID teaches (needs [console.courses])
nomad facts course GROUP              # one course
nomad facts busy --days 90 --each     # when each machine is busiest, each workstation too

They read the hub's combined.db when there is one, else this host's own database (--db to choose). Nothing is written.

docs.title: What every answer carries
docs.text:
{
  "api": "nomad.facts/1",
  "kind": "sites",
  "generated_at": "2026-10-11T07:00:00",
  "window": {"days": 30, "since": "2026-09-11T07:00:00", "until": "2026-10-11T07:00:00"},
  "notes": ["..."]
}

api changes only when a field changes meaning or goes away; new fields can appear at any time.

Two rules hold throughout:

  • Nothing measured, no number. A share that rests on no measurement is null; "CPU used" is over the jobs whose CPU use nomad measured, and says how many those were (jobs_measured). Nothing is shown as 0 for lack of data.
  • Each site against its own latest reading. A site that has not reported for two hours is stale: its figures are what it last said, never averaged in as if current, and it is never dropped. Its nodes, GPUs and queue are judged by the node collector's own latest reading; jobs "running now" at a site that stopped reporting are listed, marked stale, and left out of the totals.
  • No figure that is one person's in disguise. Where the caller says so (the Console does, for anyone but staff), a site's job figures resting on 3 people or fewer, and a lab's totals (and how many members ran jobs) resting on fewer than 3 members besides the one asking, are left out ("suppressed": true and why). The Console also gives anyone but staff fixed windows (7, 30, 90 or 365 days), so answers a day apart can't be subtracted. That stops reading one person off one answer, not combining several: two windows, two labs, or a site's total and a lab's can still come down to one person. These figures are not anonymised; what a PI may see of each student is the institution's decision.

docs.title: Jobs, wherever they appear
docs.text:
The same calculation for a site, a person and a lab, over the jobs that ended in the window:

Field Meaning finished jobs that ended in the window outcomes completed, failed, timeout, out_of_memory, node_fail, cancelled, preempted, other ran_to_an_end finished, less cancelled, preempted and other failed_pct failed, timed out or out of memory, of those that ran to an end; node failures are the machine's and in neither count (the Console's Dashboard counts them as failures, of every job that ended, until it reads these facts) people how many people's jobs these are (a count, never names) core_hours.requested cores × run time asked for, all jobs core_hours.used_pct core-hours used over core-hours requested, over the jobs measured memory.used_pct memory at peak over memory requested, by memory-hours, over the jobs measured memory.set_aside peaks larger than any node at the job's site: not measurements (Slurm's jobacct_gather/linux counts shared memory once per process) gpus.jobs, gpus.gpu_hours_requested GPUs asked for; their use per job is not measured here wait_minutes.median, .p90 time from submission to start

docs.title: sites
docs.text:
For each site (the hub's sync_sites, so a site whose sync fails is still listed):

  • note: what the site is, when [console.machines] says (1.17.7).
  • status: ok, stale or no_data; last_data and age_minutes, from its newest reading in any table; sync.failing and sync.last_success on a hub (the reason stays in the hub's sync log).
  • For a Slurm site: nodes (up, drained, down, not reporting, and the unavailable ones; Slurm's reason for each only when asked for, since an admin's free text can name people: the Console gives it to staff), cpu and memory (allocated_pct: what Slurm has handed out, not what jobs use), gpus (busy_pct from DCGM, over the GPUs it measured: nvidia-smi's "utilization" is any kernel running at all, and is not used), queue (running and waiting now) and jobs over the window.
  • workstations: how many it collects and how many are online now.
  • storage: each filesystem read in the last week: size, use, how fast it is filling over 30 days (least squares over daily averages of the fall in free space, which also catches a shared pool filling while this filesystem's own use stays flat) and days until full at that rate; same_as when another site or path reports the same size and use.
  • alerts: conditions holding now, by severity (counts only: an alert's message can name things a viewer should not see).

docs.title: me
docs.text: person.username, jobs (as above), jobs_by_site, now (running and waiting, by site, with whether that site is stale), and score and advice: the same as nomad edu me and the Console's My Activity, from the same code.

docs.title: lab
docs.text:
For each lab the person leads, by nomad.toml's rules ([console.labs], [console.storage]; the same labs as nomad console roles NETID and the Console's My Lab):

  • members: current members (seen in the groups collector's latest run, with an account), how many ran jobs in the window, how many the group lists without an account or no longer lists.
  • jobs and now: the members' jobs taken together.
  • workstations: the lab's machines, online or not, last seen, when they last answered (last_online), and what each is (note, from [console.machines], 1.17.7).
  • storage: each server or export the lab has, with its size and use, and what it is (note); shares_free_with for exports of one pool (their free space is one).

  • condos (when report.toml's condo settings are given, as nomad facts lab and the Console do, 1.17.9): the lab's own condos. Only confirmed ones; when a condo's members name groups ("group:NAME"), it is those labs' only; otherwise its owner's: the lab group_pattern names for the owner, or the one lab they lead (an owner leading several, none named for them, needs members to say which). Each has the cluster, the partition, its nodes (report.toml's, else the partition's) as the cluster's latest reading has them (up, drained or down; gone when that reading no longer lists the node; cores, cores allocated, memory, GPUs), the totals, and of the cores on nodes that are up (cores_up) how many are allocated to jobs now (cores_allocated, guests' jobs included) and that share. stale when the cluster's latest reading is over 2 hours old: then the nodes are as it last reported them, and no share is given. On a hub, report.toml's clusters are its sites.

  • each (with names=True, --each on the command line): a row per member by NetID: jobs finished in the window, core-hours held and the share used, memory used of what was asked, GPU-hours, the median wait, and jobs running and waiting now. Most core-hours first.

  • attention (with names too, 1.17.6): what needs the PI's attention now, most pressing first, each item with who (user, or none for a machine), how many, up to three of the jobs it is about (job_id, site, submit_time), and a sentence saying it (says); attention_days is the window it looks at. From the last 7 days, what is waiting now, and the latest storage readings:
kind When waiting a member's jobs waiting more than 24 hours (and under 60 days) for something that won't change by itself: a job it depends on that can never run, a hold (also REQUEUE_HOLD and the like), a request beyond a partition's or a per-job limit, an account or QOS that won't take it. Not limits that lift as jobs end (per user or per group), nor the cluster's own reasons (its turn, free nodes, nodes down, drained or reserved, a partition down), nor at a site that stopped reporting. One item a member, the longest wait first out_of_memory a member's jobs that ran out of memory timeout a member's jobs that hit their time limit or their --deadline failing 3 or more failed jobs, at least half of a member's jobs that ran to an end (node failures aside) quota a member at 90% or more of a quota, where there are quotas storage a lab storage server or export 90% full or more (a current reading) data the lab's 3 biggest holders of data (100 GB or more each), and anyone whose data grew by 100 GB or more in the last 7 days: how much, where (server and path, with the note [console.storage] gives the server, and "the lab's" on its own storage), how much it changed, and how much the latest scans (of the last 8 days) found unchanged for a year (modified, not read). From the servers the storage_use collector reads; copies (backups, replicas) and owners the server can only number are left out. A reading more than 2 days old is said with its date, and no change is said from it, nor from readings much further apart than the window over_cpu a member whose measured jobs held 100 core-hours or more and used under 25% of them over_memory a member whose jobs used under 20% of the memory they asked for, over 3 measured jobs or more, where Slurm holds the memory a job asks for workstation a lab workstation that hasn't answered for 2 hours

Every limit is nomad.toml's to change, [console.labs.attention] (see configuration). Nothing else is listed, and nothing says "all fine": an empty list is a lab where none of these checks found anything, which may be because nothing was measured; attention_unchecked names a check that couldn't be made (storage: the readings couldn't be read just then). The one asking is left out (their own jobs and data are on their Home and in nomad facts me), and a research assistant isn't told about the lab's leaders, as in each; staff, naming the lab, see every member.

Lab-wide figures unless names are asked for. How much a PI sees of each student is the institution's decision: the Console gives each member's row to staff and to the lab's own PI, for that lab. Without names, no row is about one member. A member's jobs count wholly toward the lab, and someone in two labs counts in both: group membership is all there is to go on.

docs.title: course
docs.text:
For each course the person teaches this term, by nomad.toml's [console.courses] (see docs/config.md, Courses):

  • students: the course's people who are not faculty (listed: its group's members, and whoever used its environments this term, on two days or more); this term's (this_term: joined since the term began, or used an interactive server or a cluster since; for a course whose environment's users are mostly not in its group, by_environment: joined, or used the environment); those left out, as from earlier terms (nomad saw them join before) or not known (in the group since before nomad 1.11 recorded join dates, and not active: earlier students, or some who haven't started); used_a_server, not_yet, and open_never_computing (had sessions open while computing was measured, and never computed: possibly stuck).
  • interactive: hours open and computing for the class, week by week, and from when each was recorded.
  • each_student: one row per student, busiest first: hours open in a typical week (the median over the term's complete weeks) and the range of their weeks (10th to 90th percentile), the same for hours computing over the weeks it was measured, CPU-hours, peak memory, memory kills, weeks active. This is what a caterpillar plot draws: one row per student, a dot for the typical week, a bar for the range. nomad facts course prints it. Rows are "student 1", "student 2"... unless [console.courses] names is true (the institution's decision).
  • when: students on, and computing, on average at each hour of each weekday (from nomad 1.11.1's hourly totals).
  • oom: the students' sessions the kernel killed for lack of memory.
  • jobs: their cluster jobs, taken together.

Each course says who teaches it and why (instructors_why: added by name, confirmed (they said so this term), only faculty member among its people, joined its group this term, environment: used its environment this term, active this term where its students work, those sites in active_on; see Courses in config.md), and how many of its faculty members were left out or said no. environments lists the environments whose users this term are among its people (nomad 1.12.5). Asked for every course, one nobody teaches this term is left out and listed in not_shown with the reason. answers (from nomad.config.course_answers.load) is what faculty members said this term.

For the Console's questions: facts.courses.questions(conn, config, netid, answers) lists the courses that have netid as a faculty member, in its group or a user of the environment named for it (with students this term, or already answered): their answer and whether nomad takes them as teaching it; facts.courses.may_answer(conn, config, netid, group) says whether they may answer for a course. facts.teaches(conn, config, netid, answers) names the courses a person teaches without their figures (a menu), and facts.every_course(conn, config) every course this term, for staff to choose from.

For whoever sets courses up: facts.courses.discover(conn, config) (what nomad course discover prints) lists the environments people had a session in this term (people, faculty members among them, the courses each counts for, whether it is named like a course, the group most of its other users are in) and the groups that are not courses with a faculty member and people active this term (whose own group each is, the environment most of them used), with how many courses there are and how many nobody teaches. It names NetIDs, groups and environments.

A week before a figure was recorded is left out of it, never counted as zero: hours open from nomad 1.11 (earlier weeks once nomad interactive backfill has rebuilt them), computing from 1.11, hours of the week from 1.11.1. With min_students set, a course with fewer students this term shows counts only. Unnamed rows are not anonymous to an instructor who knows the class: in a course of three, the rows are three people.

docs.title: busy
docs.text:
For each cluster, interactive server and group of workstations over the window: the most in use at once and when, the average, a typical week (each weekday's hour averaged over the window) and the three busiest and quietest hours. Machines only, never a person. Workstations go by lab: a machine [console.labs.resources] lists for a lab, or its collector tags with the lab's group (its latest department, as for My Lab), is the lab's, in every lab that lists or tags it; machines in no lab go by the site that collects them. A machine read by two sites counts once. Anything nomad.toml lists as storage (a lab's storage, [console.storage] servers and their names, the storage collector's devices) is left out, even when the workstation collector reads it too; names match in any case and without their domain (a NAS another site collects needs its [console.storage] entry on the hub). Machines and labs are listed by name (each, label), and both can be named for people, so the Console shows a lab to staff and to its own PI only, and --mask numbers them. CPUs are as each system counts them: Slurm's CPUs on the clusters, and a hardware thread on servers and workstations (two per core with hyperthreading).

  • Clusters (node_state): cores allocated (CPUAlloc) of the cores of the nodes in service. A node down, not responding, failing, in maintenance, or drained with nothing running is out of service: left out of the totals and counted apart (nodes_out: on average and at most).
  • Load (CPULoad): each node's counts up to its cores, for the most at once as for the average. Load counts threads ready to run as well as running, and processes waiting on storage, so a node whose storage stalls can read far above its cores; over_cores_pct and over_cores_readings say how often a node read above its cores. Where jobs are held to their cores (task/cgroup), that means jobs started more threads than cores they asked for, or were waiting on storage. Load is not cores in use.
  • Memory allocated (AllocMem), or "tracked": false where Slurm doesn't count memory (SelectTypeParameters without _Memory), never 0%.
  • Memory held: on the nodes running jobs, each node's memory less what Slurm reports free, as a share of the memory of all the nodes in service. Slurm's free memory is the kernel's free memory (MemFree), which counts the file cache as used, so this is the most the jobs could have used: jobs used this much or less. Nodes running nothing count as none (whatever they hold is cache, or left behind, not a job's). A free figure of 0 (Slurm's FreeMem=N/A, from a node that hasn't reported) is not counted.
  • A cluster whose every reading in the window had every node out of service has no figures; it is listed in clusters_all_out instead.
  • Readings that aren't numbers (text in a number column) are not counted.
  • Interactive servers (interactive_hourly): people with a session open (the most in an hour, and the hour's average), people computing, the memory their sessions held, and the machine's own busy cores (mpstat_summary) where the collector runs on it (one server at the site).
  • Workstations: the cores people's sessions kept busy, from each person's CPU counters (workstation_user_snapshot, accounts from uid 1000): everything in their user slice, logins, terminals and cron jobs; the machine's own services are not included. Memory in use is the machine's, cache left out (workstation_state). A machine is busy with a core or more in use. The group's figures add each machine's ten-minute averages (machines aren't read at the same instant). The workstation collector's own CPU percentages were never measured, and are not used. A machine whose per-person probe read only its own accounts (the collector's root login, the login screen: uid below 1000) reads 0, nobody used it; one with no per-person readings at all says its CPU is not measured.

An hour of the week is ranked busiest or quietest only with readings on two different days or more, and nothing is ranked when every hour is the same. A site whose last reading is more than two hours old is marked stopped. Times are as the collectors wrote them: each site's local time.

docs.title: Using the functions
docs.text:
from nomad import facts
conn = facts.open_readonly("~/.local/share/nomad/combined.db")
facts.sites(conn, days=30, config=config)
facts.person(conn, "jdoe", days=30, config=config, db_path=path)   # db_path: score and advice
facts.labs(conn, config, "pi1", days=30, min_others=3)             # what a PI is given
facts.labs(conn, config, groups=["pi1$"])                            # staff, by group
facts.sites(conn, reasons=True)                                      # staff: node reasons
facts.busy(conn, days=30, names=False)                               # machines numbered, not named

The functions decide nothing about who may ask: the caller does.

docs.title: GPU Monitoring
docs.text: NØMAÐ collects GPU metrics from NVIDIA GPUs using nvidia-smi as the standard source, with optional enhanced metrics via DCGM (NVIDIA Data Center GPU Manager) when available. The two sources are transparent to the user — NØMAÐ detects DCGM automatically and falls back to nvidia-smi silently.

docs.title: Data Sources
docs.text:
Source Metrics Availability nvidia-smi Utilization, memory, temperature, power Any NVIDIA GPU node DCGM All of the above + Real Util, pipeline counters, hardware health Datacenter GPUs with DCGM installed

The data_source column in gpu_stats records which source was used for each record. The dashboard shows a DCGM pill next to the GPU name when enhanced metrics are active.

docs.title: Real Utilization
docs.text:
nvidia-smi reports GPU utilization as the fraction of time at least one kernel was running — a kernel-launch duty cycle. A GPU can show 100% utilization while its tensor cores are completely idle.

Real Utilization is a weighted composite of DCGM pipeline activity counters that reflects what the GPU is actually doing:

Real Util = clamp(0, 100,
    W_sm     × SM_ACTIVE
  + W_tensor × TENSOR_ACTIVE
  + W_dram   × DRAM_ACTIVE
  + W_gr     × GR_ENGINE_ACTIVE)

Three presets are available, configurable in nomad.toml:

[collectors.gpu]
real_util_weights = "ai"   # ai | hpc | memory | [custom list]
Preset Weights (SM, Tensor, DRAM, GR) Best for ai 0.35, 0.35, 0.20, 0.10 DL training, LLM inference hpc 0.45, 0.15, 0.25, 0.15 Scientific computing, mixed CUDA memory 0.35, 0.10, 0.40, 0.15 Bandwidth-heavy, stencil codes

Custom weights are also supported:

real_util_weights = [0.40, 0.30, 0.20, 0.10]  # SM, Tensor, DRAM, GR

Weights are auto-normalized to sum to 1.

The Real Utilization metric and workload classification framework are adapted from KempnerPulse (Kempner Institute, MIT license), based on NVIDIA DCGM profiling metric guidance.

docs.title: Workload Classification
docs.text:
When DCGM data is available, each GPU record is assigned one of 12 workload categories based on pipeline counter patterns. Categories are evaluated in priority order; the first match wins.

Category Signal Meaning tensor-heavy compute Tensor ≥ 50%, SM ≥ 60% DL training, large-scale inference. GPU used for its intended purpose. tensor compute Tensor ≥ 15%, SM ≥ 40% Mixed-precision, moderate neural network activity. FP64 / HPC compute FP64 ≥ 20%, SM ≥ 50% Classical scientific computing: molecular dynamics, quantum chemistry, climate simulation. I/O or data-loading PCIe ≥ 1 GB/s, SM < 30% GPU waiting for data. Common during dataset loading or checkpoint I/O. memory-bound DRAM ≥ 50%, SM < 50% Bandwidth is the bottleneck. The workload may benefit from data layout optimization. compute-heavy SM ≥ 80% High SM occupancy. General CUDA compute, older code without tensor core use. compute-active SM ≥ 50% Moderate SM activity. Mixed or general-purpose CUDA kernels. memory-active DRAM ≥ 40% Significant DRAM traffic without SM saturation. busy, low SM use GR ≥ 40%, SM < 25% Kernel launch overhead, synchronization barriers, or driver activity. low utilization GR < 15%, SM < 15%, DRAM < 15% Barely active — job may be stalled or using the GPU incidentally. idle Real Util < 5%, all counters low Nothing running. mixed / moderate (fallthrough) No single dominant pattern.

The dashboard displays the workload category as a color-coded badge using the Okabe-Ito colorblind-safe palette:

  • Blue — tensor workloads (tensor-heavy, tensor)
  • Teal — FP64 / HPC compute
  • Amber — memory and I/O workloads
  • Mauve — compute workloads
  • Orange — I/O or data-loading
  • Gray — idle, low utilization, mixed

docs.title: Interpreting the utilization gap
docs.text:
The difference between nvidia-smi utilization and Real Utilization is often the most actionable signal:

  • Small gap (< 10 pts): GPU is well-utilized; pipeline stages match the workload type.
  • Large gap (> 20 pts) with memory-bound: Data movement is the bottleneck. Consider larger batch sizes, prefetching, or NVLink if available.
  • Large gap with busy, low SM use: Many small kernels or excessive synchronization. Kernel fusion or async execution may help.
  • High nvidia-smi, low Real Util, idle: A single process holds the GPU but is not actively computing (e.g., a job in a data-loading loop).

docs.title: Hardware Health Monitoring
docs.text:
When DCGM is active, NØMAÐ collects hardware health signals that precede visible performance degradation:

Signal Meaning PCIe replay rate Link errors causing retransmissions. Any sustained rate > 0/s indicates link issues. ECC correctable errors Transient memory bit flips. Monitor for trends. ECC uncorrectable errors Serious memory failures. Investigate immediately. Row remap failure HBM memory (A100, H100) permanently degraded. Remove from production.

Health status per GPU:

Status Condition OK Normal operation WARN PCIe replay rate > 0/s HOT Temperature at or above model threshold (A100: 93°C, RTX 6000 Ada: 92°C, H100: 95°C) CRIT Row remap failure or uncorrectable ECC errors

The dashboard shows a colored health badge (WARN/HOT/CRIT) next to the GPU name in the node detail panel. CRIT nodes should be removed from production.

docs.title: SSH Mode
docs.text:
For headnode deployments where GPUs are on compute nodes, configure SSH mode:

[collectors.gpu]
enabled = true
ssh_user = "zeus"
gpu_nodes = ["node51", "node52", "node53"]

NØMAÐ SSHes to each node and runs nvidia-smi (and dcgmi if available) remotely. The same fallback logic applies per node.

docs.title: SLURM / CUDA GPU Visibility
docs.text:
User-facing commands (nomad edu explain_job, etc.) filter GPU data to the GPUs visible to the current job. Detection priority:

  1. CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
  2. NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES
  3. SLURM_STEP_GPUS
  4. SLURM_JOB_GPUS
  5. All GPUs (admin mode)

docs.title: nomad diag gpu
docs.text:
Utilization summary, workload distribution, and temperature status.

nomad diag gpu                    # All nodes, last 24h
nomad diag gpu --node node51      # Specific node
nomad diag gpu --hours 48         # Longer window
nomad diag gpu --health           # Hardware health only (PCIe, ECC, remap)

docs.title: nomad insights gpu
docs.text:
Narrative summary of GPU usage patterns and health concerns. Flags the utilization gap when nvidia-smi reports significantly higher utilization than Real Util.

nomad insights gpu                # All nodes, last 6h
nomad insights gpu --hours 12     # Longer window
nomad insights gpu --node spdr16  # Specific node

docs.title: Installing DCGM
docs.text:
DCGM is free and available for all supported datacenter GPUs.

Rocky Linux / RHEL: 

dnf install -y epel-release
dnf install -y datacenter-gpu-manager
systemctl enable --now nvidia-dcgm

Ubuntu / Debian: 

apt-get install -y datacenter-gpu-manager
systemctl enable --now nvidia-dcgm

Verify: 

dcgmi discovery -l
dcgmi dmon -e 1001 -c 1

NØMAÐ detects dcgmi in PATH automatically on the next collection cycle. No configuration change is required.

docs.title: Supported GPUs
docs.text:
GPU nvidia-smi DCGM NVIDIA A100 ✓ ✓ NVIDIA A40 ✓ ✓ NVIDIA H100 / H200 ✓ ✓ NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada ✓ ✓ (DCGM 3.3.9+, field IDs 1001-1005) NVIDIA RTX 4090 / 3090 / 3050 ✓ Management only — profiling not supported NVIDIA GTX series (Maxwell/Pascal) ✓ — AWS p3/p4/g4dn/g5 instances ✓ ✓ (if installed) AMD GPUs — —

Profiling counter availability is GPU-class dependent. NVIDIA gates the profiling fields (SM_ACTIVE, TENSOR_ACTIVE, DRAM_ACTIVE, GR_ENGINE_ACTIVE) to datacenter and professional GPUs. Consumer GeForce cards (RTX 40/30/20 series) support DCGM for management metrics (utilization, memory, temperature, power) but profiling counters return error -36 ("Profiling is not supported"). The collector detects this automatically and falls back to nvidia-smi data with no DCGM enrichment fields populated. Real Utilization and workload classification are unavailable for these GPUs.

NØMAÐ has been verified with DCGM on: - NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation with DCGM 3.3.9 (full profiling support) - NVIDIA A100, A40, H100 (full profiling support — datacenter GPUs) - NVIDIA RTX 4090 (DCGM 4.5+ — management only, no profiling)

AMD GPU support is a future initiative (ROCm).

docs.title: Insight Engine Integration
docs.text: GPU signals are automatically included in nomad insights brief, nomad insights detail, and the dashboard Insights tab. No configuration is required — signals fire when the relevant data is present in the database.

docs.title: Signals
docs.text: Signal Severity Condition Requires DCGM GPU Job Failures WARNING > 20% of GPU jobs failing No GPU Out of Memory WARNING/NOTICE Any GPU jobs hit VRAM limit No GPU Utilization Gap WARNING/NOTICE nvidia-smi avg > 30%, Real Util lags > 20 pts Yes GPU Workload Pattern NOTICE memory-bound ≥ 50% or idle ≥ 70% of samples Yes GPU Workload Pattern INFO tensor-heavy or FP64 dominant ≥ 60% Yes GPU Hardware Health CRITICAL Row remap failure or uncorrectable ECC Yes GPU Hardware Health WARNING Temperature at or above model threshold Yes GPU Hardware Health NOTICE PCIe replay errors detected Yes

docs.title: Example narratives
docs.text:
GPU Utilization Gap (NOTICE):

node51 shows a 30-point gap between nvidia-smi utilization (54%) and Real Utilization (24%). The GPU appears busy but the compute pipeline is underused. Consider larger batch sizes, kernel fusion, or data prefetching.

GPU Workload Pattern — memory-bound (NOTICE):

node51 has been running memory-bound workloads 65% of the time. GPU compute pipeline is underutilized relative to memory bandwidth. Possible improvements: increase batch size, optimize data layout, or use prefetching to overlap compute and data transfer.

GPU Workload Pattern — productive (INFO):

spdr16 is running tensor-heavy compute workloads 72% of the time — GPU resources are being used effectively.

GPU Hardware Health — CRITICAL:

node51 GPU 2 has a row remap failure — HBM memory is permanently degraded. This GPU should be removed from production and scheduled for replacement.

GPU Hardware Health — NOTICE:

spdr17 GPU 0 is logging PCIe replay errors (0.023/s). This indicates link instability — check the PCIe slot, riser card, or cable. Left unaddressed, this typically escalates to link failure.

docs.title: Signal thresholds
docs.text:
Utilization gap and workload pattern signals require at least 3 samples within the analysis window before firing, avoiding false positives from transient conditions. Hardware health signals fire on any occurrence within the window — PCIe errors and ECC events are always worth flagging.

-- Extended gpu_stats table
CREATE TABLE gpu_stats (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
    timestamp DATETIME NOT NULL,
    node_name TEXT,
    gpu_index INTEGER,
    gpu_name TEXT,
    gpu_util_percent REAL,       -- nvidia-smi kernel duty cycle
    memory_util_percent REAL,
    memory_used_mb INTEGER,
    memory_total_mb INTEGER,
    memory_free_mb INTEGER,
    temperature_c INTEGER,
    power_draw_w REAL,
    power_limit_w REAL,
    compute_processes INTEGER,
    -- DCGM fields (NULL when nvidia-smi only)
    sm_active_pct REAL,          -- Streaming multiprocessor activity
    tensor_active_pct REAL,      -- Tensor core activity
    dram_active_pct REAL,        -- DRAM bandwidth utilization
    gr_engine_active_pct REAL,   -- Graphics engine activity
    fp64_active_pct REAL,        -- FP64 pipeline activity
    real_util_pct REAL,          -- Weighted composite (see above)
    workload_class TEXT,         -- 12-category classification
    data_source TEXT             -- 'nvidia-smi' or 'dcgm'
);

-- Hardware health time series
CREATE TABLE gpu_health (
    timestamp DATETIME NOT NULL,
    node TEXT NOT NULL,
    gpu_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
    pcie_replay_count INTEGER,
    pcie_replay_rate_per_sec REAL,
    ecc_correctable_total INTEGER,
    ecc_uncorrectable_total INTEGER,
    rows_remapped_correctable INTEGER,
    rows_remapped_uncorrectable INTEGER,
    rows_remapped_pending INTEGER,
    row_remap_failure INTEGER,
    health_status TEXT,          -- OK | WARN | HOT | CRIT
    PRIMARY KEY (timestamp, node, gpu_id)
);

Existing databases are migrated automatically on the next nomad collect run. No manual schema changes are required.

docs.title: Impact: before and after NØMAÐ
docs.text:
A year or more after people start getting NØMAÐ's feedback, the question is what changed: do jobs ask for closer to what they use, do fewer fail or run out of memory, do they wait less? [impact] in nomad.toml records when that feedback began and what else changed along the way; nomad impact compares the jobs before and after.

[impact]
launch = 2026-10-19            # when people started getting NØMAÐ's feedback
baseline_from = 2025-08-24     # where "before" starts (default: a year before launch)
events = [
  { date = 2026-10-06, what = "Console open to staff" },
  { date = 2027-01-11, what = "four nodes added to the large partition" },
]
exclude_users = ["svc-backup"] # accounts that aren't people (1.13.2)

launch splits the jobs into before and after. events is a log of everything else that changes how people use the machines: nodes added, a Slurm limit, a workshop, a new part of NØMAÐ itself. Write them down when they happen; a report a year later names them instead of crediting NØMAÐ with what they did. exclude_users names accounts that aren't people (a service account that runs test jobs, signs in to every workstation, or holds a login session open): they are left out of every figure. nomad config check says what in the section it can't use.

docs.title: What the before period needs
docs.text:
nomad impact status

For each site, the jobs that ended before and after launch: how many, how many measured, how many measured the 1.13 way, how many with an eligible time. Then what to run:

  • Jobs the database doesn't reach back to. Slurm's accounting usually keeps far more than nomad has collected. On the site, nomad import sacct --from BASELINE (a dry run, then --apply) brings them, with their eligible times.
  • Measurements read the old way. Before 1.13, CPU use came from Slurm's AveCPU, the average over a step's tasks: a job running 16 tasks read about a sixteenth of its use. Set against 1.13's figures, that would look like an improvement NØMAÐ didn't make. On the site, nomad impact backfill (a dry run, then --apply) reads the before period again from Slurm, a week at a time, and stores CPU and memory as the collector does now. Slurm keeps step usage only as long as slurmdbd's purge settings allow, often far less time than it keeps the jobs; a job whose usage it no longer has keeps what nomad stored (1.13.2), and the status says how much is still unmeasured.

Both run on each site, not on the hub; the next sync brings the results.

docs.title: Bringing back measurements from an older copy
docs.text:
In 1.13.0 and 1.13.1, a job read again without usage (Slurm had purged its steps) was stored as "not measured" over the measurement nomad had taken when the job ended: nomad impact backfill could erase months of them. 1.13.2 never writes an empty reading over a stored one. What was erased can come back from an older copy of the site's database, or of a hub's combined database, from before the backfill:

nomad impact extract --from OLD/combined.db --site SITE --out SITE-measurements.db
nomad impact restore --from SITE-measurements.db            # on the site: a dry run
nomad impact restore --from SITE-measurements.db --apply

extract reads the copy (read-only) and writes a small file with one row per measured job: its number, submit time and measurements, nothing else. restore runs on the site: it fills in only jobs that have no measurement now, and only the same job: the submit times are known on both sides and agree (a job kept under NUMBER@SUBMIT when a later job took its number is found there). A value the copy doesn't have never replaces one stored. It counts the rest: measured since, another job under the same number, no submit time to tell (left alone), not on the site. Restored rows were measured the old way and the report counts them so (below). An older copy of the site's own database works as --from too, without extract. Not on the hub: the next sync brings them there. --apply first copies the database next to itself (--backup PATH elsewhere; SQLite's backup, safe while the collector writes) and stops if it can't.

docs.title: The report
docs.text:
nomad impact report [--site SITE] [--source PART] [--advice-db PATH] [--json]

--source is clusters, interactive, workstations, login, advice or all (the default: every part that has data).

docs.title: Clusters
docs.text: Month by month from baseline_from: jobs, people and how many were new, the share of jobs measured (of those that ran 10 s or more: the others' figures rest on them), CPU used of the core-hours measured jobs held, memory peak of what was asked for, time used of the time limits of completed jobs, the share that failed, timed out or ran out of memory, out-of-memory jobs, and the median wait from when a job could start. Events appear in their month. Then the periods side by side: before launch, after it, and the same days a year earlier where the data reaches back (students and courses follow the academic year). The figures are the ones the Console and nomad facts use. When more than a fifth of the measured jobs before launch were measured before 1.13 (CPU from AveCPU, which reads jobs running several tasks low), the report says their CPU can't be set against after launch; memory, time, failures and waits can. Counts and shares only: no names.

docs.title: Interactive servers
docs.text: From the interactive collector's daily totals: people, hours with at least one session open (in all and per person), the share of the measured time notebooks, kernels and RStudio sessions were computing, and their measured session-hours that weren't. The Jupyter server's own process isn't counted: it polls all the time, a few percent of a core, which until 1.13.2 made anyone with JupyterLab open look busy all the time (the report reads the sessions' own rows, so this holds for the history too). Days rebuilt from the raw snapshots (nomad interactive backfill) have hours but no CPU, so the computing share starts where the collector began keeping CPU; the report says from when.

docs.title: Lab workstations
docs.text:
From the workstation collector's per-person snapshots: sessions (from signing in to the last program ending, counted in the month they ended), hours, core-hours used, long CPU-heavy runs (12 hours or more keeping half the machine's cores busy: what the Console advises moving to a cluster) and sessions whose programs held 80% or more of the machine's memory.

A session is the person's slice on the machine (systemd's user-UID.slice) for as long as it lives. Until 1.13.2 sessions were told apart by the slice directory's change time, which the kernel moves whenever a login, terminal, ssh connection or cron job starts or ends there: one person's day came out as many sessions. Now a session runs while the slice's CPU time and memory peak keep growing, as they do until it is made again, and ends after two hours without a reading; this holds for the readings already collected too.

A session can then last weeks (anything left running keeps the slice), so its average says little about a two-day job inside it. Long runs are found inside sessions (1.13.3): stretches in which every reading kept three quarters of the cores needed busy, with pauses of up to 30 minutes, and the whole stretch averaged half the machine's cores (at least 2) for 12 hours or more. Each run counts in the month it ended. The Console's advice to move long runs to a cluster uses the same runs.

Memory is the programs' own (memory.stat anon + shmem, read from 1.13.2 on). memory.peak, all there was before, counts the file cache: a session that read large files looked as if it had filled the machine. Sessions without the new reading aren't counted as pressured or not (a dash), and the Console doesn't advise on their memory.

docs.title: Shared login hosts
docs.text: From the per_user collector: heavy-use episodes as nomad per-user merges them (and how many were actionable), the people flagged, everyone who used the host and the core-hours they used there.

docs.title: Advice shown and taken
docs.text:
The Console notes, once a day, the advice it showed someone about their own work (Console fix 33 and later; the Console account's ~/.nomad-console/activity.db, or [impact] advice_db = "PATH", or --advice-db). For each piece of advice on a cluster partition, the person's typical request there in the 60 days before they first saw it and the 60 days after: "took it" when it moved at least half the way to the suggestion, "partly", "no change", or "too early" while there aren't three later jobs yet. For the advice to move long workstation runs to a cluster: whether the person's long runs fell to half or less and their jobs on that cluster grew. Plus how many people opened their own pages each month.

There is no comparison group here (people with the same advice who never saw it), so part of a change may be requests drifting toward use anyway.

docs.title: Reading it
docs.text: What the report can say is what changed after launch, not why. The people and courses change from one term to the next, and the events changed things too. The closest thing to cause is whether a person's next jobs changed after they were shown advice (above). The other sources started at different times (workstations and login hosts only recently, at most sites), so their before periods can be short: nomad impact status says from when each has data, and the same months a year apart will say more than the first before and after.

docs.title: Infrastructure Monitoring
docs.text: NØMAÐ extends beyond compute nodes to monitor research workstations and storage systems, providing a holistic view of your computing environment.

docs.title: Dashboard Views
docs.text:
Access these views from the web dashboard tabs: 

nomad dashboard
# Then click: Workstations | Storage

docs.title: Workstation Monitoring
docs.text: Track departmental workstations across your institution.

docs.title: What's Monitored
docs.text: Metric Description Status Online/offline/unreachable CPU Load Current utilization percentage Memory Used/total RAM Disk Root filesystem usage Users Currently logged-in users Uptime Time since last reboot

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Add workstations to your config file: 

# ~/.config/nomad/nomad.toml

[[workstations]]
name = "bio-ws1"
host = "bio-ws1.dept.edu"
department = "Biology"

[[workstations]]
name = "bio-ws2"
host = "bio-ws2.dept.edu"
department = "Biology"

[[workstations]]
name = "chem-ws1"
host = "chem-ws1.dept.edu"
department = "Chemistry"

Or use the collector: 

nomad collect workstations --discover   # Auto-discover via DNS
nomad collect workstations --add bio-ws1.dept.edu

docs.title: Storage Monitoring
docs.text: Monitor NFS servers, ZFS pools, and storage capacity.

docs.title: What's Monitored
docs.text: Metric Description Capacity Total/used/available space Utilization Percentage used ZFS Health Pool status (online/degraded/faulted) IOPS Read/write operations per second Throughput MB/s read/write Latency Average I/O response time NFS Clients Connected client count

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
# ~/.config/nomad/nomad.toml

[[storage]]
name = "storage01"
host = "storage01.cluster.edu"
type = "nfs"
pools = ["tank/home", "tank/apps"]

[[storage]]
name = "storage02"
host = "storage02.cluster.edu"
type = "nfs"
pools = ["scratch"]

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
Set up alerts for storage conditions: 

[alerts.storage]
capacity_warning = 80      # Warn at 80% full
capacity_critical = 95     # Critical at 95% full
inode_warning = 80
inode_critical = 95
latency_warning_ms = 50    # Warn if latency > 50ms
pool_degraded = true       # Alert on ZFS degraded state

docs.title: Correlating Job Failures
docs.text:
When jobs fail, check infrastructure:

  1. Job failed with I/O errors - Check Storage tab for NFS issues
  2. Job timed out - Check if storage latency spiked
  3. Multiple failures from one department - Check their workstations

docs.title: Capacity Planning
docs.text:
Track trends over time: 

nomad report storage --days 30    # 30-day storage trend
nomad report workstations --idle  # Find underutilized machines

docs.title: Proactive Maintenance
docs.text:
Get notified before problems occur:

  • Storage at 80% - Plan cleanup or expansion
  • ZFS pool degraded - Replace failing drive
  • Workstation offline - Check before users complain

docs.title: Insight Engine
docs.text: The NØMAÐ Insight Engine translates analytical output into actionable, human-readable narratives. Instead of presenting raw numbers, charts, and threshold alerts, the engine explains what is happening, why it matters, and what to do about it.

docs.title: The Distinction
docs.text:
Layer Example Role Alerts WARN: /scratch usage 92% Reactive threshold triggers Reports 94.2% success rate this week Backward-looking, descriptive Insights /scratch is 87% full (40.3 TB free). Growing about 10.2 TB a month; full in about 4 months at that rate. Interpretive, forward-looking

Reports provide evidence. Insights provide understanding. Both coexist.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# Generate demo data with stress scenarios
nomad demo --no-launch

# Get a concise operational briefing
nomad insights brief --db ~/nomad_demo.db --cluster demo-cluster --hours 168

# Full detailed report
nomad insights detail --db ~/nomad_demo.db --hours 168

# One site of a hub's combined database
nomad insights brief --db ~/.local/share/nomad/combined.db --site spydur --hours 168

# JSON output (for API/Console integration)
nomad insights json --db ~/nomad_demo.db

# Slack-formatted message
nomad insights slack --db ~/nomad_demo.db --cluster demo-cluster

# Email digest
nomad insights digest --db ~/nomad_demo.db --period daily

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
The engine runs a four-step pipeline: 

DB tables → Signal Readers → Template Narration → Correlation Engine → Output
              (Level 1)         (Level 1)            (Level 2)

docs.title: Step 1: Signal Readers
docs.text:
Ten domain-specific readers query the database and produce typed Signal objects with severity, metrics, and affected entities.

Reader Data Source Signals Produced Jobs jobs How jobs ended, the partition where problems concentrate, out of memory, out of time, change against the previous window Storage filesystems, storage_state How full each filesystem is, its growth over 30 days and time to full at that rate GPU jobs (GPU subset) GPU jobs that failed or hit a limit, and whether they are one person's Queue queue_state, jobs Backlog in the latest snapshot, median wait to start Network network_perf Latency, packet loss Alerts alerts Alerts raised in the window, grouped by condition Nodes node_state Nodes down, not responding or drained in the latest snapshot Cloud cloud_metrics Cost summary, underutilized instances Workstations workstation_state Load, memory, disk, zombie processes Dynamics jobs, node_state, ... One person running most jobs, a resource near its limit, resilience (see dynamics)

docs.title: How jobs are counted
docs.text:
A job counts once, by how it ended: completed; failed (FAILED, BOOT_FAIL); hit a limit (TIMEOUT, OUT_OF_MEMORY, DEADLINE); lost to a node failure (NODE_FAIL). Cancelled jobs (Slurm writes CANCELLED by <uid>) and preempted ones are reported but not counted as failures. The rate is "failed or hit a limit" over the jobs that ran to an end.

Below 50 such jobs (MIN_JOBS) nothing about jobs rises above a notice and no change is reported between windows: 2 failures in 31 jobs is 6.5%, which says nothing. A partition is singled out only with at least 50 jobs of its own, 10 problems, and a rate at least twice the rest of the site's.

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text: nomad stores alerts but never marks them resolved, so none is called "active": the reader reports alerts raised in the window, grouped by condition, with how many times and when last. A condition that persists is raised again once a day (reminder_hours; every cooldown_minutes before 1.7.16); that is not flapping, and nothing claims it is. Alerts from 1.7.16 name their condition (dedup_key: source, host, what on the host, metric) and are grouped by it; for older ones, measured values don't split a condition: "Disk usage at 86.0% on /scratch" and "at 87.1%" are one; numbers in names do ("GPU 0" and "GPU 3", /data1 and /data2 stay apart). Alerts stored by nomad test-alerts (category test) prove that mail works and are not counted. Both column layouts are read: nomad's (category, source = host) and the demo database's (source, host).

docs.title: What was measured
docs.text:
Next to the signals the engine keeps a coverage list: for each source, measured, stale (a snapshot source — nodes, filesystems, queue, workstations — whose newest reading is over 2 hours old), stopped (a snapshot source silent for over 7 days — a retired collector, listed with its last reading; storage counts as current while either filesystems or storage_state reports), no data (not collected here, or nothing in the window), or failed (the reader raised; the error is given). A missing table is "no data"; any other database error is reported as a failure instead of being swallowed.

Health rests on it: with nothing measured it is unknown, not "good". A stale or failed source counts as a warning, and a data_stale signal names what stopped updating (No new readings from spydur: nodes (last reading 13:05, 3h ago)). A stopped source is not read and does not lower health: a workstation collector retired in April is not a warning every day since.

Sizes are in decimal units, as on the Console's Dashboard (1 TB = 1012 bytes).

docs.title: Step 2: Template Narration (Level 1)
docs.text:
Each signal is passed through a narrative template that states what the data shows:

  • "7,896 jobs ended in the last 7 days (and 50 were cancelled, which is not counted as a failure); 2.5% failed or hit a limit. 191 failed, 3 ran out of time."
  • "In the 'gpu' partition 400 of 2,000 jobs failed or hit a limit (20.0%), against 1.5% in the other partitions."
  • "20% of GPU jobs failed or hit a limit (400 of 2,000). 95% of them are one person's (of 6 people)."

Templates say only what the numbers support. A template that fails falls back to the signal's own detail, so one malformed signal can't take down the brief or the Console page.

docs.title: Step 3: Correlation Engine (Level 2)
docs.text:
The engine examines multiple signals together to find causal or co-occurring patterns. Instead of three separate alerts, it produces one coherent finding:

Correlation Rule Signals Combined Insight Disk pressure + job failures disk_fill_projection + job_success_rate The two may be connected: check whether failing jobs write there GPU jobs out of memory + partition failures gpu_oom + partition_failure_concentration GPU jobs stopped for memory (--mem, the node's memory, not GPU memory) Queue pressure + wait times queue_pressure + high_wait_time Partition bottleneck Network issues + job failures high_network_latency + job_success_rate I/O-related failures Cloud cost + underutilization cloud_cost_summary + underutilized_instance Cost optimization Several workstations busy workstation_high_cpu / workstation_high_memory on 2+ machines People working on them will find them slow

Correlated insights include a recommendation with specific actions. Signals are correlated within one site only.

docs.title: Step 4: Output Formatting
docs.text: Format Use Case CLI brief Concise terminal briefing CLI detail Full report with metrics JSON API and Console integration Slack Channel notifications (supports webhook) Email digest Daily/weekly summaries

docs.title: Signal Suppression
docs.text: Some signals only make sense when there's enough activity or appropriate cluster type to support them. The engine suppresses signals that would be misleading or noisy in low-data conditions.

docs.title: Concentration
docs.text: The diversity signal is by person: "One person ran 94% of the 7,946 jobs submitted in this window". It fires with at least 50 jobs, two people, and one of them over 60%. It matters for reading everything else: figures counted over jobs then mostly describe that person's work. Group-based signals (niche overlap, externalities) appear only where each job can be placed in one group; see dynamics.

docs.title: Capacity binding constraint
docs.text: A resource is called the binding constraint only at 75% or more (BINDING_AT). Below that nothing binds, and no signal is raised; Dynamics names the busiest resource instead.

docs.title: Cluster type considerations
docs.text: NØMAÐ monitors three cluster types: HPC clusters (SLURM), workstation groups (per-user processes), and interactive servers (RStudio/Jupyter sessions). Some signals only fire for specific types — for example, SLURM-related signals only run when there are jobs in the database, and workstation pressure signals only run when workstation_state has data.

docs.title: CLI Reference
docs.text: All commands accept --db PATH, --hours N, --cluster NAME and --site NAME.

docs.title: One site of a combined database
docs.text:
A hub's combined database (nomad sync) holds every site's rows. --site (InsightEngine(..., site=...)) reads one site through read-only views — nothing is copied — and labels the report with it; a site the database doesn't hold is an error. Without it, every site is read separately and each finding is labelled with its site; sites are never pooled, since pooling mixes one site's filesystems and nodes with another's.

A filesystem is reported only while it is still reported: a path whose last reading is more than a day older than the site's newest is taken as retired. Node states from a snapshot over 2 hours old are worded as "was ... at the last report".

docs.title: nomad insights brief
docs.text: Concise operational briefing with health assessment, correlated findings, and individual signals.

docs.title: nomad insights detail
docs.text: Full report with all signals, metrics, and affected entities.

JSON output for programmatic use:

  "site": "spydur",
  "hours": 168,
  "measured": true,
  "overall_health": "degraded",
  "coverage": [{"source": "jobs", "label": "Jobs", "status": "measured", "newest": "...", "detail": "", "signals": 3}, ...],
  "signal_count": 15,
  "insight_count": 3,
  "insights": [...],
  "signals": [...]
}

docs.text: Slack-formatted message. Add --webhook URL to post directly.

docs.title: Dashboard Integration
docs.text: Available in nomad dashboard as the Insights tab, and through the /api/insights endpoint.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
nomad/insights/
    engine.py         — InsightEngine orchestrator
    signals.py        — 10 signal readers, coverage
    templates.py      — narrative templates
    correlator.py     — correlation rules (within one site)
    formatters.py     — Output formatters
    inject_stress.py  — Demo stress scenarios

docs.title: Implementation Levels
docs.text: Level Description Status Level 1 Template-based narratives Implemented Level 2 Multi-signal correlation Implemented Level 3 LLM-powered interpretation Planned (CSSI Year 2-3)

docs.title: Programmatic Use
docs.text:
from nomad.insights import InsightEngine

engine = InsightEngine("/path/to/nomad.db", hours=168, cluster_name="mycluster")
engine = InsightEngine("/path/to/combined.db", hours=168, site="spydur")

print(engine.overall_health)    # "good", "nominal", "degraded", "impaired", "unknown"
print(engine.coverage)          # per source: measured / stale / stopped / no_data / failed
print(engine.signal_count)
data = engine.to_dict()         # Python dict
print(engine.to_slack())        # Slack markdown
subject, body = engine.to_email("daily")

docs.text: NØMAÐ tracks interactive computing sessions to identify: - Idle sessions consuming resources - Memory-heavy notebooks - Stale sessions (no activity for days) - Resource hogs

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
# Full report
nomad report-interactive

# Alerts only (idle/stale sessions)
nomad report-interactive --quiet

# JSON output
nomad report-interactive --json
