docs.title: Issue Reporting
docs.text: NØMAÐ includes an integrated issue reporting system that lets you submit bug reports, feature requests, and questions directly from the CLI, dashboard, or Console without leaving your workflow.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The issue system operates in three tiers:

  • CLI (nomad issue): Interactive form with duplicate detection
  • Dashboard: "Report Issue" tab with structured fields
  • Console (paid): Direct API submission + private support channel

All tiers auto-populate system information (NØMAÐ version, Python version, OS, active collectors, active alerts, cluster count) for better diagnostics.

docs.title: Report an Issue
docs.text:
nomad issue report                     # Interactive form
nomad issue report -c bug -m alerts    # Pre-select category and component
nomad issue report --email             # Send via email
nomad issue report --json              # Output as JSON (no submission)

The interactive form walks you through:

  1. Category: bug, feature, or question
  2. Component: collectors, alerts, dashboard, tessera, cli, console, dynamics, insights, reference, other
  3. Title: brief description
  4. Category-specific fields: steps to reproduce, expected/actual behavior (bugs), problem statement (features), question details (questions)
  5. Duplicate check: searches existing open issues for similar reports
  6. Submission: via GitHub API (with token) or browser link (without token)

docs.title: Search Existing Issues
docs.text:
nomad issue search disk collector
nomad issue search gpu memory --max 10

docs.title: Preview System Info
docs.text:
nomad issue info
nomad issue info --db /var/lib/nomad/cluster.db
nomad issue info --json

docs.title: Dashboard Integration
docs.text:
The dashboard includes a "Report Issue" tab with:

  • Category selection (Bug Report / Feature Request / Question)
  • Component dropdown
  • Structured input fields that adapt to the selected category
  • Duplicate detection that warns about similar open issues
  • Auto-populated system info preview
  • "Submit Issue" and "Open in GitHub" buttons

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Configure direct API submission in nomad.toml:

[issue_reporting]
enabled = true
github_token_file = "~/.config/nomad/github_token"   # a file holding the token (chmod 600)
contact_email = "hpc-team@your-institution.edu"

[support]
email = "hpc-support@your-institution.edu"   # where `nomad issue report --email` goes
institution = "Your Institution"

github_token = "..." written into the TOML still works, but a file keeps the token out of a config that is often copied and shared. The older institution_name and support_email keys in [issue_reporting] are still read when [support] doesn't set them.

The GitHub token should be a fine-grained Personal Access Token scoped only to issue creation on the jtonini/nomad-hpc repository.

docs.title: Without a Token
docs.text: Without a token configured, nomad issue report and the dashboard both fall back to opening a pre-filled GitHub issue form in your browser. The --email flag provides an additional fallback for users without GitHub accounts.

docs.title: Auto-Labeling
docs.text:
Issues submitted via the API are automatically labeled with:

  • Source: source:cli, source:dashboard, or source:console
  • Category: bug, enhancement, or question
  • Component: component:alerts, component:collectors, etc.
  • Version: v1.3.1
  • Institution: inst:university-of-richmond

docs.title: GitHub Issue Templates
docs.text:
The repository includes structured YAML form templates for:

  • Bug Report (bug_report.yml): component, version, description, steps to reproduce, expected/actual behavior
  • Feature Request (feature_request.yml): component, problem statement, proposed solution
  • Question (question.yml): topic area, question, what you have already tried

These templates are used both by the GitHub web interface and by the pre-filled URLs generated by nomad issue report.

docs.title: Noise Reduction
docs.text:
The system includes several mechanisms to keep the issue tracker clean:

  • Duplicate detection: searches open issues before submission
  • Structured templates: required fields produce consistent, useful reports
  • Auto-labeling: enables fast triage by component, version, and institution
  • Institutional token as quality gate: direct API submission comes from production deployments
  • Acknowledgment bot: auto-responds with triage timeline and nomad ref hints

docs.title: ML Framework
docs.text: NØMAÐ's machine learning framework combines multiple models for robust job failure prediction.

docs.title: 1. Graph Neural Network (GNN)
docs.text:
The GNN leverages the job similarity network structure to propagate failure signals.

Intuition: Jobs connected in the similarity network share behavioral profiles. If a job's neighbors have high failure rates, the job itself is at elevated risk.

Architecture: 

Input: Node features (17-dim) + Adjacency matrix
  │
  ▼
GraphConv Layer (17 → 64, ReLU)
  │
  ▼
GraphConv Layer (64 → 32, ReLU)
  │
  ▼
Global Mean Pooling
  │
  ▼
Dense Layer (32 → 1, Sigmoid)
  │
  ▼
Output: Failure probability

Key insight: The GNN learns that certain network neighborhoods are "failure-prone regions" in feature space.

docs.title: 2. LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory)
docs.text:
The LSTM detects temporal patterns and early warning trajectories.

Intuition: Job failures often have precursors—accelerating memory pressure, increasing I/O wait, declining CPU efficiency. The LSTM learns these temporal signatures.

Architecture: 

Input: Time series of metrics (sequence_length × features)
  │
  ▼
LSTM Layer (hidden_size=64)
  │
  ▼
LSTM Layer (hidden_size=32)
  │
  ▼
Dense Layer (32 → 16, ReLU)
  │
  ▼
Dense Layer (16 → 1, Sigmoid)
  │
  ▼
Output: Failure probability

Sequence construction: For each job, we collect metrics at regular intervals (default: every 30 seconds) and form a time series.

docs.title: 3. Autoencoder (Anomaly Detection)
docs.text:
The autoencoder identifies jobs that deviate from normal behavior.

Intuition: Train on successful jobs to learn "normal" patterns. Jobs that reconstruct poorly are anomalous—and anomalies correlate with failures.

Architecture: 

Input: Feature vector (17-dim)
  │
  ▼
Encoder:
  Dense (17 → 12, ReLU)
  Dense (12 → 8, ReLU)
  Dense (8 → 4, ReLU)  ← Latent space
  │
  ▼
Decoder:
  Dense (4 → 8, ReLU)
  Dense (8 → 12, ReLU)
  Dense (12 → 17, Sigmoid)
  │
  ▼
Reconstruction Error = MSE(input, output)
  │
  ▼
Output: Anomaly score (higher = more anomalous)

Training: Only on COMPLETED (successful) jobs. The model learns what "normal" looks like.

Inference: High reconstruction error suggests the job doesn't fit normal patterns.

docs.title: Ensemble Combination
docs.text:
Individual model predictions are combined using weighted averaging:

\[\text{Risk Score} = w_1 \cdot P_{GNN} + w_2 \cdot P_{LSTM} + w_3 \cdot S_{AE}\]

Default weights:

Model Weight Rationale GNN 0.4 Strong structural signal LSTM 0.35 Good temporal patterns Autoencoder 0.25 Catches outliers

Weights are tunable via configuration or can be learned via cross-validation.

docs.title: Data Preparation
docs.text:
nomad train --prepare
  1. Extract completed jobs from database
  2. Compute feature vectors
  3. Label: COMPLETED=0, FAILED/TIMEOUT/CANCELLED=1
  4. Split: 80% train, 10% validation, 10% test
  5. Handle class imbalance (failures are rare):
  6. Oversample failures
  7. Or use class weights

docs.title: Model Training
docs.text:
nomad train

For each model:

  1. GNN: Train on similarity graph with node labels
  2. LSTM: Train on metric time series
  3. Autoencoder: Train reconstruction on successful jobs only

Training outputs: 

~/.local/share/nomad/models/
├── gnn_model.pt
├── lstm_model.pt
├── autoencoder_model.pt
└── ensemble_weights.json

docs.title: Hyperparameters
docs.text: Parameter Default Description learning_rate 0.001 Adam optimizer LR epochs 100 Training epochs batch_size 32 Mini-batch size hidden_dim 64 Hidden layer size dropout 0.2 Dropout rate similarity_threshold 0.7 For GNN graph

docs.title: Real-Time Scoring
docs.text:
nomad predict

For running jobs:

  1. Compute current feature vector
  2. Query similar historical jobs
  3. Run through ensemble
  4. Output risk score (0.0 - 1.0)

docs.title: Risk Score Interpretation
docs.text: Score Level Recommended Action 0.0 - 0.3 Low No action needed 0.3 - 0.6 Moderate Monitor more frequently 0.6 - 0.8 High Alert user, suggest changes 0.8 - 1.0 Critical Immediate intervention

docs.title: Actionable Recommendations
docs.text:
When risk is elevated, NØMAÐ provides specific recommendations based on which features contribute most: 

⚠️ Job 12345 has elevated failure risk (0.72)

Contributing factors:
  • High NFS write ratio (0.89) — 3x normal
  • Low CPU efficiency (23%) — below 50% threshold

Recommendations:
  • Consider using local scratch: export TMPDIR=/scratch/$USER
  • Reduce core count if not using parallelism

docs.title: Classification Metrics
docs.text: Metric Formula Target Precision TP / (TP + FP) > 0.7 Recall TP / (TP + FN) > 0.8 F1 Score 2 × P × R / (P + R) > 0.75 AUC-ROC Area under ROC curve > 0.85

docs.title: Operational Metrics
docs.text: Metric Description Lead time How early before failure is risk elevated? False alarm rate Alerts that didn't result in failure Coverage % of failures that were predicted

docs.title: CLI Commands
docs.text:
# Train all models
nomad train

# Train specific model
nomad train --model gnn
nomad train --model lstm
nomad train --model autoencoder

# Run predictions
nomad predict

# Generate report
nomad report

# View model performance
nomad ml status

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
In nomad.toml: 

[ml]
enabled = true
similarity_threshold = 0.7
retrain_interval_days = 7

[ml.ensemble]
gnn_weight = 0.4
lstm_weight = 0.35
autoencoder_weight = 0.25

[ml.alerts]
high_risk_threshold = 0.7
alert_on_prediction = true

docs.title: Network Methodology
docs.text: NØMAÐ's prediction engine uses similarity networks to identify job failure patterns. This approach draws inspiration from biogeographical network analysis.

docs.title: From Biogeography to HPC
docs.text:
The methodology is inspired by Vilhena & Antonelli (2015), who used network analysis to identify biogeographical regions from species distribution data. Just as biogeographical regions emerge from species patterns rather than being predefined, NØMAÐ allows job behavior patterns to emerge from metric data.

Biogeography Concept NØMAÐ Analog Species Jobs Geographic regions Compute resources (nodes, partitions) Emergent biomes Job behavior clusters Species ranges Resource usage patterns Transition zones Domain boundaries (CPU↔GPU, NFS↔local)

docs.title: Why Cosine Similarity?
docs.text:
NØMAÐ uses cosine similarity on continuous feature vectors rather than Simpson similarity on categorical presence/absence data:

  • Magnitude matters: CPU efficiency of 80% vs 20% is significant, not just "used CPU"
  • Multi-dimensional: Jobs have 17+ continuous metrics
  • Shape over scale: Cosine similarity captures resource profiles, not absolute consumption

A job requesting 64GB with 50% utilization has a similar profile to one requesting 8GB with 50% utilization—both represent reasonable memory sizing—even though absolute consumption differs by 8x.

docs.title: Step 2: Cosine Similarity Matrix
docs.text:
For jobs \(a\) and \(b\) with feature vectors \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\):

\[\text{similarity}(a, b) = \frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}| \cdot |\vec{b}|}\]

Values range from -1 (opposite profiles) to +1 (identical profiles).

docs.title: Step 3: Edge Creation
docs.text:
Edges connect jobs with similarity ≥ threshold (default: 0.7): 

if cosine_similarity(job_a, job_b) >= 0.7:
    network.add_edge(job_a, job_b)

Threshold trade-offs:

Threshold Network Density Clusters Use Case 0.9+ Sparse Tight, specific Anomaly detection 0.7 (default) Moderate Balanced General prediction 0.5 Dense Broad patterns Exploratory analysis

docs.title: Step 4: Community Detection
docs.text: Connected components and modularity-based clustering identify job communities—groups with similar resource profiles.

docs.title: Bipartite Network Approach
docs.text:
For advanced analysis, NØMAÐ implements Vilhena & Antonelli's bipartite approach: 

┌──────────────┐          ┌──────────────┐
│    Jobs      │──────────│ Resource Bins│
├──────────────┤          ├──────────────┤
│ job_1001     │────┬────▶│ cpu_high     │
│ job_1002     │────┤     │ cpu_low      │
│ job_1003     │────┼────▶│ mem_high     │
│ job_1004     │────┤     │ mem_low      │
│ ...          │────┴────▶│ io_nfs_heavy │
└──────────────┘          └──────────────┘

  1. Discretize features into bins (e.g., cpu_high, cpu_low)
  2. Create bipartite graph: jobs connected to their resource bins
  3. Project onto job-job network: jobs sharing bins are connected
  4. Weight by overlap: more shared bins = stronger connection

This approach:

  • Treats each resource bin as a "site" (biogeography analogy)
  • Reveals emergent behavioral regions
  • Handles missing data gracefully

docs.title: Assortativity
docs.text:
Measures whether failed jobs cluster together:

\[r = \frac{\sum_{ij}(A_{ij} - k_i k_j / 2m) \delta(c_i, c_j)}{2m - \sum_{ij}(k_i k_j / 2m) \delta(c_i, c_j)}\]
  • Positive: Failed jobs connect to failed jobs (pattern exists)
  • Zero: Random mixing (no predictive signal)
  • Negative: Failed jobs connect to successful jobs (unusual)

docs.title: Clustering Coefficient
docs.text:
Local clustering indicates behavioral cohesion:

\[C_i = \frac{2 |\{e_{jk}\}|}{k_i(k_i - 1)}\]

High clustering = consistent failure patterns.

docs.title: Statistical Significance
docs.text:
NØMAÐ tests whether observed patterns exceed random chance using permutation tests:

  1. Shuffle failure labels 1000 times
  2. Compute metric for each shuffle
  3. Calculate z-score: \(z = (observed - \mu_{null}) / \sigma_{null}\)
  4. Report significance if \(|z| > 2\)

docs.title: Visualization
docs.text:
The dashboard provides a 3D force-directed network visualization:

  • Node color: Green (healthy) to Red (failed)
  • Node position: Fruchterman-Reingold layout
  • Axes: NFS ratio, local I/O, I/O wait
  • Regions: "Safe zone" vs "danger zone" emerge from data

docs.title: References
docs.text: Vilhena, D.A., Antonelli, A. (2015). A network approach for identifying and delimiting biogeographical regions. Nature Communications 6:6848. DOI: 10.1038/ncomms7848

docs.title: Policy watch
docs.text: What runs on a cluster's login and compute nodes that its rules usually forbid, for an administrator to look at (1.19). It reads; it never stops, changes or reports anything to anyone but the site's admins.

docs.title: What it finds
docs.text:
Of accounts from min_uid (1000) up -- system services aren't people; nor are Slurm's and munge's accounts, nor the collector's own (ignore_users, watch_self):

Kind What Alerted tunnel a program that opens a way in or out: ngrok, cloudflared, frp, chisel, Tailscale, ZeroTier, sshuttle, wstunnel, iodine, ... (and ssh -w); generic names (bore, gost, naive, xray, ...) only with an argument that listens or proxies warning ssh_reverse an ssh client forwarding a port from outside to here (-R, RemoteForward), before or after the destination, as ssh reads them (checked against ssh -G) warning ssh_socks an ssh SOCKS proxy (-D, DynamicForward): this host's traffic carried out through another warning code_tunnel code tunnel: VS Code's relay through Microsoft (Remote-SSH's server isn't one) warning miner a miner by name (xmrig, t-rex, lolMiner, ...), xmrig's --donate-level, or a stratum+tcp:// pool on the command line of a program that isn't a text tool (grep stratum+tcp:// isn't a miner) critical relay a relay or proxy: socat listening, 3proxy, v2ray, shadowsocks, sing-box, ... warning listening a person's program listening on a port open to the network, on a login node warning escalation a process running as root whose parent is owned by a regular account and isn't a sanctioned helper (sudo, su, pkexec, ...): the shape of a process that reached root outside the usual path (1.20) critical agent an AI agent command-line program (Claude Code, Codex, aider, ...): listed, not alerted -- AI use is not misuse (1.20) listed auth_failures, setuid_new repeated failed sudo/su per account, and setuid/setgid files of a person's in the places scanned — read unprivileged where the collector's account may (1.23), or from the root helper (below) where root is available (1.20) warning gpu a GPU compute process (nvidia-smi): listed, not alerted -- the note says the memory held, whether it is detached (no terminal: the shape of an unattended job), and whether it is an AI agent (1.21) listed gpu_served a GPU compute process reachable from the network: it listens on a port open to the network, or its account also runs a tunnel/relay/forward -- the shape of reselling or an open inference server (1.21) warning heavy a user process holding real CPU (by lifetime average: its whole CPU time / its age) of at least heavy_cpu cores on a login node -- a computation run where it shouldn't be (1.22) warning job_burst at least burst_jobs sbatches within burst_minutes by one user (an array counts as one) -- listed, not alerted, since a parameter sweep bursts too (1.22) listed fail_fast at least fail_fast_jobs of a user's jobs that FAILED within fail_fast_seconds of starting -- the shape of an agent resubmitting what it doesn't understand (1.22) warning job_churn the same job name resubmitted at least churn_repeats times by one user with cancellations between (1.22) warning

A program is known by its name as it started (argv[0]), its kernel name (comm: what exec -a doesn't change), a download's suffix aside (cloudflared-linux-amd64, chisel_1.10.1_linux_amd64), and, for an interpreter (python, node, java, sh, ...), the script or module it runs, by its exact name (python3 -m sshuttle, sh pagekite.py; rigel_fit.py isn't the rigel miner). An ignore_programs entry leaves a finding out only if it names every name the process goes by.

What a user writes never lowers a finding. Each ssh forward says where its account's connections on that host go, from what the kernel shows (/proc/net), not from the destination on its command line (a user's own ~/.ssh/config can map any name anywhere): stays inside (this host, the cluster's own networks, the servers you list), on campus (private addresses beyond the cluster, and campus_networks), or connects outside. That is a label; it changes nothing by itself.

docs.title: Forwards to servers you trust (1.19.1)
docs.text:
An ssh -R to a server you list in trusted_hosts (and to the cluster's own login hosts: this one and login_hosts) is verified: shown by nomad watch list as info, with why, and not alerted. Only when all of this holds, on that host, at that sweep:

  • the forward opens one port that leads to this host (-R 2222:localhost:22; any port here: what it exposes is the user's choice, and the note says the far end), asks for loopback on the far end (no bind address, or localhost), and has no -J, -W, -F or -o HostName/ProxyJump/ProxyCommand/ProxyUseFdpass of its own; a SOCKS proxy on either end (-R 2222, -D) never is;
  • every connection its account has there goes to a listed server (on a port below 1024, which only root opens, or the one you give: "vadur:2222"), into the cluster below port 1024, or to a service on this host of a system account (below min_uid, or in ignore_users) -- and at least one to a listed server or into the cluster. A connection anywhere else, to a port of a person's on this host (its own -L, say: a relay) or above 1023 on a node, keeps it a warning. Connections into the account's own listening ports count only by where they come from (from this host, the cluster or a listed server: fine); a UDP socket counts by where it is connected to;
  • the account has at least as many such connections as ssh processes (an ssh with no connection of its own, between connection attempts, could be going anywhere);
  • no ssh of that account has a child process (ProxyCommand and ProxyJump from ~/.ssh/config start one: a jump through a listed server to somewhere else) or relays (-W, -J, a proxy, a local forward from a socket);
  • the account has no UDP socket open that isn't connected (it may send anywhere) beyond loopback, and no raw or ICMP socket.

The names in trusted_hosts are resolved by the collector (its own DNS and /etc/hosts), each sweep; nomad watch probe and nomad config check say what they resolve to. The far end is what was asked: that server's sshd decides (with GatewayPorts).

Once verified, it stays verified while the same ssh runs. An ssh keeps the connection it made for as long as it runs, so what its account does afterwards (a Jupyter reached through ssh -L, a name that doesn't resolve at one sweep) can't move its far end: the note says what is new ("... (the same ssh since; now: 1 connection to a person's port on this host)"). The probe names a forward's processes by a key (a hash of the boot, their pids and start times), only when each is ssh by its kernel name (exec -a ssh changes argv[0] alone; a user can set the kernel name too, so this stops only the simplest pose; where the probe runs as root, the program file must be the system's /usr/bin/ssh). It stops being kept when its account reaches anywhere at two of its last four sweeps -- campus, outside, a person's port on a listed server or a node, an open UDP or raw socket, no connection to a listed server (one such sweep, a git pull, is fine; a program posing as ssh that carries the forward elsewhere would show at more) -- or when you take its server off trusted_hosts. Without limit it rides through only what carries nothing elsewhere by itself: a connection to a person's port on this host (a Jupyter through ssh -L), and the account's other ssh processes, which are themselves counted. A new ssh (a new one on the same port, or autossh starting it again) is checked afresh: until a sweep finds its account quiet it is a warning, and alerts, its note saying why ("not verified: 1 connection outside; far end loopback"). An autossh row is verified when its ssh is ("as its ssh: ...").

The cluster's own networks are the private ones each host reaches directly, on an interface with no default route for that IP version (one with a default route is a way out, shared with whatever else is there); where a compute node's way out is the cluster network (through the head node), or a spare default route is on it, list it: cluster_networks = ["10.1.1.0/24"].

A site's own ProxyCommand (FreeIPA's /etc/ssh/ssh_config.d/04-ipa.conf on older clients: ProxyCommand /usr/bin/sss_ssh_knownhostsproxy) gives every ssh a child process, so nothing is verified there; the note names the child by its kernel name, cut at 15 characters ("an ssh with a child process (sss_ssh_knownho: ...)"). The probe can't tell a site's proxy from a user's copy of it without root, so it doesn't try; newer sssd uses KnownHostsCommand, which starts no child. To see whether a host has one: grep -ri proxycommand /etc/ssh/ssh_config /etc/ssh/ssh_config.d/.

What it can't see without root: which process holds which connection. An account that hands ssh a ready connection through a socket of its own (ProxyUseFdpass in its ~/.ssh/config, a relay of its own making), or runs a program of its own that poses as ssh, can hide where a forward goes, and so can two accounts working together; the check makes that deliberate, not easy. Like everything the watch sees, it sees only what runs when it looks: what runs between sweeps, it doesn't.

On compute nodes, programs listening are not findings unless listeners_on_nodes = true: MPI, NCCL, Dask and Ray open ports of their own there (and with it, a port in the kernel's ephemeral range is listed only). Listening on loopback only (VS Code's server, a Jupyter reached through ssh -L) is never one, nor is a local forward (ssh -L).

A host that answered before and hasn't for 3 sweeps raises its own alert: a probe that can't finish there sees nothing, and someone may be hiding.

Not seen: a forward set in someone's ~/.ssh/config (it isn't on the command line), and what runs between sweeps.

docs.title: How
docs.text: Every interval_minutes (15), a probe (watch_probe.py, standard library only, Python 3.6 or later) runs on the login node the collector runs on and, over ssh (BatchMode, no agent or X forwarding), on each compute node Slurm lists that is up, a few at a time, for at most max_seconds. It is piped to a fixed interpreter, the first of python (/usr/bin/python3, /usr/libexec/platform-python) that exists, with -I -S: not whatever python3 comes first on the account's PATH, and no site-packages or .pth files, so nothing a user could put in the collector's way runs as its account. Nothing is installed on the nodes. It reads /proc as the collector's account: every account's processes and their command lines (at most 64 KB each), and the listening sockets with their owners (/proc/net/tcp, readable by every account). No root is needed, unless /proc is mounted with hidepid: then only the collector's own processes are seen (sockets still are), and nomad watch status says so. Which program listens on a port is known only to root (another account's sockets are its own): elsewhere a listener is its owner and port, and ignore_ports leaves out a sanctioned one.

docs.title: What is kept
docs.text:
The host, the account, the kind, the program's name (a short word: letters, digits, . _ + -; at most five per account and kind on a host, listeners too, then +N more), the port it forwards or listens on, and for an ssh forward where its account's connections go (inside, campus, outside), whether it is verified and why, as last seen (in the watch's own words, naming only the servers you listed, by the name or network you gave without its port, the cluster's own hosts, and the kernel name of a child process), and a key of its processes (a hash): never a command line, or an address or host a user gave. --mask replaces the server names in notes too, and nomad watch probe --mask shows no addresses or settings. Each finding has a first and a last time seen, and how many sweeps saw it, in policy_findings, which the hub gets with every other table: admins see NetIDs, as elsewhere in the Console. policy_watch_hosts keeps, per sweep, which hosts answered and what the probe could see there.

Findings raise one alert per account and kind, on whatever hosts (renaming a program, or the same thing on many nodes, makes no new one; something new in it makes one more, itself deduplicated; deduplicated, with reminders as for every alert) that names no one unless owners_in_alerts = true: alerts also go to Slack and webhooks, and their key is the finding's number on the site, which says nothing of the account. policy_watch_hosts (7 days) and policy_watch_sweeps stay on the site.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
[collectors.policy_watch]
enabled = true
# interval_minutes = 15
# nodes = "slurm"              # every node Slurm lists that is up; or a list; or [] for this host only
# login_hosts = []             # other login nodes, asked over ssh
# min_uid = 1000
# listeners_on_nodes = false
# ignore_users = ["slurm", "munge"]   # services' accounts above min_uid (the default)
# watch_self = false           # the collector's own account (an admin's: it may run services) left out
# ignore_programs = []         # e.g. ["tailscaled"] where IT runs it
# ignore_ports = []
# owners_in_alerts = false
# parallel = 8
# timeout = 15
# max_seconds = 180
# ssh_user = "..."
# python = ["/usr/bin/python3", "/usr/libexec/platform-python"]
# trusted_hosts = []           # servers an ssh -R may go to, verified: ["vadur"], "vadur:2222",
#                              # an address or a network (ports below 1024 unless one is given)
# campus_networks = []         # public ranges that are campus, a label: ["141.166.0.0/16"]
# cluster_networks = []        # the cluster's own, where a host's default route is on it: ["10.1.1.0/24"]
# workstations = []            # GPU workstations to ask over ssh (role "workstation"): ["ml-ws01"]
# watch_gpu = true             # GPU compute processes (nvidia-smi); nothing where there is no GPU
# gpu_min_mem = 256            # a compute context smaller than this (MiB) is a probe, not a workload
# gpu_serve_hosts = []         # boxes where serving a GPU is sanctioned (then listed): ["shared-infer01"]
# watch_auth = true            # failed sudo/su from the auth log, where the collector may read it (1.23)
# auth_log = ""                # the auth log path (default: /var/log/secure or /var/log/auth.log)
# auth_window_hours = 24       # how far back failed attempts are counted
# setuid_roots = []            # scan these for a person's setuid files, off until set: ["/localscratch"]
# watch_heavy = true           # heavy use of a login node (a user process holding real CPU)
# heavy_cpu = 2.0              # cores (by lifetime average) at or above which it is heavy
# heavy_min_seconds = 600      # CPU-seconds the process must have used (so a brief spike doesn't count)
# watch_jobs = true            # job-submission patterns from this site's jobs table
# job_window_hours = 24
# burst_jobs = 60              # sbatches within burst_minutes to list a burst (an array is one)
# burst_minutes = 10
# fail_fast_jobs = 15          # jobs that FAILED within fail_fast_seconds to warn
# fail_fast_seconds = 60
# churn_repeats = 8            # resubmissions of one job (with cancellations) to warn
# keep_days = 365              # findings not seen for this long are removed

The collector's account needs ssh to the nodes without a password (as node_disks does). Before turning it on, nomad watch probe (here) and nomad watch probe NODE show what a sweep would find, storing nothing.

docs.title: Looking at it
docs.text:
nomad watch list              findings of the last 7 days, the most serious first (* seen in the last sweep),
                              and verified forwards
nomad watch list --all        also what is only listed (ephemeral ports on compute nodes, agents, GPU processes)
nomad watch list --mask       stand-ins for people and hosts, for anything shared outside ARC
nomad watch list --json
nomad watch status            the last sweep: each host, whether it answered, what it could see
nomad watch probe [HOST]      look now

docs.title: AI agents and getting root (1.20)
docs.text:
The meeting that prompted this named two harms, and neither depends on which tool a person used, so the watch keys on what happens, not on the agent.

An agent (or anyone) trying to reach root. The result is the strong signal: a process running as root whose parent is owned by a regular account, where the parent isn't one of the sanctioned ways up (sudo, su, runuser, pkexec, doas, and the service managers that start a user's work — sshd, systemd, slurmstepd, ...). That is the escalation kind, a critical finding; its note names the program that spawned it. It reads /proc, so under hidepid the collector sees only its own tree unless it runs as root (nomad watch status says when a host is blind). The attempts, rather than the result — failed sudo/su, new setuid files — are in root-only logs, so they come from the root helper below. The surest defence isn't detection, though: an unpatched node (vadur is RHEL 7.9, no security updates since June 2024) is the likeliest way up whatever the agent, so patching or retiring it does more than any alert.

Reselling the cluster's time through an agent. This is mostly what the watch already does: tunnels, relays and miners, and a service open to the network. Turn on listeners_on_nodes = true so a service open to the network on a compute node is a warning (a port in the kernel's ephemeral range, which MPI/Dask/Ray use, is listed, not alerted). The firmer controls are the cluster's: compute nodes reaching the internet only through a proxy, and per-user job and query limits in Slurm.

AI agents themselves are listed, not alerted. Using an agent is not misuse; what matters is what it does. The agent kind names agent command-line programs (Claude Code, Codex, aider, Gemini CLI, ollama, ...) so an admin can see them in nomad watch list --all; agents = [...] adds a site's own. An agent on a login or compute node is seen this way. An agent on a laptop driving the cluster over the user's own ssh looks, from the cluster, like the person typing — so the watch aims at the behaviour (bursts of submissions, jobs that fail in seconds over and over, cancel/resubmit loops, query rates), which catches a careless script just the same.

docs.title: Failed sudo/su and new setuid files
docs.text:
Two of these signals — failed privilege attempts (auth_failures) and a person's setuid/setgid files (setuid_new) — are what the ordinary /proc walk can't see. There are two ways to get them; prefer the first.

Unprivileged (1.23), no root, no cron. The probe reads them itself, as the collector's account, wherever it's allowed to:

  • auth_failures — failed sudo/su in the last auth_window_hours (24), counted per account, straight from the auth log (/var/log/secure, or auth_log). This needs read access to the auth log, which installer often already has: on spydur /var/log/secure is root:securegrp 0640 and installer is in securegrp, so it just works on the login node (watch_auth = true, the default). On a host where the log is root-only it reads nothing and says nothing — no error. The actor is taken from the log's structured fields and matched on the line's head before any COMMAND=, so a command string can't inject a fake account, and su to root is counted against whoever ran it (not dropped as "root").
  • setuid_new — set setuid_roots = ["/localscratch"] (off until set) and the probe lists a person's setuid/setgid files there (basename only), staying on each root's own filesystem, following no symlink, bounded. "New" comes for free from the finding's first-seen: a file that appears is a new finding (and alerts once); one that persists just updates its last-seen.

Note that the auth log is per host and usually not forwarded, so this covers the login node (where interactive sudo happens); to cover the compute nodes too, make their /var/log/secure group-readable to the collector the same way (chgrp securegrp … && chmod 0640, plus a matching create line in logrotate) — a config change, not a cron or a script. The setuid scan needs no such grant and runs on every host.

docs.title: The root helper (off by default, needs root)
docs.text:
Where the auth log can't be made readable and root is available, scripts/watch_root_probe.py feeds the same two signals from a root context instead. It is off until a site turns it on. Run it as root by cron on each node, writing a counts-only JSON that the probe reads back:

*/15 * * * * /usr/bin/python3 -I /path/to/watch_root_probe.py \
    --out /var/lib/nomad-watch/root_signals.json --roots /home,/scratch,/localscratch

Then point the collector at the same path: root_report = "/var/lib/nomad-watch/root_signals.json". It writes, for review, never a command line or a file's contents: auth_failures (failed sudo/su per account, read on from where it stopped last run) and setuid_new (setuid/setgid files under --roots owned by a person that weren't there last run, by basename). The output is world-readable (the collector isn't root); its state file, beside it, is 0600. What the helper needs from the site's administrators (an IS ticket at UR) is the one cron entry as root on each node and a writable --out directory; it installs nothing and keeps nothing secret.

docs.title: GPU workstations (1.21)
docs.text:
On a GPU workstation the person usually already has sudo on their own box, so reaching root isn't the worry — the GPU being served out is. The money threat is a card turned into an inference API or a rented machine, and the quiet one is a job pegging the GPU with nobody at the keyboard. So the watch goes to the workstations and keys on what the GPU shows.

Where it looks. workstations = ["ml-ws01", ...] lists GPU boxes to ask over ssh, with the role workstation (login and compute nodes aside). Their findings reach the hub and the Console the same way everything else does. The collector's account needs passwordless ssh to them, as to the nodes.

What it reads. With watch_gpu (on by default), the probe runs nvidia-smi — unprivileged, and nothing where there is no GPU, so it costs a host without one nothing. It reads the compute processes (--query-compute-apps): CUDA contexts — training, inference, miners — not graphics, so Xorg and a browser's GPU use never show. A context below gpu_min_mem (256 MiB) is a probe, not a workload, and is left out.

  • gpu (listed, not alerted): a GPU compute process, with its owner, program and the memory it holds. The note says detached when it has no controlling terminal and is parented to init or systemd — the shape of an unattended job (nohup, a service, a detached agent) — and an AI agent when the program is one. This is the inventory: it makes no claim of misuse.
  • gpu_served (warning): a GPU compute process reachable from the network — it listens on a port open to the network, or its account also runs a tunnel, relay, SOCKS or an unverified reverse forward (a verified -R is the admin's own and doesn't count). This is the reselling / open-inference signal.

On a compute node a GPU job opens ports of its own — a distributed job's rendezvous (PyTorch, NCCL, Dask, Ray) — so a gpu_served that is only a listener there is listed, not a warning, exactly as a plain listener is, unless listeners_on_nodes = true; and even then a port in the kernel's ephemeral range (where that rendezvous lands) is listed. A GPU served through its account's tunnel still warns, on any host. On a workstation, a served GPU is always a warning — that is the box the signal is for.

GPU miners don't need a kind of their own: a miner is caught by name on any host (the miner kind, critical), GPU or not.

Allowing what is meant to be there. gpu_serve_hosts = ["shared-infer01"] names boxes where serving a GPU is sanctioned: there a served GPU is listed, not a warning. ignore_programs (e.g. ["ollama"]) and ignore_users apply as everywhere, so a lab's own shared server or a service account is left out.

What it can't see, honestly. Per-process GPU attribution goes opaque under MIG, and when the compute app runs in a container or a separate PID namespace. Reading which port a GPU process listens on needs to read that process's sockets — the probe's own, or any as root — so where it doesn't run as root, a GPU another account serves is caught through that account's exposure (a tunnel or forward it also runs), not its listener directly. Detached is a heuristic: an overnight training run looks the same as a rented job, which is why it only annotates a finding and never alerts on its own. As everywhere, these are signs to judge, not verdicts, and the watch sees only what runs when it looks.

docs.title: Behaviour: the agent the /proc watch can't see (1.22)
docs.text:
An agent on a login or compute node shows up as agent. But an agent (or a careless script) running on someone's laptop and driving the cluster over the user's own ssh looks, from the cluster, exactly like the person typing — there's no agent process on the cluster to find. So the watch also reads what was done, not who typed it, from two things it already has: the process table, and this site's jobs table.

  • heavy (warning): a user process holding real CPU — by lifetime average, its whole CPU time (utime+stime) over its age, so a steady computation shows and a brief spike doesn't — of at least heavy_cpu cores (default 2), having used at least heavy_min_seconds CPU-seconds (default 600). Only on a login node: a compute node is where jobs are meant to be heavy, so heavy is dropped there (as a plain listener is). This is the long-standing "someone's running their work on the head node" catch, and it needs no root. ignore_users / ignore_programs leave out a sanctioned service.
  • From the jobs table (watch_jobs, read on the site each sweep; nothing where there's no Slurm):
  • job_burst (listed, not alerted): at least burst_jobs (default 60) sbatches by one user within burst_minutes (default 10). An array counts as one (its tasks share a submit time), so a 1,000-task array isn't a burst. It's listed rather than alerted because a legitimate parameter sweep bursts the same way — it surfaces who is submitting heavily, for you to glance at.
  • fail_fast (warning): at least fail_fast_jobs (default 15) of a user's jobs that FAILED within fail_fast_seconds (default 60) of starting. The shape of an agent resubmitting something it doesn't understand (node failures don't count — those aren't the user's doing).
  • job_churn (warning): the same job name resubmitted at least churn_repeats (default 8) times by one user, with cancellations between — a cancel/resubmit loop.

The job findings are attributed to the login host where the collector runs, with the user's NetID, and raise one alert per user and kind (as every finding does). Thresholds are all in the TOML; raise them, or ignore_users a service account, if a site's normal work trips one. As everywhere: signs to judge, not verdicts — a burst or a run of failures can be an ordinary bad day. We don't watch query rates (sacct/squeue hammering): nomad doesn't record user queries, so there's no honest signal there.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text: It is a set of signs for a person to judge, not a verdict: an administrator's own tunnel, a sanctioned service or a research server may well be fine (ignore_*). It sees what runs while it looks (every 15 minutes), not what ran in between. Without root it can't tell which process holds which socket, and an account determined to hide where a forward or a root shell came from still can; the checks make that deliberate, not easy. It doesn't stop anything: closing these doors (compute nodes reachable only through Slurm with pam_slurm_adopt, outbound traffic from compute nodes allowed only where needed, limits on login nodes) is the cluster's configuration, and what is allowed is the site's policy. an administrator's own tunnel, a sanctioned service or a research server may well be fine (ignore_*). It sees what runs while it looks (every 15 minutes), not what ran in between. It doesn't stop anything: closing these doors (compute nodes reachable only through Slurm with pam_slurm_adopt, outbound traffic from compute nodes allowed only where needed, limits on login nodes) is the cluster's configuration, and what is allowed is the site's policy.

docs.title: Proficiency Scoring
docs.text: NØMAÐ's Educational Analytics module tracks computational proficiency development through per-job behavioral fingerprints.

docs.title: Philosophy
docs.text:
Traditional HPC monitoring answers: "Did the job run?"

NØMAÐ Edu answers: "Did the user learn to use HPC effectively?"

This shift enables:

  • Instructors to measure learning outcomes, not just resource consumption
  • Mentors to identify specific skill gaps in research trainees
  • Users to self-assess and improve their HPC practices
  • Institutions to evaluate training program effectiveness

docs.title: The Five Dimensions
docs.text:
Every completed job is scored across five proficiency dimensions: 

  NØMAÐ Group Report — cs101
  Last 90 days · 4 members · 4 ran jobs · 4 scored · 935 of 935 jobs measured · demo-cluster

  Median overall: 72/100 across 4 people (middle half 69–73)
  Over the period: 1 of 4 improved, 3 steady, 0 declined

  By dimension (median, people):
    CPU        51   (4)
    Memory     87   (4)
    Time       81   (4)
    I/O        69   (4)
    GPU        70   (4)

  Most common to work on:
    CPU: 4 of 4
    I/O: 2 of 4

  Member             Jobs  Measured  Overall  Change  Weakest
  diana               200       200       66      +1  I/O
  charlie             243       243       70      +9  CPU
  alice               260       260       73      +2  CPU
  bob                 232       232       73      -2  CPU

The Console's Group Reports page shows the same figures; see edu.

docs.title: 1. CPU Efficiency
docs.text:
What it measures: How well did the user utilize requested CPU cores?

Formula: $\(\text{CPU Score} = \min\left(100, \frac{\text{CPU Time Used}}{\text{Cores} \times \text{Walltime}} \times 100\right)\)$

Scoring rubric:

Efficiency Score Level Interpretation ≥ 80% 85-100 Excellent Efficient parallelization 50-79% 65-84 Good Reasonable usage 25-49% 40-64 Developing Some waste, learning < 25% 0-39 Needs Work Significant over-allocation

Common issues:

  • Requesting 16 cores for single-threaded code
  • I/O-bound jobs with idle CPUs
  • Poor parallel scaling

Recommendations generated: 

CPU Efficiency: Very low CPU utilization at 21% — requested 4 
cores but used ~1. This wastes resources and may delay other 
users' jobs.

Try: #SBATCH --ntasks=1
     If your code is single-threaded, request 1 core.

docs.title: 2. Memory Efficiency
docs.text:
What it measures: How well did the user size their memory request?

Formula: $\(\text{Memory Score} = \begin{cases} 100 - (100 - \text{Utilization}) \times 0.5 & \text{if utilization} \geq 50\% \\ \text{Utilization} \times 1.5 & \text{if utilization} < 50\% \end{cases}\)$

The asymmetric formula penalizes under-utilization more harshly than slight over-utilization (better to have headroom than OOM kills).

Scoring rubric:

Utilization Score Level Interpretation 70-95% 85-100 Excellent Well-sized 50-69% 65-84 Good Acceptable headroom 30-49% 40-64 Developing Over-allocated < 30% 0-39 Needs Work Significant waste

Common issues:

  • Requesting 64GB when job uses 2GB
  • Copy-pasting scripts without adjusting memory
  • Not profiling memory requirements

Used more than requested: where Slurm doesn't enforce memory limits a job can peak above its request. It scores low and the advice is to request what it uses; it is not described as waste.

Readings no node could hold are not scored. Slurm's jobacct_gather/linux adds up the RSS of every process in a job, so memory the processes share (a data loader's forked workers, a memory-mapped dataset) is counted once per process -- one arachne job reported 7 TB. A peak above the largest node's memory at that site (from node_state) is shown as "not a measurement" and left out. Readings inflated less than that can't be told apart; the fix is at the source: JobAcctGatherParams=UsePss in slurm.conf, which counts shared memory in proportion. (jobacct_gather/cgroup avoids the multiplying too, but on Slurm 22.05 with cgroup v2 it counts transparent huge pages twice: arachne reported 2.0 GB for a job the kernel measured at 1.0 GB. With UsePss the same job read 1.0 GB.)

docs.title: 3. Time Estimation
docs.text:
What it measures: How accurately did the user estimate walltime?

Formula: $\(\text{Time Score} = \begin{cases} 95 + 5 \times (1 - \frac{\text{Runtime}}{\text{Requested}}) & \text{if ratio} \geq 0.7 \\ 70 \times \frac{\text{Runtime}}{\text{Requested}} & \text{if ratio} < 0.7 \end{cases}\)$

Using close to requested time (without exceeding) is optimal.

Scoring rubric:

Runtime/Requested Score Level Interpretation 70-100% 85-100 Excellent Accurate estimation 40-69% 65-84 Good Conservative but reasonable 20-39% 40-64 Developing Significant overestimation < 20% 0-39 Needs Work Gross overestimation

Why it matters:

  • Backfill scheduling depends on accurate time estimates
  • Over-requesting blocks resources from others
  • Under-requesting causes job kills

docs.title: 4. I/O Awareness
docs.text:
What it measures: Did the user choose appropriate storage for their workload?

Formula: $\(\text{I/O Score} = 100 - (\text{NFS Ratio} \times 50) - (\text{IO Wait} \times 2)\)$

Where: - NFS Ratio = NFS writes / Total writes - IO Wait = percentage of time waiting on I/O

Scoring rubric:

NFS Ratio IO Wait Score Level < 20% < 5% 85-100 Excellent 20-50% 5-15% 65-84 Good 50-80% 15-30% 40-64 Developing > 80% > 30% 0-39 Needs Work

Applicability: Scored only when NFS traffic was measured for the job. Slurm accounting has no NFS/local breakdown, so jobs measured only by the job collector show "not measured" rather than a score (before 1.7.5 the collector wrote an NFS ratio of 0 as a placeholder, which scored every job Excellent).

Common issues:

  • Writing temp files to NFS instead of local scratch
  • Not using $TMPDIR or /scratch
  • Reading input files repeatedly from network storage

Recommendations generated: 

I/O Awareness: High NFS write ratio (78%) causing I/O wait. 
Jobs with this pattern have 3x higher failure rates.

Try: export TMPDIR=/scratch/$USER/$SLURM_JOB_ID
     Write temporary files to local scratch, copy results 
     back at job end.

docs.title: 5. GPU Utilization
docs.text:
What it measures: Did the user effectively utilize requested GPUs?

Formula: $\(\text{GPU Score} = \frac{\text{GPU Utilization} + \text{GPU Memory Utilization}}{2}\)$

Scoring rubric:

GPU Util Score Level Interpretation ≥ 70% 85-100 Excellent Efficient GPU usage 40-69% 65-84 Good Acceptable 20-39% 40-64 Developing Under-utilizing expensive resource < 20% 0-39 Needs Work GPU mostly idle

Applicability: Only scored if the job requested GPUs and its GPU utilization was measured (DCGM data for its nodes and time window). A GPU job without that data shows "not measured": the request alone says nothing about how the GPUs were used.

Common issues:

  • CPU preprocessing starving GPU
  • Small batch sizes
  • Requesting GPU for CPU-only code

docs.title: Proficiency Levels
docs.text:
Scores map to four proficiency levels:

Score Range Level Description 85-100 Excellent Demonstrates strong HPC understanding 65-84 Good Reasonable usage with minor inefficiencies 40-64 Developing Learning, with clear room for improvement 0-39 Needs Work Significant resource waste or misconfiguration

docs.title: Overall Score
docs.text:
The overall score is the plain mean of the dimensions that apply to the job and were measured:

\[\text{Overall} = \frac{1}{|A|}\sum_{d \in A} s_d \qquad A = \text{applicable, measured dimensions}\]

A dimension that was not measured is left out, never counted as zero or as a default. For a person or a period, dimensions are averaged over their measured jobs first, and the overall is the mean of those averages. Only jobs NØMAÐ measured (with a job_summary row) are scored; the rest are counted, not scored.

docs.title: Database Storage
docs.text:
nomad edu explain records each job it explains in proficiency_scores. Trajectories, group reports and the Console's lists do not read this table: they score every measured job directly, so they cover everyone, not only the jobs someone happened to explain.

CREATE TABLE proficiency_scores (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    timestamp DATETIME,
    job_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    user_name TEXT NOT NULL,
    cluster TEXT,

    -- Dimension scores
    cpu_score REAL,
    cpu_level TEXT,
    memory_score REAL,
    memory_level TEXT,
    time_score REAL,
    time_level TEXT,
    io_score REAL,
    io_level TEXT,
    gpu_score REAL,
    gpu_level TEXT,
    gpu_applicable INTEGER,

    -- Overall
    overall_score REAL,
    overall_level TEXT,

    -- Recommendations
    needs_work TEXT,  -- JSON array of dimension names
    strengths TEXT,   -- JSON array of dimension names

    UNIQUE(job_id)
);

docs.title: CLI Commands
docs.text:
# Explain a single job
nomad edu explain <job_id>
nomad edu explain <job_id> --json
nomad edu explain <job_id> --no-progress

# User trajectory
nomad edu trajectory <username>
nomad edu trajectory <username> --days 30
nomad edu trajectory <username> --json

# Group report
nomad edu report <group_name>
nomad edu report <group_name> --days 90
nomad edu report <group_name> --json

docs.title: Integration with SLURM
docs.text:
For automatic scoring, add to SLURM epilog: 

#!/bin/bash
# /etc/slurm/epilog.d/nomad-edu.sh

nomad edu explain $SLURM_JOB_ID --json >> /var/log/nomad/edu.log 2>&1

Users can then view their proficiency in the dashboard or via CLI.

docs.title: Try Without HPC
docs.text:
pip install nomad-hpc
nomad demo

This launches a dashboard at http://localhost:8050 with synthetic data.

docs.title: The Console's demo (1.17.4)
docs.text:
nomad demo --console ~/nomad-demo

writes a demo for the Console in ~/nomad-demo: the demo cluster's data with a cast of made-up people in it (nomad_demo.db), and the nomad.toml that makes each what they are (.config/nomad/nomad.toml):

Who Is Sees bob a student in CS 101 his own jobs, some running now eve the Grace Lab's research assistant its members one by one, as its PI does, but not Grace's own work grace the PI of the Grace Lab (grace$) her lab's members one by one, their work, and what needs her attention: a job of charlie's that will never start, jobs out of memory, who holds the lab's data and where (nas-01, everyone's $HOME; nas-02, the lab's own) henry the instructor of CS 101 his class olive an operator everything; changes no settings adam an admin everything, settings included

Start the Console on it from the Console's backend folder, with the Python the Console runs on (its venv's: HOME= also moves where Python looks for packages installed with pip install --user):

HOME=~/nomad-demo NOMAD_CONSOLE_DEMO=1 /path/to/console/venv/bin/python -m uvicorn app.main:app --port 8000

The demo is "now" as it was made: its running jobs and its nodes' reading are of that moment, and after a couple of hours the Console says the cluster hasn't reported since. Make it again just before a session.

Its sign-in page then offers each of them, one click and no password: for trying the Console, for tutorials and for screenshots. The sign-in picker appears only with NOMAD_CONSOLE_DEMO=1 and a database nomad demo --console made (it says so in its demo_info table), so it can't open a real Console. Running the command again replaces its own demo, never another database or nomad.toml, and never in your home folder (whose nomad.toml nomad reads). A hub never syncs a demo's marker, so a hub's database is never taken for a demo.
