docs.title: Data Readiness
docs.text: The nomad readiness command helps administrators determine when sufficient data has been collected for reliable ML predictions.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
nomad readiness              # Basic readiness report
nomad readiness -v           # Verbose with feature details
nomad readiness --db mydata.db   # Specify database

docs.title: What It Assesses
docs.text: The readiness estimator evaluates four dimensions:

docs.title: 1. Sample Size
docs.text: Level Jobs Score Minimum 100+ 40% Recommended 500+ 70% Optimal 1000+ 100%

docs.title: 2. Class Balance
docs.text: Compares successful vs failed jobs. Ideal ratio is between 60:40 and 90:10. Extremely imbalanced data (>95% one class) reduces prediction reliability.

docs.title: 3. Feature Coverage
docs.text:
Checks that all 17 feature dimensions have sufficient variance:

  • CPU efficiency
  • Memory utilization
  • I/O wait percentage
  • NFS write ratio
  • Runtime characteristics
  • Exit signals
  • And more...

Features with zero variance (all same value) don't contribute to predictions.

docs.title: 4. Data Recency
docs.text:
Recent data is weighted more heavily. The estimator checks:

  • Jobs from last 24 hours
  • Jobs from last 7 days
  • Jobs from last 30 days

Stale data (>30 days old only) triggers a warning.

docs.title: Verbose Mode
docs.text:
With -v or --verbose, see per-feature statistics: 

nomad readiness -v

Shows coefficient of variation (CV%) for each feature, helping identify which metrics contribute most to predictions.

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
The command provides actionable recommendations:

  • Low sample size: "Continue collecting data. Run nomad collect to gather more jobs."
  • Class imbalance: "Dataset is heavily skewed toward successful jobs. Consider longer collection period to capture more failure modes."
  • Missing features: "GPU metrics unavailable. Install nvidia-smi for GPU-enabled nodes."
  • Stale data: "Most recent job is 15 days old. Ensure collectors are running."

docs.title: Reference System
docs.text: The nomad ref command provides built-in documentation and code navigation without leaving the terminal.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
nomad ref                          # Browse all topics
nomad ref alerts                   # Alert system overview
nomad ref dyn diversity            # Dynamics diversity command
nomad ref collectors disk          # Disk collector details
nomad ref config                   # Configuration reference
nomad ref search regime divergence # Search across all documentation
nomad ref tessera                  # TESSERA methodology
nomad ref concepts governance      # Ostrom governance framework

docs.title: Knowledge Base
docs.text:
The reference system includes 60 entries across 5 categories:

Category Count Description Commands 32 All CLI commands and subcommands Collectors 9 Data collection modules Concepts 11 TESSERA, diversity indices, governance Config 5 nomad.toml configuration sections Alerts 3 Alert system, thresholds, backends

Each entry includes:

  • Description — plain language explanation
  • Source files — paths in the repository
  • Configuration — relevant nomad.toml keys
  • Mathematical basis — formulas where applicable
  • Examples — CLI usage examples
  • Related — cross-references to related entries

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
Full-text search with relevance scoring across all entries:

nomad ref search "disk alert"
nomad ref search "simpson diversity"
nomad ref search "SLURM collector"

docs.title: Console Integration
docs.text: In the NØMAÐ Console (paid product), the Reference page provides a graphical interface with category filters, live search, and clickable cross-references.

docs.title: Adding Entries
docs.text:
Reference entries are stored as YAML files in nomad/reference/entries/. To add a new entry:

entries:
  my.new.topic:
    title: "My New Topic"
    summary: "One-line description."
    description: "Longer explanation."
    source_files:
      - nomad/my_module.py
    config_section: "my_section"
    examples:
      - "nomad my-command --flag"
    tags:
      - my-tag
    category: commands

The entry is immediately available in nomad ref and nomad ref search.

docs.title: Setup Wizard
docs.text:
The nomad init wizard configures NØMAÐ for your environment. It detects available tools, asks about your infrastructure, and generates a configuration file at ~/.config/nomad/nomad.toml.

nomad init

This guide walks through each step of the wizard with explanations and recommendations.

docs.title: Step 1: Connection Mode
docs.text:
Where is NØMAÐ running?
  1) On the cluster headnode
  2) On a separate machine (laptop, desktop, etc.)

Option 1 — On the headnode is the most common choice. NØMAÐ runs directly on the machine that has access to SLURM commands (sinfo, squeue, sacct) and local filesystems. This is the simplest setup with no SSH configuration needed for the local cluster.

Option 2 — Remote machine is for cases where you want to run NØMAÐ from a laptop or desktop that connects to the cluster via SSH. NØMAÐ will SSH into the cluster to run commands. You will need to provide SSH credentials (hostname, user, key path).

Recommendation

Choose Option 1 whenever possible. Running on the headnode gives direct access to SLURM, filesystems, and system tools without SSH overhead.

docs.title: Step 2: Deployment Strategy
docs.text: NØMAÐ supports two deployment strategies. The wizard explains both and asks how many systems this instance will monitor.

docs.title: Strategy A — One NØMAÐ per machine + sync
docs.text:
Install NØMAÐ on each machine independently. Each instance monitors its own environment and stores data in its own database. Use nomad sync on a central machine to merge all databases into a unified dashboard.

This is the recommended approach when each machine has a different role — for example, an HPC cluster with SLURM, an interactive server with Jupyter/RStudio, and a workstation management server.

In this case, answer 1 on each machine:

  • HPC headnode: 1 cluster (HPC type) — monitors partitions, jobs, nodes
  • Interactive server: 1 cluster (HPC type, SLURM auto-skipped) — monitors sessions, disk, CPU
  • Workstation manager: 1 cluster (Workstation type) — monitors lab machines via SSH

Then on a central machine, configure nomad sync to pull all databases together:

nomad sync                        # Merge all site databases
nomad dashboard --db combined.db  # Unified view across all sites

docs.title: Strategy B — One NØMAÐ monitors everything
docs.text:
A single NØMAÐ instance monitors multiple systems from one machine, using SSH for remote access. This works when you have a machine that can reach all targets.

For example, to monitor both an HPC cluster and a set of workstations from the same headnode, answer 2:

  • Cluster 1: HPC cluster (SLURM, local)
  • Cluster 2: Workstation group (department machines, via SSH)

docs.title: Which strategy to choose?
docs.text:
Scenario Strategy Why Machines have different roles (HPC, interactive, workstations) A — one per machine + sync Each instance uses the right collectors for its environment Everything is reachable from one machine B — single instance Simpler setup, no sync needed Machines are on different networks A — one per machine + sync SSH may not work across network boundaries You want resilience (one site going down doesn't stop others) A — one per machine + sync Each site collects independently

You can always start with Strategy B and split later

If you start with a single instance monitoring everything and later want to split, just run nomad init on each machine separately and set up nomad sync. The data format is the same either way.

docs.title: Step 3: Cluster Configuration
docs.text: For each cluster, the wizard asks for a name and type.

docs.title: Cluster Name
docs.text:
Cluster name [cluster-1]: spydur

Choose a short, descriptive name. This appears in the dashboard navigation tabs and in the combined database when using nomad sync. Use lowercase with no spaces.

docs.title: Cluster Type
docs.text:
What type of system is this?
  1) HPC cluster (managed by SLURM)
  2) Workstation group (department machines, not SLURM)

Option 1 — HPC cluster enables SLURM collectors (squeue, sacct, sinfo), job metrics, node state, group membership, and job accounting. The wizard will auto-detect SLURM partitions.

Option 2 — Workstation group disables SLURM collectors and enables the WorkstationCollector, which monitors remote machines via SSH. You will be asked for department names and hostnames. Workstation data appears in the Workstations page of the dashboard.

What gets disabled for workstation groups

When you select workstation group, the following collectors are automatically disabled since they require SLURM: slurm, job_metrics, node_state. The disk, vmstat, gpu, nfs, groups (membership only; job accounting needs Slurm) and workstation collectors remain active.

docs.title: Step 3a: HPC Cluster — Partition Detection
docs.text:
If you selected HPC cluster, the wizard auto-detects SLURM partitions:

Detecting SLURM partitions...
Found partitions: basic, medium, large, gpunodes, chemlab

If auto-detection fails (SLURM not installed locally, or running in remote mode), you can type partition names manually:

Type your partition names separated by commas:
Partitions: basic, medium, large, gpunodes

Tip

You can find partition names by running sinfo -h -o "%P" on the cluster headnode.

docs.title: Step 3b: Workstation Group — Departments and Machines
docs.text:
If you selected workstation group, the wizard asks for department organization:

Type your department/lab names, separated by commas:
Departments: smith-lab

Then for each department, provide the hostnames of machines to monitor:

Type the hostnames for 'smith-lab', separated by commas:
Nodes for smith-lab: ws01, ws02, ws03, ws04, ws05, ws06

The WorkstationCollector will SSH to each machine and collect CPU, memory, disk, load, and user session data.

SSH Access Required

The current user must be able to SSH to each workstation with key-based authentication (no password). Test with: ssh -o BatchMode=yes hostname "hostname". The wizard writes the current username as ssh_user in the configuration.

docs.title: Step 4: Filesystem Monitoring
docs.text:
Which filesystems should NØMAÐ monitor for disk usage?
Filesystems (comma-separated) [/, /home]: /, /home, /scratch

These are the local filesystems on the machine running NØMAÐ. The DiskCollector monitors these paths, computes fill rates using derivative analysis, and fires alerts when usage exceeds thresholds.

Common paths:

  • / — Root filesystem
  • /home — User home directories
  • /scratch — Scratch storage (often the most critical to monitor)
  • /localscratch — Node-local scratch

Workstation filesystems

For workstation groups, this setting applies to the machine running NØMAÐ (not the workstations). The WorkstationCollector independently collects disk usage from each remote workstation via SSH.

docs.title: Step 5: Optional Features
docs.text: The wizard probes for available tools and asks about optional collectors:

docs.title: GPU Monitoring
docs.text:
✓ nvidia-smi found (NVIDIA GPU detected)
Enable GPU monitoring? [Y/n]: y

Enabled when nvidia-smi is available. Collects GPU utilization, memory, temperature, and power draw.

docs.title: NFS Monitoring
docs.text:
✓ NFS monitoring available (nfsiostat found)
Enable NFS monitoring? [Y/n]: y

Enabled when nfsiostat is found. Monitors NFS mount performance including read/write throughput and latency.

docs.title: Interactive Sessions
docs.text:
✓ JupyterHub detected
Enable interactive session monitoring? [Y/n]: y

Detects running JupyterHub or RStudio Server processes. When enabled, the InteractiveCollector tracks active sessions, memory usage, idle time, and session type.

docs.title: Step 6: Alerts
docs.text:
NØMAÐ can send you email alerts when something needs
attention (disk filling up, nodes going down, etc.).
Your email address (press Enter to skip): admin@example.com

Providing an email address enables the alert pipeline. Alerts are always stored in the database and visible in the dashboard regardless of email configuration.

For email delivery, NØMAÐ uses the system mail command if available. No SMTP server configuration is required. You can set up a daily report via cron:

0 8 * * * /path/to/nomad insights brief | mail -s "NØMAÐ Daily Report" admin@example.com

Advanced alert configuration

After the wizard, you can edit ~/.config/nomad/nomad.toml to configure Slack webhooks, custom thresholds, severity filters, and cooldown periods. See the Alerts documentation for details.

docs.title: Step 7: Dashboard Port
docs.text:
The NØMAÐ dashboard is a web page you open in your
browser to view cluster status, node health, and alerts.
Dashboard port [8050]:

The default port 8050 works for most installations. Choose a different port if 8050 is already in use.

For remote access, set up an SSH tunnel:

ssh -L 8050:localhost:8050 user@headnode

Then open http://localhost:8050 in your browser.

docs.title: Step 8: Condo reports
docs.text:
Register condos for the monthly condo reports? [y/N]:

A condo is a set of nodes a lab bought, lent to everyone else through a guest partition while the lab isn't using them. Answer yes and the wizard asks, for each Slurm cluster, which partition is the guest partition (the one named like "condo" by default), lists the condos in it (the partitions whose nodes all sit inside it), and asks each one's owner NetID; then the owners' mail domain and who should review the reports first. It writes report.toml beside nomad.toml, the cluster named as in nomad.toml (condos on several clusters monitored from one machine go together as this-cluster: that machine's database holds them all); written as root, the nomad account can read it. See Condo reports.

docs.title: Summary and Next Steps
docs.text:
After completing the wizard, you will see a summary:

✓ NØMAÐ configured!

Config:  ~/.config/nomad/nomad.toml
Data:    ~/.local/share/nomad

Clusters:
  • spydur: 5 partitions, 30 nodes (local)

Enabled: GPU monitoring, NFS monitoring

What to do next:
  1. Review your config:     nano ~/.config/nomad/nomad.toml
  2. Verify environment:     nomad syscheck
  3. Start collecting data:  nomad collect
  4. Open the dashboard:     nomad dashboard

docs.title: Verify Your Environment
docs.text:
nomad syscheck

This checks Python version, SLURM availability, system tools, database state, and filesystem access. Fix any warnings before starting collection.

docs.title: Test Collection
docs.text:
nomad collect --once

Run a single collection cycle to verify everything works. Check for errors in the output — successful collectors show ✓ with a record count.

docs.title: Start Continuous Collection
docs.text:
nohup nomad collect > ~/.local/share/nomad/logs/collect.log 2>&1 &

For production, consider running the collector as a systemd user service for automatic restart on failure.

docs.title: Launch the Dashboard
docs.text:
nomad dashboard

Open http://localhost:8050 in your browser.

docs.title: Multi-Site Setup
docs.text:
To monitor multiple sites from a single dashboard:

  1. Install and configure NØMAÐ on each site using nomad init
  2. On a central machine (the hub), list the sites under [hub] in its nomad.toml (~/.config/nomad/nomad.toml, or /etc/nomad/nomad.toml for a service account; nomad -c FILE sync names another):
[hub]
output_db = "~/.local/share/nomad/combined.db"   # the default

[[hub.sites]]
name = "cluster-a"
host = "headnode-a"
ssh_user = "monitor"
db_path = "~/.local/share/nomad/cluster-a.db"

[[hub.sites]]
name = "cluster-b"
host = "headnode-b"
ssh_user = "monitor"
db_path = "~/.local/share/nomad/cluster-b.db"

[[hub.sites]]
name = "hub"                  # collectors on the hub itself (lab workstations, say)
host = "localhost"            # read directly: no ssh to itself
db_path = "/var/lib/nomad/nomad.db"

A relative output_db is in the data directory (~/.local/share/nomad). A localhost site's partitions come from the nomad.toml in use, and an action run on it (nomad actions run --site) runs on the hub itself, without the agent key. ~/.config/nomad/sync.toml with top-level [[sites]] still works, with a warning.

A site reached through a jump host (ProxyJump in the hub account's ~/.ssh/config) works from a service account too: ssh runs a jump through $SHELL, which for an account with no login shell is /sbin/nologin, so since 1.17.3 nomad sets SHELL=/bin/sh for itself and its ssh and scp when $SHELL is missing or can't run one. A shell that works is left as it is.

A site that can't send its own alerts (no way to the mail server, or set up with nomad init --quick, which writes no [alerts]) can have the hub send its node alerts: alerts = "hub" in its [[hub.sites]] entry (alerts).

  1. Run sync and launch the combined dashboard:
nomad sync
nomad dashboard --db ~/.local/share/nomad/combined.db
  1. Set up a cron for automatic syncing:
*/10 * * * * /path/to/nomad sync 2>/dev/null
  1. See how the syncs go (it only reads; the Console's sync.status action runs it):
nomad sync status

For each site in [hub] sites: when its data was last brought up to date, how (only what changed, copied whole, or kept what the hub had because the sync failed), how many rows, the last live pull, whether it is late (more than alert_after_minutes, 120), what the next sync will ask for, how many attempts failed in a row and the last error. A site never synced, and one no longer in [hub] sites (its rows go at the next sync), are said too. nomad sync -c FILE -o DB status reads the hub a sync with those options would.

How a site's database reaches the hub, and what happens when it doesn't:

  • Only what changed (1.17). Each site keeps a log of the rows its collectors add, change and delete (triggers on its tables, in its own database: the tables _nomad_changes, _nomad_capture and _nomad_capture_meta, and triggers named _nomad_*). Each sync asks for what is in the log past the point the hub has, and the hub applies it to the combined database in place, one transaction per site; the log is then dropped up to that point. A run writes megabytes. Until 1.16 every sync copied every site's whole database and rebuilt the combined database: on a four-site hub about 24 GB of writes a run, which wore out the hub's SSD, and each site wrote a full snapshot of its database for every pull.
  • The site needs only python3 (3.6 or later): the hub sends the exporter (nomad/db/delta_site.py) with each request and runs it there with python3 -, so nothing else is installed for it. A site where it can't run (no python3, or one without its sqlite3 module) is copied whole at every sync, as before, and so is one whose changes could not be had three syncs in a row; each sync tries the log again first.
  • The exporter never keeps a collector waiting: it reads a batch per statement and holds nothing open while the hub reads its answer, and it drops the log a batch at a time; it reads the log a part at a time, so it needs a few tens of MB however far behind the hub is. The hub spools each answer to a file and applies it a record at a time, so a table sent whole (after a migration) takes no more memory than a few rows.
  • A site is copied whole once (a snapshot, as below, removed when applied): the first time; when its log was put back (its database replaced); when its database was restored from a backup (each answer carries a token the hub sends back, which a restored database doesn't know); when the hub is more than 3 million changes behind (silent for a day or more); or when the log no longer reaches back to where the hub is. A hub whose combined database moved, or that moved to another host, is a new hub to the sites: each is copied whole once. A table recreated, renamed or given new columns or unique keys by a migration is sent whole, once. A migration that drops a column must first call nomad.db.delta_site.untrack(conn, table) (the triggers name the columns); the next sync puts the triggers back and sends the table whole.
  • nomad sync --full copies every site whole again, into the combined database in place. The first sync after upgrading to 1.17 builds the combined database whole once, in the form later syncs update, and copies it into the published file with SQLite's backup (one write the Console sees whole or not at all) instead of renaming a new file over it: a file renamed over one in use, under its write-ahead log, comes out corrupted once the hub writes in place. The site copies it was built from are not kept.
  • Each hub has its own place in a site's log (by host and combined database), so a trial nomad sync -o /tmp/x.db does not make the real hub copy everything again; the log is kept back to the oldest place among the hubs heard from in the last two days. Once more than 6 million changes wait, the hubs more than 3 million behind stop holding the log back (each copies the site if it comes back); the others are not affected.
  • A site whose sync fails keeps what the hub had of it (sync_sites.source says kept, synced_at and last_success stay at the last good sync) and is asked again next time, from where it was. A site taken out of [hub] sites has its rows removed at the next sync, and is told: its log and triggers are taken out there unless another hub reads it. If it can't be told, its own nomad collect (1.17) takes out a log no hub has read for a week.
  • After each sync the hub folds its write-ahead log into the combined database and cuts it back (after a whole copy it would otherwise stay the size of that site's data).
  • Going back to a nomad older than 1.17: run nomad sync --remove-logs on the hub first (with 1.17). It takes the log and triggers out of every site's database and empties the combined database's write-ahead log, which the older nomad's rebuild needs (it renames its new file over the old one); if something kept reading it, stop the Console before that first older sync.

The copies the full rebuild, and a site's first sync, are made of:

  • Each site writes a consistent snapshot of its database (SQLite's .backup, safe while its collectors keep writing; with the sqlite3 command, or with its python3 3.7+ when it has no sqlite3 command) in /tmp when it has ample room, otherwise beside the database, and the hub copies it. A site with neither is copied as its live file, which can be torn without looking it: such a copy is not trusted to say where the site's log stands: instead, when the log could be set up there, the site's exporter sends every table whole, as of a place in its log, and from then on only changes come. If that fails (it can take long on a big database), the live file is copied after all, and the exporter is not asked again for a day. A login node's /tmp is often a few GB shared by everyone, smaller than the database. When there is room in neither, the reason says so ("no room for a snapshot: the database is 6.0 GB; …").
  • The snapshot is always removed afterwards; any left by a run that died are removed after two hours. Time limits follow the database's size.
  • The copy replaces the hub's cached copy of that site only once it is complete. In a full rebuild, when a site's pull fails, its cached copy stands in (marked as such in sync_sites, its last_success left at the last live pull), so one site's trouble doesn't hold back the others. Once the hub syncs only changes it keeps no copies (sync_cache is emptied).
  • A site whose last live pull is older than alert_after_minutes (120 by default) raises a sync alert through the hub's [alerts] settings: a warning, critical after a day, with the reason, then reminders while it lasts:
[hub]
alert_after_minutes = 120
  • A site that syncs but has stopped collecting, a collector that stopped or fails every run, a GPU node gone quiet and a GPU node whose DCGM stopped answering raise collection alerts after the sync (1.14.5; see alerts); nomad collection-check lists them.

docs.title: Configuration Reference
docs.text:
The wizard generates ~/.config/nomad/nomad.toml. Key sections:

Section Purpose [general] Data directory, cluster name [database] Database filename [collectors.disk] Filesystem paths to monitor [collectors.slurm] SLURM partitions (HPC only) [collectors.workstation] SSH user, workstation hostnames [collectors.gpu] GPU monitoring toggle [collectors.nfs] NFS mount monitoring [collectors.interactive] Jupyter/RStudio session detection [alerts] Email, Slack, webhook, thresholds [dashboard] Port, host binding [clusters.*] Cluster metadata and partition descriptions

See the Configuration documentation for the full reference.

docs.title: Storage use
docs.text:
Who holds each storage server's space, and on what (1.16): for each path a server exports (/home, /scratch, a NAS's datasets),

  • each owner's space now, and how it changed over the last 7, 30 or 90 days;
  • their quota, where one is set (ZFS user, group and dataset quotas; XFS user, group and project limits);
  • for each folder at the top of the path (/home/USER), the folders inside it (/home/USER/FOLDER): size, number of files, the newest change, and how much hasn't changed in 180 and in 365 days;
  • when each owner last ran a job, on any cluster nomad collects.

It is meant to inform: what is filling a filesystem and how fast, what has lain untouched for a year, and whose it is, including people who no longer run anything. It changes nothing on the servers.

This is separate from the storage collector ([collectors.storage], in Collectors), which reads a server's pools and capacity, and from disk, which reads df on each host.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Seeing everyone's files takes root on the storage server (or sudo, or an account given just those rights: see Who runs it), and nomad itself never runs with them. So the part that reads runs there: a short POSIX sh script, nomad-storage.sh, that only reads (df, xfs_quota report, zfs list, zfs get, zfs userspace and groupspace, and for the scan find and stat) and writes what it read to a folder that its owner and one group can read (/var/lib/nomad-storage by default, mode 750, files 640). The storage_use collector, on a site or on the hub, picks those files up with an ordinary account in that group, over ssh or from the same machine, and stores them.

The script runs on Linux (GNU find and stat) and on FreeBSD, as TrueNAS CORE is (BSD find and stat); it needs nothing else installed. It writes:

  • usage.txt, from the filesystem's own accounting: fast, so run it hourly. ZFS always keeps per-owner counts; XFS keeps them when user or group accounting is on (the uquota/gquota or uqnoenforce/gqnoenforce mount options; limits are not needed). Other filesystems (ext4, NFS) are listed with their size, and say that the scan counts them by folder instead. The counts are the whole dataset's or filesystem's: for a path inside one (not its mount point), the file says so, and so does nomad storage use.
  • scan.txt, from walking the files: run it nightly. It works at the lowest priority (nice 19, and ionice idle on Linux), stays on one filesystem, and stops after its time budget (3 hours by default). The top folders tried longest ago go first, and each try, finished or stopped at the budget, goes to the back of the line: a large filesystem is covered over a few nights, and a folder too big for one night can't hold up the others (nomad storage use says how many never finish; give the scan more time with -s). A file with several hard links counts once in its top folder. A folder at the top of a path that is itself another of the paths given to the same run (/mnt/pool/home when the run has /mnt/pool and /mnt/pool/home, or a symbolic link to it) is left to that path, so its files are counted once, and a path given twice is scanned once; nomad storage status lists both. A top folder that holds another of the paths deeper down (/mnt/pool/labs when the run also has /mnt/pool/labs/shared) is still counted whole, so that path's files are counted in both: nomad storage status says so, and the fix is to leave one of the two out of the run.

Sizes are the space files take on disk (as du says, after ZFS compression), in both files. Snapshots aren't counted.

The script makes its folder itself, with a .nomad-storage file in it, and refuses an existing folder it didn't make, so that a mistyped --dir can't change the permissions of a pool or a home. The script, its folder and every folder above them must be changeable only by root (or the account running it), or it refuses to run, naming the folder and what to do: anyone else could swap them for something else. A folder its group may write is refused (even a group of one: accounts sharing its number don't always show), as is one with an access list (ACL) that may let others write it; a umask of 002 leaves new folders group-writable, so chmod g-w the folders you make for it. It sets its own PATH, whatever the caller's. One run of each kind goes at a time: a scan still going when the next is due is left to finish. Folders at the top of a path whose names hold a tab, a line break or a backslash, and symbolic links, are left out (and counted); files inside a top folder whose paths hold a line break are counted together, in a folder of their own. A path the scan can't list says so, and its folders keep their last figures.

docs.title: Setting it up
docs.text:
On a machine with nomad, print the script and how to run it:

nomad storage script > nomad-storage.sh
nomad storage cron /home /scratch --group nomadread --server fs1

cron prints the lines for root's crontab, the same for TrueNAS's Tasks > Cron Jobs, and the nomad.toml part for the collector. --group is a group on the storage server that the collecting account is in (the files are not readable by anyone else); --seconds is the scan's budget; --dir where the files go; --run-as who runs it.

docs.title: Who runs it
docs.text:
--run-as How For root (default) root's crontab; on TrueNAS, Cron Jobs with Run As User root a server where you are root sudo --user NAME NAME's crontab runs it with sudo -n; the sudoers lines it prints allow exactly those two command lines and nothing else a server where you work through sudo sudo-readers --user NAME --dir D NAME's crontab runs it as NAME (-S), and it asks sudo -n only for xfs_quota and zfs (usage) and GNU du (the scan) a Linux server where sudo already lets NAME run those, and nothing else as root owners --user NAME --dir D NAME's crontab runs it as NAME, and the scan measures each top folder as its owner (-O: sudo -n -u OWNER find) a Linux server where sudo lets NAME act as the other accounts but not as root (see Measuring as each owner) user --user NAME systemd runs it as NAME with only the right to read every file and folder (CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH), writing only to its folder a Linux server where nothing should run as root

In every case the script is owned by root and writable only by root (install -o root -m 755), in folders only root can change: whoever can change it can make it do anything its runner can. For sudo, the sudoers lines name the folder, the group and the paths, and cron takes only paths of letters, digits and . _ / + @ , : = -, which sudoers, cron and systemd all read as written; with sudo's usual env_reset, the caller's environment doesn't reach the script either.

With sudo-readers, the script and its folder belong to NAME (in NAME's home, say) and nothing of nomad's runs as root but xfs_quota, zfs and du themselves. The scan's figures are the same as with find, except that an empty folder counts as a file and the owners of the folders inside each top folder aren't read (the top folder's owner is).

Run as an account without root, the scan reads what that account may read, and each top folder says how many files or folders it couldn't (nomad storage use: "couldn't read"). On XFS, each owner's counts need root (xfs_quota's report): run usage as root or through sudo there, with a folder of its own (root's runs won't write into a folder another account owns), and the scan as the account; give the source usage_dir for the usage folder. On ZFS, zfs allow -u NAME userused,groupused,userquota,groupquota DATASET lets the account read the counts. Every file says which account wrote it (nomad storage status).

docs.title: Measuring as each owner
docs.text:
Some servers give an account the right to act as the other accounts through sudo (to install software for them, say), but not as root. There, -O (nomad storage cron --run-as owners) measures each top folder as the account that owns it, which may read all of it even when no one else may.

  • What it runs: for each owner, one sudo -n -u '#UID' find (by number, so it is exactly the folder's owner), for all of that owner's top folders on every path, from /, read only, at the lowest priority (nice 19, ionice idle) and within the scan's budget. It prints each folder's depth, owner and path and each file's size, time, links and inode, nothing else. Paths are passed as arguments, never through a shell, and an owner is acted as only when the system gives it a name made of letters, digits and . _ -. A folder of the account running the script is read without sudo.
  • The sudo rule it relies on: either one sudo already has, letting the account run commands as people's accounts (sudo -l as the account shows a rule such as (%GROUP) ALL), or, where there is none, a rule for nomad-storage-find alone. Never give it find itself: find can run any program (-exec), delete and write files, so a rule for find is a rule for anything, as any account it names, slurm's and munge's included. nomad-storage-find is a few lines of sh that take absolute folder paths and run find over them with the fixed, printing-only expression above. As root (sudo 1.8.28 or later):
nomad storage script --find > nomad-storage-find
install -o root -g root -m 755 nomad-storage-find /usr/local/sbin/nomad-storage-find
visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/nomad-storage
    NAME ALL=(ALL,!root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/sbin/nomad-storage-find

and give the script -F /usr/local/sbin/nomad-storage-find (nomad storage cron --run-as owners --find-wrapper /usr/local/sbin/nomad-storage-find). It refuses a wrapper that isn't nomad-storage-find, or that anyone but root could change or swap: give its real path, with no link in it (sudoers names that path), and the file and every folder from / down to it must be root's and writable by root only. (%GROUP) in place of (ALL,!root) narrows it to one group's accounts. Where sudoers has Defaults requiretty (older RHEL), add Defaults:NAME !requiretty: cron has no terminal, and sudo would refuse every owner. - How often: each top folder weekly, on a night of its own (spread over the seven by its path), and nightly when it is large (10 GB or more, -L GB, --large) or changed since it was last measured (a plain stat of it: an entry made, removed or renamed directly in it, or a new owner or mode; not its ctime, which backups that keep access times change every night). A folder whose last measurement didn't finish is measured again the next night, and one missed for more than a week is caught up. The others keep their last measurement, shown with when it was taken (measured in nomad storage use). Each night's file holds only that night's measurements, so the collector must read it before the next night's run (it reads every few minutes): a night it misses leaves those folders at their earlier figures until they are measured again. - What isn't measured: top folders of root and of system accounts (numbered below 1000, -U UID, --min-uid), for which sudo isn't even asked; of owners sudo refuses (an account the rule leaves out), asked again only after a week, or sooner if the folder changes hands, since sudo logs every refusal; and of owners with no name. Their last figures stand, if there are any, and nomad storage status says how many owners and top folders weren't measured, and why. A folder inside a top folder that belongs to someone else is read only as far as the owner of the top folder may read it (couldn't read, counted from find's own output, in any locale). Such a measurement is short of what is there: nomad storage status and nomad storage use flag it. It is still at least what is there, so it stands when it is larger than the folder's last whole measurement (the folder grew); when it is smaller (an owner may make a folder unreadable to hide it), the last whole one stands, for four weeks at most (a lab folder holding a member's private folder is never read whole, and a real cleanup has to show), and never once the top folder has a new owner (the old owner's figure says nothing of the new one's). A folder with no earlier figure (new, or renamed: where people make their own top folders, as on a shared scratch) has nothing to hold, so its first short figure stands, flagged. When the scan's time runs out, the folders the owner's find had finished count as measured, the one it was in is short, and the rest wait for the next night. - Each owner's total comes from the scan, as on a filesystem without per-owner accounting (usage, run as an ordinary account, reads only df). The collector reads the files on the server itself (a source without host) or over ssh, as for the other ways of running it.

It needs GNU find (Linux), and can't be combined with -S. The alternative is one line in sudoers that lets the account run the script itself as root (--run-as sudo): root owns the script, and the account can't change it. That reads everything, every night, within the budget, in one pass.

docs.title: On a Linux file server
docs.text:
As root on the server:

install -o root -m 755 nomad-storage.sh /usr/local/sbin/nomad-storage.sh
sh /usr/local/sbin/nomad-storage.sh -g nomadread usage /home /scratch
head /var/lib/nomad-storage/usage.txt
crontab -e

and add the two lines nomad storage cron printed:

17 * * * * /bin/sh /usr/local/sbin/nomad-storage.sh -d /var/lib/nomad-storage -g nomadread usage /home /scratch
30 1 * * * /bin/sh /usr/local/sbin/nomad-storage.sh -d /var/lib/nomad-storage -g nomadread -s 10800 scan /home /scratch

cron's short PATH is fine: the script looks in /usr/sbin and /sbin for xfs_quota and zfs itself.

docs.title: On TrueNAS
docs.text: Changes on TrueNAS go through its web interface: the system disk is replaced at upgrades, and anything put there by hand is lost. Put the script on a pool (say /mnt/POOL/nomad-storage/nomad-storage.sh) and give it a folder there that doesn't exist yet (/mnt/POOL/nomad-storage/out; the script makes it), then in Tasks > Cron Jobs > Add, with Run As User root, add the usage line (hourly) and the scan line (daily) that nomad storage cron ... --script /mnt/POOL/nomad-storage/nomad-storage.sh --dir /mnt/POOL/nomad-storage/out prints. The collecting account is a TrueNAS user in the group given to -g, with SSH on; the folders above the output folder must let it through (execute permission), and only root may change them (/mnt/POOL/nomad-storage owned by root, not a share's dataset). On a dataset with NFSv4 ACLs, its ACL mode must allow chmod (the script stops and says so otherwise).

docs.title: The collector
docs.text:
In nomad.toml where the collector runs (a site, or the hub):

[collectors.storage_use]
enabled = true
# every_minutes = 60          # how often each server's files are read
# keep_days = 30              # every reading kept this long; one a day after
# timeout = 30                # seconds a server has to answer

[[collectors.storage_use.sources]]
server = "fs1"                # the name nomad shows
host = "fs1"                  # ssh to it; leave out when the files are on this machine
dir = "/var/lib/nomad-storage"
# ssh_user = "..."            # default: the account nomad collects as
# usage_dir = "..."           # usage.txt's own folder, when it isn't dir
# scan_dir = "..."            # (usage run as root, the scan as another account)
# copy_of = "fs0"             # it holds copies of fs0's files (see below)
# copies = {"/backup/home" = "fs0:/home"}   # or only some of its paths do
# same_accounts = true        # it and this machine share their accounts (see Names)
# account_floor = 1000        # ... from this number up (see Names); also above, for all

The account needs a key for ssh with no password prompt (BatchMode), as for the other collectors that reach servers. It reads the two files and nothing else. A file is stored once, by when its run started; a run that didn't finish leaves no new file (the script writes to a temporary file and moves it into place at the end); a file that can't be stored is noted (nomad storage status) without holding up the others. nomad sync copies the tables to the hub. Read each server from one site: when two read the same one, the hub shows the one that read it last, and status says so.

nomad collect -C storage_use
nomad storage status

docs.title: A server that holds copies
docs.text:
A server that holds replicas or backups of another's files (a second copy of the homes, a transition copy kept until it is checked) is listed with copy_of: it is read and shown like any other — whose files, how big, how old, which helps when deciding what to keep — and marked as copies, never added to anyone's totals.

When only some of its paths hold copies (a backup of the homes beside a scratch area of its own), name them with copies, each with the server and path it copies (or just the server, when the path is the same there):

copies = {"/backup/home" = "fs0:/home"}

Those paths are shown as copies of fs0:/home and left out of totals; the server's other paths count as usual.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
nomad storage use                  # each path, its owners, largest first
nomad storage use --days 7         # the change over 7 days (30 by default; 90...)
nomad storage use --over 1T        # only owners holding more than 1 TiB
nomad storage use --over 500GB --list   # tab-separated lines to paste: folders, owner, used, last job, change
nomad storage use --binary         # sizes in KiB, MiB, GiB, TiB, as du -h and xfs_quota -h show them
nomad storage use --groups         # by group instead (--projects: XFS projects)
nomad storage use --server fs1 --top 30
nomad storage use --path /home     # one path, on every server that has it
nomad storage use --mask           # stand-ins for names and long paths, for sharing the output
nomad storage status               # what was read from each server, by whom, and when

fs1:/home  xfs  13.0 TB of 20.0 TB (65%)  read 2026-10-21 12:17
  scans: 780 of 800 top folders finished in the last 7 days, scanned 2026-10-12 to 2026-10-21
  owners as of 2026-10-21 12:17; the change is since 2026-09-21 12:17
  owner                used    30 days     quota   >365 days newest change   last job
  user 1            12.0 TB    +2.0 TB      none     40.2 GB    2026-10-20 2026-10-20
  user 2             1.0 TB        0 B      none    900.0 GB    2025-01-01       none

Every figure says when it is from: the reading, the reading the change is from (the one nearest before 30 days ago, or --days), and the dates of the scans behind the folders' figures. last job is the latest job anyone with that username submitted on a cluster nomad collects, so none can also mean someone who only uses the storage. A path without per-owner counts lists its owners by what the scans found in their top folders instead, each with when it was measured (the oldest scan behind its figures). ZFS datasets with a quota are listed under their path; an owner with space in several datasets shows several for quota.

docs.title: Sizes
docs.text: nomad shows sizes in powers of 1000 (KB, MB, GB, TB), as df -H does; --binary shows them in powers of 1024 (KiB, MiB, GiB, TiB), as du -h and xfs_quota -h do, so 1.7 TB is 1.5 TiB, which xfs_quota -h writes 1.5T. --over takes either way of writing a size: a bare letter (500M, 20G, 1T) or MiB, GiB, TiB count in powers of 1024, as those tools write them; 500MB, 20GB, 1TB count in powers of 1000. --list gives one line per owner (all of them, or those over --over; --top cuts it), its folders as the scans found them (/home/USER, or wherever its top folders are; the server and path until the first scan), and a note when the server holds copies or the counts cover more than the path.

docs.title: Names
docs.text:
The usage file names owners as the storage server knows them, and a number for an account it can't name, shown as uid N (gid N, project N): often an account since deleted. The scan records each folder's owner as a number. Which numbers the collecting machine names, as it knows them:

  • The files of the machine itself (a source without host, written by this machine): all of them. A source without host whose files another machine wrote (a folder shared over NFS, say: the file names the machine that ran the script) is named as a server sharing its accounts, below.
  • A server sharing its accounts (one directory, LDAP or AD: same_accounts = true on the source): those from account_floor up (1000 by default, where most Linux systems start their people's accounts; set it for every source under [collectors.storage_use], or on one). Below it are each machine's own system accounts, which may be other accounts on the server than here, so they stay numbers.
  • Any other server (a NAS with accounts of its own): none, or another person's name could be put on them. Its owners are shown as uid N, and are best read by folder name; nomad storage status says so, for a server that in fact shares this machine's accounts and only lacks same_accounts = true. (Before 1.17.1 a scan's owners were named whatever the server, so after the upgrade such a server's scan owners turn to numbers until it is set.)

Folder names one level inside each top folder are stored (/home/USER/FOLDER), never anything deeper, and stay where nomad's other data does. A top folder that is gone from its path (a departed account's home, removed) goes from the tables at the next scan. A top folder whose owner the collecting machine can't name is counted as uid N, never under the person its folder is named after. Use --mask for output that leaves your site.

docs.title: Quotas
docs.text: None need to be set for any of this. Where they are, they are read and shown: ZFS userquota and groupquota beside each owner, and dataset quota and refquota under their path; XFS user, group and project soft and hard limits beside each owner (--groups, --projects). A filesystem with no accounting has no per-owner figures at all, quotas or not, and is covered by the scan.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
Table Holds storage_reports each file read: server, usage or scan, when its run started and finished, who ran it, copy_of, copies (per path), how numbered owners were named (naming: local, same or none); for a scan, the folders left out as other paths (nested), those holding another path (contains), how many were measured short (short_tops), and with -O (scan_as owner) those kept from earlier nights (carried) and those not measured storage_paths each path's filesystem, size and use, what the counts cover, at each reading storage_owners each owner's space on each path (and ZFS dataset), quotas, at each reading storage_datasets ZFS filesystems under each path: use, quota, refquota storage_tops each scan of a top folder: owner, size, files, older than the two ages, whether it finished (and if not, why: why_short, time or unreadable), what it couldn't read, when storage_folders the latest scan of each top folder's folders storage_reads each read, and what it found (working state, not copied to the hub)

Every reading is kept for keep_days (30); after that, one whole reading a day, and one scan of each top folder a week (the week's latest finished one, else its latest). A short scan (stopped at its budget, or as an owner who can't read everything) replaces a finished one of the same folder only when it found more.

docs.title: Sizing and submitting jobs
docs.text:
nomad size says what a job should ask for, and nomad submit sends it with that. People run them themselves, on a cluster's login node: nomad reads their script, the input file it names, their own past jobs from Slurm's accounting, and the cluster's partitions. Nothing is stored, and nothing needs changing in Slurm.

nomad size job.sh                 what job.sh should ask for
nomad size --job 4815162          a job of yours that ran, to run it again
nomad submit job.sh [ARGS...]     size it, show the sbatch command, ask, submit
nomad submit --again 4815162      a job of yours, sent again (an array: 5005, or one task: 5005_7)
nomad submit --mem 12G job.sh     your own value for memory (and --cpus, --time, --gpus, --partition)
nomad submit --keep job.sh        the script's own values: nomad only checks and tags

Options for nomad submit go before the script, as with sbatch; what follows the script is its arguments (nomad warns, and won't submit without asking, when one of its own options comes after the script). --dry-run shows the command without running it, and --yes submits without asking.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
job.sh: Gaussian (g16), input w.com
  compared with your 5 runs of this script

             asked         nomad         why
  CPUs       4             8*            the input sets 8 threads of one task (%nprocshared=8): 4 CPUs would make them share cores
  memory     8G            20G*          what the input sets (%mem 16 GB, and a fifth more: Gaussian needs room beyond %mem); your 3 runs of this script peaked at 10.7G
  time       04:00:00      02:30:00*     the longest of your 3 runs of this script took 01:30:00: a shorter limit starts sooner
  GPUs       -             -             none asked
  partition  basic         basic         it fits basic
  (* nomad would change it)

Memory is per node. Each value says where it comes from:

  • The input file or the command line, for programs that state their sizes there:
Program CPUs Memory Gaussian %nprocshared (%nproc, %cpu): threads %mem, and a fifth more ORCA %pal nprocs, ! PALn: processes %maxcore × processes, and a quarter more Q-Chem qchem -nt (threads) or -np (processes) MEM_TOTAL in $rem (for each process), and a fifth more Columbus runc -nproc: processes runc -m (for each process), and a fifth more GROMACS mdrun -nt, or -ntmpi × -ntomp: threads — NAMD +pN: processes under charmrun or mpirun, else threads —

Threads are asked as one task with that many CPUs (--ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=N), processes as that many tasks of a CPU each (--ntasks=N): a job asking the other way is told so. A value given by a shell variable (-nt $SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK) is left to the job's own request. The input file is read where the job will run: the folder sbatch is run in (or --chdir), after a literal cd in the script; nomad says when it is only found next to the script. - How the job ended, for one run again: out of memory, half as much memory again; out of time, half as long again; or what the input says, or your past runs of it needed, or what its script asks now, whichever is more. A job that stopped with an error is sized as usual, with a note that more resources won't fix it; one whose node failed or that was preempted runs as it was. - Your past runs like this one: the same script; else the same program in the very same folder; else the same job name; else the same program. An interpreter (python, R, Julia, MATLAB) or a program nomad doesn't know isn't "the same program": two python scripts can be anything. Memory is the highest peak × 1.5, time the longest run × 1.5 (the room nomad's scores ask for), rounded to values people type. History may lower a value only from at least three runs that completed, of the same script or of the same program in the same folder; the weaker matches (the same job name, the same program anywhere) may only raise one. A value the job doesn't ask for is weighed against the partition's default (its DefaultTime, else MaxTime; DefMemPerNode or DefMemPerCPU): where that isn't known, only runs close enough to lower a value set one. A run that failed never counts, nor a memory reading larger than its nodes have (Slurm can count memory processes share more than once). CPUs are lowered only as CPUs per task of a one-task job, never as tasks (an MPI launch counts on them), and only from runs that had at least as many CPUs as now asked. Where the runs of this script had other arguments, nomad says so. - The program: an executable built for GPUs (pmemd.cuda, mdrun -nb gpu) gets one when none is asked. - The partition: when the one asked (or the default) doesn't fit -- too long for its limit, no node with the CPUs, memory and GPUs one node needs together (a task's GPUs are on its node), too few GPUs in all, or one the job's account may not use (its AllowGroups, AllowAccounts; the job's --account, else the person's default account) -- nomad names one that fits, preferring ones the person may use, not preemptible, with the smallest nodes. A partition Slurm doesn't list is kept (Slurm checks it), and one whose nodes couldn't be read isn't offered. With a list (-p a,b), Slurm picks; nomad checks that one of them fits. A time or memory nomad works out that the partition can't give is asked at what it gives (its time limit, its biggest node), with a note.

A job on several nodes (--nodes above 1) keeps its CPUs and memory; nomad checks its time and partition. Tasks Slurm places over as many nodes as it takes (--ntasks without --nodes), or on several, with memory per CPU or per GPU have no one node's figure: their memory is weighed a CPU (or GPU) at a time, and shown so (2G/CPU) -- the input's memory over the CPUs the job will have, or, when the job ran out, half as much again a CPU from Slurm's record (never below what the script asks now); past runs' readings (a node at a time) aren't weighed, a change of their CPUs keeps memory per CPU, and a partition fits them when its nodes hold them all, a task (its CPUs and their memory) at a time. --ntasks-per-node alone (no --ntasks, no --nodes) is that many tasks on one node; with --ntasks, it is the most a node takes. CPUs asked per GPU (--cpus-per-gpu) or through --tres-per-task=cpu=N are kept, and so is no time limit (--time=UNLIMITED, 0 or -1; nomad says when a partition has a limit).

nomad never changes how a job asks: memory asked per CPU or per GPU stays so (rounded up to 64 MB, or down to whole megabytes when it is a node's memory: sbatch takes no fractions), GPUs stay --gpus, --gpus-per-node, --gpus-per-task, --tres-per-task or --gres, with their type and the job's other gres. Memory is decided per node: when CPUs or GPUs change (nomad's or yours), memory asked per CPU or per GPU is written again for them, so the node gets the memory the table shows. #SBATCH lines (and #SLURM, #SBATCH--x) are read as sbatch reads them: at the very start of a line (an indented one is a comment), before the first command.

docs.title: Submitting
docs.text:
nomad submit shows the same table, then the exact sbatch command, and asks. Only the values that change are set on the command line (sbatch reads the rest from the script's #SBATCH lines), and what is sent is checked again: a value you give that no node can hold is said before you submit. sbatch runs in the folder you run nomad in, as it would by hand (a relative --chdir in the script is its own). --cpus sets CPUs the way the script asks them (CPUs per task for one task, else tasks; tasks of several CPUs each keep their CPUs per task: a multiple of them; tasks per node stay per node: a multiple of the nodes); --gpus too (per task or per node, --gres on several nodes included: a multiple of the tasks or nodes; --gpus on several nodes: at least one a node). nomad can't take an option away: --gpus 0 on a script that asks for GPUs says to remove its line. --mem is per node (0: all of a node's memory), so it isn't taken for tasks Slurm places over its nodes with memory per CPU or per GPU: change that in the script. What the job doesn't ask (time, memory) is weighed against the defaults of the partition it goes to, yours included.

A job sent again gets its own command line's other options and its folder (--chdir), and runs its script as it is on disk now (nomad says when it changed since). Slurm keeps the folder the job ran in, not the one sbatch ran in: a script that moves itself (#SBATCH --chdir) is found in the folder its --chdir leads from. Not sent again: its --dependency (on jobs long gone; singleton is kept), --begin and --deadline (times for its first run), --wait, and an array's other tasks (--again 5005_7 runs task 7 alone, as --array=7; --again 5005 runs the whole array again). A job nomad sent before gets a new tag, and values it keeps from that job's own command line keep the code they had. Slurm keeps the command line without the quotes it was typed with, so a job sent again with arguments, or whose script nomad had to find among the line's words (or found from a folder Slurm doesn't keep, or where two scripts could have been the one), is never submitted without asking.

The job is tagged, in Slurm's --extra field, with who chose each value:

--extra=nomad=1.18.0;via=cli;cpus=i;mem=i;time=h;gpus=d;part=s

s the script's own, u the person on nomad's command line, h nomad from past runs, i the input file or command line, o how the job run again ended, g what the program needs, p a partition that fits, d left to Slurm's defaults; again=N for a job sent again. Slurm keeps it in its accounting where AccountingStoreFlags includes job_extra, so nomad can later tell the person's choices from its own. No tag where Slurm is older than 23.02 (no --extra; and should sbatch refuse it anyway, nomad sends the job once more untagged), where SchedulerParameters include extra_constraints (Slurm then reads --extra as node constraints) or nomad can't read them, or where the job sets --extra itself.

docs.title: Where the output goes
docs.text:
Each job's Slurm output (its .out file, with what it writes to stderr unless the job splits them) goes in a folder of its own, /scratch/USER/jobs/JOBID-NAME/slurm-JOBID.out (slurm-JOBID_TASK.out for each task of an array), so the folder the job runs in fills with its own results only. nomad says where, before and after submitting.

Slurm never makes the folder an output file goes in (a job whose folder is missing fails with no output at all), and a job's number is known only once it is submitted. So nomad sends the job to start two minutes from now (--begin=now+120), reads back from Slurm where its output would go, makes its folder, and in one update (scontrol update ... StdOut=... StartTime=now) points its output there and lets it start at once. Should nomad be stopped in between (Ctrl-C, a dropped ssh session, a kill), or Slurm not take the folder, nothing is left waiting: the job starts on its own within the two minutes, its output where Slurm puts it. nomad never holds or releases a job, and a start time a site's job_submit plugin set is left as it is. What nomad then says is what Slurm holds (an update can report an error after it took effect: nomad reads the job back). The command nomad shows is the one to run by hand, without its --begin.

The job's number and name are Slurm's own (JobName, after -J, $SBATCH_JOB_NAME or the script's name), kept to letters, digits and . _ + - in the folder's name; a folder already there (a job number Slurm used before) gets .2, .3, ... jobs/ is made private (0700): change its mode to share it (folders you give with --logs follow your umask). Scratch may be purged after a while: so are the logs in it.

Left where the job or Slurm says:

  • a job that sets its own output: #SBATCH --output or --error (or --out=: sbatch takes any prefix that is only one option's), #PBS -o or -e, its command line's (a job sent again), $SBATCH_OUTPUT or $SBATCH_ERROR; and an output a site's job_submit plugin set: nomad changes it only when Slurm reports its own default (slurm-JOBID.out in the job's folder);
  • a job that sets its own start time (--begin, #PBS -a) or a --deadline (a later start could miss it), one sbatch waits for (--wait, $SBATCH_WAIT), a --test-only, a heterogeneous job;
  • the person who has no /scratch/USER (nomad never makes it), or whose /scratch/USER isn't on a filesystem compute nodes share (NFS, Lustre, GPFS, BeeGFS, Ceph, ...; a login node that serves /scratch itself sees its own disk: a site where it is shared anyway sets NOMAD_LOGS): the output goes beside the job, and nomad says so.

A job that asks to be held (#SBATCH --hold) gets its folder and stays held, for the person to release. A job sent again doesn't get nomad's --begin (or --quiet) from its own command line.

The choice, the first one given: nomad submit --logs, then $NOMAD_LOGS, then the default. Each is here (Slurm's own place, beside the job), a folder (each job's own folder goes in it: --logs ~/runs gives ~/runs/JOBID-NAME/; a relative one is from the folder you run nomad in), or a pattern with {user}, {jobid} and {name} ({jobid} is required: each job its own folder). A site can set NOMAD_LOGS for everyone (/etc/profile.d), and a person in their own shell setup; --dry-run shows where it will go (JOBID for the number to come).

docs.title: What it reads
docs.text:
• The script, and the input file it names (at most 2 MB), as the person: their own run of nomad reads their own files.
  • Slurm's accounting: the person's own jobs of the last 180 days (--days), with sacct -u and the person's own user name (from the system, never from $USER). The full folder and submit line let nomad find each past job's script and name its program. Slurm before 21.08 has no submit line: jobs are then compared by name only.
  • The partitions: scontrol --all show partition and sinfo -a -e (hidden ones too; each kind of node on its own line), the person's groups and Slurm accounts (sacctmgr show assoc, show user).

nomad size --db PATH --user NETID sizes a script from nomad's database instead (on the hub, for staff), where folders and command lines are never kept whole, so jobs are compared by name only (and so only raise values); --job looks at one's own jobs only.

docs.title: Installing it for users
docs.text:
Users run one central install on each cluster, not one of their own, and nomad size and nomad submit need no nomad.toml. scripts/install_nomad_for_users.sh makes it, as the account that owns the folder (/usr/local/sw/nomad, or NOMAD_USERS_DIR), on the cluster or from a nomad checkout:

ssh OWNER@CLUSTER 'bash -s 1.18.1' < scripts/install_nomad_for_users.sh
ssh OWNER@CLUSTER 'NOMAD_USERS_DIR=/path bash -s 1.18.1' < scripts/install_nomad_for_users.sh

Running it again with another version upgrades: that is how a cluster follows nomad's releases, one step of each release beside the hub's upgrade.

  • Each release whole in its own folder. releases/VERSION holds its own Python 3.12, installed by uv (from uv's release on GitHub, checked against a checksum fixed in the script), and its own environment, so the system's Python doesn't matter (a python3 of 3.6 is fine). uv's cache and downloads are in a private temporary folder, and one run goes at a time.
  • One step to switch. The release is built and checked first; only then is bin/nomad replaced, in one step, by one that runs it. Until then users go on with the one they had, and a release that fails is removed. The one before is kept (with its bin/nomad, as bin/nomad.before), and the script prints how to go back to it; older ones are removed. Two releases take about 0.9 GB. An install made by 1.18.0's script is replaced the same way, and its folders removed after the switch. A removal that fails then (a file still open on NFS, say) is reported and left for the next run.
  • The right folder. The script refuses a folder another account owns (run it as that account), and one that holds anything it doesn't recognise as its own or 1.18.0's script's (a wrong NOMAD_USERS_DIR, say): such a folder is left untouched.
  • bin/nomad starts nomad's Python isolated (python -I, writing no bytecode), so PYTHONHOME and PYTHONPATH a cluster sets for another Python (Anaconda's, say) don't reach it, while the jobs nomad submits get the environment as it is.
  • Nothing writable but by the owner, nor owned by anyone else; the script stops if it finds otherwise, and says so when a folder above the install is writable by others (who could then replace it).
  • On users' PATH: bin/ holds only nomad, so it can't shadow anyone's Python. A link in a folder already on everyone's PATH (ln -s /usr/local/sw/nomad/bin/nomad /usr/local/sw/bin/nomad), or a module, or /etc/profile.d; last on the PATH, an account with its own nomad keeps it.
  • check_current.sh, beside it, says when nomad-hpc has a newer release than the one installed (and prints the command that upgrades) and says nothing otherwise: for the owner's crontab, weekly, with MAILTO set. It never upgrades anything itself.

docs.title: System Install
docs.text: This guide covers deploying NØMAÐ system-wide for production HPC environments.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
System install differs from user install in several ways:

Aspect User Install System Install Config location ~/.config/nomad/ /etc/nomad/ Data location ~/.local/share/nomad/ /var/lib/nomad/ Log location ~/.local/share/nomad/logs/ /var/log/nomad/ Permissions User only Controlled by file permissions Service Manual or user systemd System systemd unit Dashboard access localhost only Configurable (proxy recommended)

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
# Install as root or with sudo
sudo pip install nomad-hpc

# Or system-wide from source
sudo pip install /path/to/nomad/

docs.title: Initialize System Configuration
docs.text:
sudo nomad init --system

This creates:

Path Purpose Permissions /etc/nomad/ Configuration directory root:root 755 /etc/nomad/nomad.toml Main configuration root:root 644 /var/lib/nomad/ Data directory root:nomad 750 /var/lib/nomad/nomad.db SQLite database root:nomad 660 /var/log/nomad/ Log directory root:nomad 750

docs.title: Required Permissions
docs.text:
Running as root: Full access to all paths.

Running as service user (recommended): 

# Create nomad group
sudo groupadd nomad

# Create service user
sudo useradd -r -g nomad -d /var/lib/nomad -s /sbin/nologin nomad

# Set ownership
sudo chown -R nomad:nomad /var/lib/nomad
sudo chown -R nomad:nomad /var/log/nomad
sudo chown root:nomad /etc/nomad/nomad.toml
sudo chmod 640 /etc/nomad/nomad.toml

Wheel group access (for admin users): 

# Allow wheel group to read config
sudo chown root:wheel /etc/nomad/nomad.toml
sudo chmod 640 /etc/nomad/nomad.toml

# Allow wheel group to read database
sudo chown nomad:wheel /var/lib/nomad/nomad.db
sudo chmod 660 /var/lib/nomad/nomad.db

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text: File Read/Write Purpose /etc/nomad/nomad.toml R Main configuration /etc/nomad/clusters/*.toml R Per-cluster configs (optional)

docs.title: Data Files
docs.text: File Read/Write Purpose /var/lib/nomad/nomad.db RW SQLite database /var/lib/nomad/models/ RW ML model files /var/lib/nomad/cache/ RW Temporary cache

docs.title: Log Files
docs.text: File Read/Write Purpose /var/log/nomad/nomad.log W Main application log /var/log/nomad/collector.log W Collector logs /var/log/nomad/alerts.log W Alert dispatch logs

docs.title: System Files Read
docs.text: File Purpose /proc/*/io Per-process I/O stats /proc/meminfo Memory information /proc/loadavg System load /sys/class/thermal/ Temperature sensors

docs.title: External Commands Executed
docs.text: Command Package Purpose iostat sysstat Disk I/O metrics mpstat sysstat CPU metrics vmstat procps Memory/swap metrics df coreutils Filesystem usage nvidia-smi nvidia-driver GPU metrics (optional) nfsiostat nfs-utils NFS metrics (optional) squeue slurm Job queue (optional) sinfo slurm Node info (optional) sacct slurm Job accounting (optional)

docs.title: Create Service Unit
docs.text:
sudo cat > /etc/systemd/system/nomad-collector.service << 'UNIT'
[Unit]
Description=NØMAÐ HPC Monitoring Collector
After=network.target slurmd.service

[Service]
Type=simple
User=nomad
Group=nomad
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/nomad collect
Restart=always
RestartSec=30

# Security hardening
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=true
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/nomad /var/log/nomad
PrivateTmp=true

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
UNIT

docs.title: Enable and Start
docs.text:
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable nomad-collector
sudo systemctl start nomad-collector
sudo systemctl status nomad-collector

docs.title: Dashboard Service (Optional)
docs.text:
sudo cat > /etc/systemd/system/nomad-dashboard.service << 'UNIT'
[Unit]
Description=NØMAÐ Dashboard
After=network.target nomad-collector.service

[Service]
Type=simple
User=nomad
Group=nomad
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/nomad dashboard --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8050
Restart=always
RestartSec=10

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
UNIT

docs.title: Localhost Only (Default)
docs.text:
Dashboard binds to 127.0.0.1:8050 by default. Access via SSH tunnel: 

# On your local machine
ssh -L 8050:localhost:8050 user@hpc-head-node

# Then open http://localhost:8050 in browser

docs.title: Reverse Proxy (Recommended for Remote Access)
docs.text:
Using Apache: 

# /etc/httpd/conf.d/nomad.conf
<VirtualHost *:443>
    ServerName hpc.example.edu

    SSLEngine on
    SSLCertificateFile /etc/pki/tls/certs/server.crt
    SSLCertificateKeyFile /etc/pki/tls/private/server.key

    <Location /nomad>
        ProxyPass http://127.0.0.1:8050/
        ProxyPassReverse http://127.0.0.1:8050/

        # Require authentication
        AuthType Basic
        AuthName "NØMAÐ Dashboard"
        AuthUserFile /etc/httpd/.htpasswd
        Require valid-user
    </Location>
</VirtualHost>

Using nginx: 

# /etc/nginx/conf.d/nomad.conf
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name hpc.example.edu;

    ssl_certificate /etc/ssl/certs/server.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/private/server.key;

    location /nomad/ {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8050/;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;

        # WebSocket support (for live updates)
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";

        # Authentication
        auth_basic "NØMAÐ Dashboard";
        auth_basic_user_file /etc/nginx/.htpasswd;
    }
}

docs.title: Prolog/Epilog Hooks
docs.text:
For per-job metrics collection: 

# Copy hook scripts
sudo cp /path/to/nomad/scripts/prolog.sh /etc/slurm/prolog.d/nomad.sh
sudo cp /path/to/nomad/scripts/epilog.sh /etc/slurm/epilog.d/nomad.sh

# Make executable
sudo chmod +x /etc/slurm/prolog.d/nomad.sh
sudo chmod +x /etc/slurm/epilog.d/nomad.sh

# Restart SLURM controller
sudo systemctl restart slurmctld

docs.title: Prolog Script
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
# /etc/slurm/prolog.d/nomad.sh
/usr/local/bin/nomad job-start $SLURM_JOB_ID 2>/dev/null || true

docs.title: Epilog Script
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
# /etc/slurm/epilog.d/nomad.sh
/usr/local/bin/nomad job-end $SLURM_JOB_ID 2>/dev/null || true

docs.title: Multi-Cluster Setup
docs.text:
For monitoring multiple clusters from one head node: 

# /etc/nomad/nomad.toml

[clusters.spydur]
name = "Spydur"
